fact: Optogenetic activation of a single gene-targeted glomerulus elicits larger and more asynchronous lateral inhibitory currents in nearby mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source_span: Here , we show that optogenetic activation of a single , gene-targeted glomerulus elicits larger and more asynchronous lateral inhibitory currents in nearby MCs than in TCs.
selection_reasoning: This is a key experimental finding about differences in lateral inhibition.

fact: Lateral inhibition affects mitral cells at intermediate firing rates (~50 Hz) but affects tufted cells at low firing rates (<25 Hz).
source_span: While MCs are affected by lateral inhibition at intermediate firing rates ( ~50 Hz ) , TCs are affected when firing at low firing rates ( <25Hz ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals distinct functional impacts of lateral inhibition on the two cell types.

fact: Differential recruitment of morphologically distinct classes of granule cells by mitral and tufted cells contributes to differences in lateral inhibition.
source_span: This difference arises , in part , due to differential recruitment of morphologically distinct classes of GCs by MCs and TCs.
selection_reasoning: This provides a mechanistic explanation for the observed differences in inhibition.

fact: Activity-dependent lateral inhibition at both low and intermediate firing rates enables mitral and tufted cells to collectively encode odors better than either population alone.
source_span: Specifically , the combination of activity-dependent lateral inhibition at both low and intermediate rates enables TCs and MCs to collectively encode odors better than either population alone ...
selection_reasoning: This highlights the functional significance of having two neuron types with distinct inhibition profiles.

fact: The combined activity-dependent lateral inhibition in mitral and tufted cells supports novel computations unlikely to occur with a single neuron type.
source_span: ... and supports novel computations that are unlikely to occur with a single neuron type .
selection_reasoning: This emphasizes the computational advantage of parallel pathways.

fact: Lateral inhibitory currents are larger and more asynchronous onto mitral cells (MCs) than onto tufted cells (TCs) in the mouse olfactory bulb.
source_span: Collectively, these results demonstrate that lateral inhibitory currents are larger and more asynchronous onto MCs than onto TCs.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about differences in inhibition between two key olfactory bulb cell types, central to the study's main claim.

fact: Mitral cells receive stronger lateral inhibition than tufted cells during both early and late phases of inhibition.
source_span: The peak amplitude was significantly larger in MCs (n = 10) than in TC (n = 10) during both the early and late phases of inhibition.
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the main difference in inhibition strength, supporting the core finding about cell-type differences.

fact: The charge transferred during the late phase of lateral inhibition is significantly larger in mitral cells than in tufted cells.
source_span: Charge transferred was significantly larger in MCs than TCs during the late phase only.
selection_reasoning: This detail about the late phase inhibition further characterizes the difference in inhibitory input, relevant to the main result.

fact: Granule cells contribute similar proportions of lateral inhibition onto mitral cells and tufted cells.
source_span: Using this pharmacological approach, we found that GCs contribute similar proportions of lateral inhibition onto MCs and TCs.
selection_reasoning: This addresses the mechanism underlying lateral inhibition differences, clarifying that granule cells are not the source of the difference.

fact: Glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in mitral cells and tufted cells and are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between these cell types.
source_span: These observations indicate that glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in MCs and TCs and thus are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between MCs and TCs.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the anatomical source of lateral inhibition differences, important for understanding the mechanism.

fact: The strength of lateral inhibition onto mitral cells and tufted cells does not depend on whether the apical dendrite was truncated during the slicing procedure.
source_span: The strength of lateral inhibition onto MCs and TCs did not depend on whether the apical dendrite was truncated during the slicing procedure.
selection_reasoning: This rules out a potential confound in the experimental preparation, supporting the validity of the main findings.

fact: Similar differences in lateral inhibition between mitral cells and tufted cells were observed when stimulating single glomeruli in both M72-ChR2-YFP and OMP-ChR2-YFP mice.
source_span: Similar to the results obtained using M72-ChR2-YFP mice, we find that only the peak amplitude of the early phase of inhibition is larger in MCs while both the amplitude and charge transferred of the late phase of inhibition are larger in MCs.
selection_reasoning: This shows that the main findings generalize across different mouse models and glomeruli, strengthening the study's significance.

fact: Photostimulation of olfactory sensory neuron axons was used to evoke lateral inhibition onto mitral cells and tufted cells.
source_span: We stimulated MCs and TCs by step current injection and measured firing rates to construct input-output curves in cells near the M72 glomerulus. On interleaved trials we activated M72 OSN axons via photostimulation.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental approach used to measure lateral inhibition, relevant to understanding how the findings were obtained.

fact: Glomerular layer circuits contribute small and uniform amounts of lateral inhibition to mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs), and are not the main source of differences in lateral inhibition between these cell types.
source_span: These observations indicate that glomerular layer circuits make small and uniform contributions to lateral inhibition in MCs and TCs and thus are not the primary source of differences in lateral inhibition between MCs and TCs.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background on the source of lateral inhibition differences, which is central to understanding the study's focus on lateral inhibition mechanisms.

fact: Lateral inhibition reduces firing rates in mitral cells (MCs) primarily when they fire at intermediate rates.
source_span: Similar to our previous results using paired MC recordings (Arevian et al., 2008), MC firing rates were reduced by lateral inhibition selectively when MCs fired at intermediate rates.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about how lateral inhibition affects MC activity, key to the study's main question.

fact: Lateral inhibition reduces firing rates in tufted cells (TCs) only when they fire at low rates.
source_span: Surprisingly, TCs were influenced by lateral inhibition only when firing at low rates.
selection_reasoning: This finding contrasts with MCs and highlights a key difference in lateral inhibition effects between cell types.

fact: The effective firing rate range over which lateral inhibition reduces firing is significantly lower in tufted cells (TCs) than in mitral cells (MCs).
source_span: Both the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition (i.e. the range of firing rates over which lateral inhibition reduces firing rates) were significantly lower in TCs than in MCs.
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the difference in lateral inhibition impact between MCs and TCs, a core comparative result.

fact: Similar proportions of mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs) are affected by lateral inhibition.
source_span: Similar proportions of MCs (16/25–64%) and TCs (12/18–67%) were affected by lateral inhibition.
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses the prevalence of lateral inhibition effects across cell populations, relevant to the study's scope.

fact: The study measured firing rates of mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs) near the M72 glomerulus by stimulating these cells with step current injections and activating M72 olfactory sensory neuron (OSN) axons via photostimulation.
source_span: To do this, we stimulated MCs and TCs by step current injection and measured firing rates to construct input-output curves in cells near the M72 glomerulus. On interleaved trials we activated M72 OSN axons via photostimulation.
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental approach used to investigate lateral inhibition effects, important for understanding the findings.

fact: Mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs) can sustain high firing rates (>50 Hz) for long periods (>500 ms) following glomerular stimulation.
source_span: MCs and TCs can sustain high firing rates (>50 Hz) for long periods (>500 ms) following glomerular stimulation.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides physiological context about the firing capabilities of these cells, relevant to interpreting lateral inhibition effects.

fact: Lateral inhibition affects firing rates differently in mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs), with a larger fractional reduction in firing rate observed in TCs.
source_span: The average fractional reduction in firing rate was much larger in TCs than in MCs ( Figure 3c ) , though the absolute firing rate decrease was not significantly different ( MC: −8 . 2 ± 2 . 5 Hz n = 16 , vs TC: −8 . 8 ± 3 . 2 Hz n = 12 ) ( Figure 3d , f ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about functional differences in lateral inhibition between two key cell types in the olfactory bulb, central to the study's main claims.

fact: The effects of lateral inhibition on firing rates in MCs and TCs are present even on the short timescale of a single 4 Hz sniff (250 ms).
source_span: Additionally , these effects of lateral inhibition on firing rate were present even in short timescales matching a single 4 Hz sniff ( Figure 3—figure supplement 3 ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the physiological relevance of lateral inhibition timing, important for understanding sensory processing.

fact: Differences in activity-dependent lateral inhibition (ADLI) between MCs and TCs likely arise from distinct lateral inhibitory circuits within the external plexiform layer (EPL).
source_span: Our finding that inhibition is largely unaffected by apical dendrite truncation suggests that differences in ADLI between MCs and TCs most likely involves inhibitory circuitry within the external plexiform layer ( EPL ) .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains the cellular basis for observed functional differences, a key conclusion.

fact: Superficial granule cells (sGCs) and deep granule cells (dGCs) are morphologically distinct subtypes that innervate different layers of the EPL and likely mediate lateral inhibition onto TCs and MCs, respectively.
source_span: Classical morphological studies suggest that GCs are subdivided into superficial GCs ( sGCs ) , which innervate the superficial EPL , and deep GCs ( dGCs ) , which innervate the deep EPL ( Mori et al . , 1983; Orona et al . , 1983 ) . This putative morphological subdivision of GCs suggests that sGCs inhibit TC lateral dendrites in the superficial EPL while dGCs inhibit MC lateral dendrites in the deep EPL ( Mori et al . , 1983; Orona et al . , 1984 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background and mechanistic detail is essential to understand the cellular circuits underlying the main findings.

fact: Low firing rates in MCs are unaffected by lateral inhibition because many granule cells require cooperative inputs from multiple glomeruli to be activated.
source_span: Given our prior results demonstrating that low firing rates in MCs are unaffected by lateral inhibition because many GCs require cooperative inputs from multiple glomeruli in order to be activated ( Arevian et al . , 2008 ) , we hypothesized that low firing rates in TCs are affected by lateral inhibition because sGCs are more strongly recruited than dGCs following activation of a single glomerulus .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key difference in how lateral inhibition operates in MCs versus TCs, central to the study's hypothesis.

fact: Granule cell soma position correlates with granule cell subtype and odor-evoked activity in vivo, with superficial granule cells showing suprathreshold odor responses and deep granule cells showing subthreshold responses.
source_span: GC soma position correlates with GC subtype ( Mori et al . , 1983; Orona et al . , 1983 ) and odor-evoked activity in vivo ( Wellis and Scott , 1990 ) . Specifically , GCs located in the MCL and upper GCL tend to exhibit sGC morphologies and suprathreshold odor responses while GCs located in the lower GCL tend to exhibit dGC morphologies and subthreshold odor responses ( Mori et al . , 1983; Orona et al . , 1983; Wellis and Scott , 1990 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact supports the proposed functional differences between granule cell subtypes relevant to lateral inhibition.

fact: Granule cells (GCs) in the olfactory bulb can be subdivided into distinct morphological subtypes called superficial GCs (sGCs) and deep GCs (dGCs).
source_span: Consistent with previous morphological accounts (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983), GCs exhibited distinct sGC or dGC morphologies upon visual inspection... Our results therefore quantitatively confirm the morphological subdivision of GCs into distinct subclasses of sGCs and dGCs.
selection_reasoning: This morphological subdivision is a core background and classification relevant to understanding the study's main question about GC subtype function.

fact: sGCs preferentially innervate the superficial external plexiform layer (EPL) while dGCs preferentially innervate the deep EPL in the olfactory bulb.
source_span: Reconstruction and visual classification of a large subset of recorded GCs and analysis of the spatial distribution of gemmules... confirmed that sGCs preferentially innervate the superficial EPL while dGCs preferentially innervate the deep EPL.
selection_reasoning: This key anatomical difference underlies functional distinctions between GC subtypes and is important for interpreting their roles.

fact: The somatic depth of granule cells significantly predicts their subtype as either sGC or dGC, although this prediction is not perfect.
source_span: Moreover, somatic depth significantly – but incompletely – predicted GC subtype... as previously observed (Mori et al., 1983; Orona et al., 1983).
selection_reasoning: This fact links anatomical position to subtype classification, relevant for understanding how GC subtypes are identified and studied.

fact: Unbiased clustering of granule cells based on their gemmule distributions identified three distinct clusters corresponding to dGCs, sGCs, and a small group of sGCs with deep glomerular layer innervation.
source_span: Clustering of GCs by the Euclidean distances among their normalized gemmule distributions... yielded 3 distinct clusters: dGCs, sGCs, and a small group of sGCs with prominent innervation of the deep glomerular layer.
selection_reasoning: This analysis supports the existence of discrete GC subtypes rather than a continuum, a key conceptual advance.

fact: sGCs are more likely than dGCs to fire action potentials in response to activation of a single nearby glomerulus.
source_span: A greater proportion of sGCs than dGCs fired in response to glomerular activation (Chi-square test, p = 4.2 × 10–3).
selection_reasoning: This functional difference in excitability is a principal finding linking morphology to physiological response.

fact: Excitatory synaptic input to sGCs exhibits larger peak currents and greater charge transfer than input to dGCs following glomerular activation.
source_span: Excitatory input to sGCs exhibited larger peak currents (rank-sum test, p = 8.5 × 10–3) and charge transferred (rank-sum test, p = 0.046) than excitatory input to dGCs.
selection_reasoning: This synaptic input difference is a key mechanistic finding explaining differential GC recruitment.

fact: There is no significant difference in the latency of excitatory input onset between sGCs and dGCs after glomerular activation.
source_span: No difference in excitation latency was observed (6.6 ± 11.6 vs. 9.7 ± 11.4 ms; rank-sum test, p = 0.12).
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that timing of input is similar, focusing attention on input strength and intrinsic properties.

fact: sGCs and dGCs show significantly different firing rate-current (FI) relationships in response to somatic current injection.
source_span: sGCs and dGCs showed significantly different firing rate-current (FI) curves in response to somatic step current injection (2-way ANOVA, p = 4.1 × 10–3).
selection_reasoning: This intrinsic excitability difference supports functional specialization of GC subtypes.

fact: sGC action potentials have more hyperpolarized thresholds, larger amplitudes, and faster rising slopes compared to dGC action potentials.
source_span: sGC action potentials exhibited more hyperpolarized thresholds (unpaired t test, p = 4.8 × 10–3), larger amplitudes (unpaired t test, p = 1.1 × 10–4), and faster rising slopes (unpaired t test, p = 2.9 × 10–4) than dGC action potentials.
selection_reasoning: These intrinsic membrane property differences contribute to the distinct firing behaviors of GC subtypes.

fact: To test GC responses, the study recorded excitatory synaptic input and spiking responses of granule cells to activation of single nearby glomeruli using extracellular stimulation.
source_span: To more directly test our above hypothesis, we recorded the excitatory synaptic input and spiking response of GCs to activation of single nearby glomeruli... we switched from selective optogenetic stimulation of M72 glomeruli to extracellular stimulation of untagged glomeruli in order to test a large number of GC-glomerulus pairs.
selection_reasoning: This high-level methodological description is important for understanding how the functional differences were experimentally assessed.

fact: Extracellular stimulation of olfactory sensory neuron axons triggers sensory-evoked input to mitral/tufted cells and granule cells comparable to optogenetic photostimulation.
source_span: We and others have previously demonstrated that optogenetic photostimulation and extracellular stimulation of OSN axons trigger comparable sensory-evoked input to both M/TCs and GCs.
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of the stimulation method used to evoke GC responses.

fact: Odor-evoked activity differences between GC subtypes in vivo may be influenced by complex glomerular activation patterns, centrifugal inputs, and anesthesia.
source_span: Whether these differences in odor-evoked activity in vivo reflect functional differences between GC subtypes and M/TC connectivity remains unclear, however, as: 1) odors activate multiple glomeruli in distinct spatiotemporal patterns... 2) GC activity in vivo is strongly influenced by centrifugal input... and anesthesia.
selection_reasoning: This background explains the motivation for the controlled experimental approach used in the study.

fact: Superficial granule cells (sGCs) fire more frequently than deep granule cells (dGCs) in response to activation of a single glomerulus in the olfactory bulb.
source_span: In agreement with our hypothesis , a strikingly higher percentage of sGCs than dGCs fired in response to activation of a single glomerulus ( Figure 4b , e , h ) due , at least partially , to stronger excitatory synaptic input to sGCs than dGCs ( Figure 4i ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a core finding about differential recruitment of granule cell subtypes following glomerular activation, central to the study's main question.

fact: Stronger excitatory synaptic input and greater intrinsic excitability contribute to the greater recruitment of superficial granule cells compared to deep granule cells.
source_span: Our results thus support the hypothesis sGCs are more strongly recruited than dGCs following activation of a single glomerulus due to stronger excitatory input and greater intrinsic excitability ...
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanism underlying the key difference in granule cell recruitment, important for understanding the circuit function.

fact: Superficial granule cells have a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold and greater intrinsic excitability than deep granule cells despite similar somatodendritic sizes and passive membrane properties.
source_span: Examination of GC biophysical properties revealed several intrinsic differences supporting greater recruitment of sGCs than dGCs , including a more hyperpolarized action potential threshold in sGCs ( Figure 4l; Figure 4—source data 1 , Table 2 ) and greater intrinsic excitability in sGCs in response to somatic step current injections ( Figure 4j , k; Figure 4—source data 1 , Table 3 ) , despite equivalent somatodendritic sizes ( Figure 4—figure supplement 1d; Figure 4—source data 1 , Table 1 ) and passive membrane properties ( Figure 4—source data 1 , Table 4 ) between sGCs and dGCs .
selection_reasoning: This provides key physiological differences that explain functional distinctions between granule cell types.

fact: Spontaneous synaptic activity frequency and amplitude are similar between superficial and deep granule cells, indicating comparable presynaptic circuit integrity.
source_span: Analysis of spontaneous synaptic activity revealed no difference in event frequency or amplitude between sGCs and dGCs ( Figure 4—source data 1 Table 5 ) ... equal spontaneous event frequencies between sGCs and dGCs suggests that their respective presynaptic circuits are comparably intact . Moreover , equal spontaneous event amplitudes suggest a comparable contribution of larger action potential-dependent and smaller action potential-independent events between sGCs and dGCs , again consistent with comparably intact presynaptic circuits .
selection_reasoning: This supports that differences in recruitment are not due to presynaptic circuit damage, strengthening the physiological relevance of findings.

fact: Activity-dependent lateral inhibition (ADLI) in mitral cells (MCs) depends on the firing rate of the recorded MC, with lateral inhibition increasing at intermediate firing rates but saturating at high firing rates.
source_span: ACTIVITY-Dependent lateral inhibition in MCs ( left panels ) : Low rates ( a , b ) : When the recorded MC is unstimulated or firing at low rates , no additional GCs are recruited during the photostimulation of the M72 glomerulus , so no lateral inhibition is evoked . Intermediate rates ( c , d ) : When the recorded MC is firing at intermediate firing rates , additional GCs are activated during the photostimulation of the M72 glomerulus and generate lateral inhibition . High rates ( e , f ) : When the recorded MC is firing at high firing rates , all shared GCs are maximally recruited so that M72 photostimulation is unable to activate any additional GCs or generate additional lateral inhibition .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key functional mechanism of lateral inhibition in mitral cells, central to the study's investigation of olfactory bulb circuitry.

fact: Activity-dependent lateral inhibition in tufted cells (TCs) occurs at low firing rates but saturates at intermediate and high firing rates, preventing additional lateral inhibition.
source_span: Activity-dependent lateral inhibition in tcs ( right panels ) :Low rates ( a , b ) : When the recorded TC is firing at low firing rates , additional GCs are activated selectively during the photostimulation of the M72 glomerulus and generate lateral inhibition . INTERMEDIATE AND HIGH RATES ( c , d , e , f ) : When the recorded TC is firing at intermediate or high firing rates , all shared GCs are maximally recruited so that M72 photostimulation is unable to activate any additional GCs or generate lateral inhibition .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a distinct pattern of lateral inhibition in tufted cells, important for understanding cell-type specific circuit function.

fact: Increasing granule cell excitability with the mGluR agonist DHPG reduces the effective activity range of lateral inhibition in mitral cells.
source_span: The effective activity range of lateral inhibition in MCs ( n=6 ) fell from 31 ( ± 9 ) –73 ( ± 10 ) Hz to 16 ( ± 12 ) –49 ( ± 23 ) Hz after adding DHPG ( Figure 5a–d ) , and the lower and upper bounds of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition were significantly reduced after the addition of DHPG ( Figure 5e ) .
selection_reasoning: This experimental manipulation demonstrates that granule cell excitability modulates lateral inhibition, a principal finding with mechanistic and potential therapeutic implications.

fact: DHPG selectively enhances the excitability of granule cells without affecting mitral cells.
source_span: At this concentration , DHPG selectively enhances the excitability of GCs ( Heinbockel et al . , 2004 ) but not MCs ( Figure 5—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the specificity of the pharmacological manipulation used to test the role of granule cell excitability in lateral inhibition.

fact: Increasing granule cell (GC) excitability shifts the effective activity range of lateral inhibition in mitral cells (MCs) to lower firing frequencies.
source_span: Increasing GC excitability shifts the effective activity range of lateral inhibition in MCs to lower frequencies . ( a–c ) Example of lateral inhibition in one example MC before and after bath applying mGluR agonist , DHPG ( 10 µM ) . ... ( e ) The lower ( LEFT , paired t-test , p = 0 . 009 ) and upper bound ( RIGHT , paired t-test , p = 0 . 009 ) of the effective activity range of lateral inhibition are significantly lower after application of DHPG .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing how modulation of GC excitability affects lateral inhibition in MCs, a core mechanism relevant to olfactory processing.

fact: The mGluR agonist DHPG does not affect the intrinsic excitability of mitral cells (MCs).
source_span: DHPG has no effect on MC excitability . Data is taken from the LIGHT OFF trials in the MCs recorded in Figure 5 before and after adding 10 μM DHPG . ( a ) MC input-output curves in response to 500 ms somatic current injections of increasing amplitudes before and after bath application of DHPG ( n = 6 MCs ) . ( b ) Average Pre-DHPG and Post-DHPG FI curves across 6 MCs indicate that DHPG has no effect on MC excitability ( p = 0 . 77; 2-way ANOVA ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that the observed changes in lateral inhibition are not due to direct changes in MC excitability, supporting the mechanism involving granule cells.

fact: Differences in granule cell populations contribute to differences in the effective activity range of lateral inhibition onto mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs).
source_span: These data ( Figures 4–5 ) provide two indirect lines of evidence that suggest that differences in GC populations provide one mechanism for differences in the effective activity range of lateral inhibition onto MCs and TCs .
selection_reasoning: This identifies a key mechanism underlying cell-type-specific lateral inhibition differences relevant to olfactory coding.

fact: Distinct odor-evoked activity observed in mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs) in vivo arises, in part, due to differences in how apical dendrite lateral inhibition (ADLI) affects each cell type.
source_span: Together these data suggest that distinct odor-evoked activity observed in MCs and TCs in vivo arises , in part , due to differences in how ADLI affects each cell type ( Figure 4—figure supplement 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This links cellular circuit differences to functional differences in odor responses, a core motivation and conclusion.

fact: Simulations of mitral cell (MC) and tufted cell (TC) networks were performed to determine how differences in apical dendrite lateral inhibition (ADLI) translate into differences in stimulus encoding during an olfactory discrimination task.
source_span: To begin assessing how these circuit-level differences between MCs and TCs impact their ability to encode olfactory information , we performed simulations of MC and TC networks to determine how differences in ADLI may translate into differences in stimulus encoding . We simulated an olfactory discrimination task in which a presented odor must be identified from a panel of similar odors .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key method used to link circuit properties to functional odor discrimination.

fact: In the simulations, odors were modeled as patterns of activated glomeruli, with differences in odor concentration represented by changes in the number and intensity of activated glomeruli.
source_span: Each odor was simulated as a pattern of inputs to populations of MCs or TCs , corresponding to activated glomeruli ( Figure 6a , b , Figure 6—figure supplement 1 ) . Differences in odor concentration were modeled as changes in the number and intensity of activated glomeruli ( Rubin and Katz , 1999; Meister and Bonhoeffer , 2001 ) ( see Materials and methods ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides necessary background on how the olfactory stimuli were represented in the computational model.

fact: Trial-to-trial variability was added in the simulations to mimic natural fluctuations in background odors and odor-evoked glomerular activation patterns.
source_span: Additionally , we added trial-to-trial variability in each presentation of a particular odor ( Figure 6b , see Materials and methods ) in order to mimic natural fluctuations in the background odors and in the patterns of odor-evoked glomerular activation ( Wachowiak et al . , 2004 ) .
selection_reasoning: This detail supports the biological relevance of the simulation approach.

fact: Mitral cells (MCs) and tufted cells (TCs) receive excitatory input from glomeruli and their firing rates can be modulated by lateral inhibition.
source_span: In this simulation, each MC or TC received excitatory input from one of the 150 glomeruli.
selection_reasoning: This background fact is necessary to understand the neural populations studied and the role of lateral inhibition in odor discrimination.

fact: The study used simulated populations of mitral cells and tufted cells to test how well these neurons discriminate between similar odors presented at the same concentration.
source_span: In our simulations, we asked how well MC and TC population activity discriminated between similar odors presented at the same odor concentration.
selection_reasoning: This describes the main research question and the high-level method used, which is central to the study.

fact: Linear discriminant analysis, a biologically plausible decoding algorithm, was applied to assess odor discrimination accuracy from MC and TC population activity.
source_span: We applied a common decoding algorithm, linear discriminant analysis, to determine the extent to which different odors were discriminable in our simulated MC and TC populations.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key analytical method used to evaluate the neural data, relevant for understanding the findings.

fact: When discriminating among 8 odors, mitral cell and tufted cell populations performed similarly to a control population without inhibition.
source_span: When the odor panel consisted of only 8 odors, both MC and TC populations discriminated between odors with an accuracy that did not differ from the control population that lacked inhibition.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the limits of lateral inhibition effects at low odor discrimination difficulty.

fact: Tufted cells and mitral cells differ in their intrinsic excitability and strength of excitatory input, which affects their odor discrimination performance.
source_span: Differences in the strength of excitatory inputs and intrinsic excitability between MCs and TCs are modeled using 2 sigmoids to translate glomerular inputs into MC/TC outputs.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key mechanistic difference between the two neuron types that underlies their functional differences.

fact: Simulations compared networks composed of only mitral cells, only tufted cells, or mixed mitral and tufted cells to evaluate odor discrimination accuracy across concentrations.
source_span: Overview of simulations comparing 3 separate output neuron configurations: 2 MCs per glomerulus, 2 TCs per glomerulus or 1 MC and 1 TC per glomerulus.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental design element that tests how different neuron populations contribute to odor discrimination.

fact: Subtractive or divisive lateral inhibition does not improve odor discrimination accuracy in the simulated neuron populations.
source_span: Subtractive or divisive lateral inhibition does not improve discrimination accuracy.

fact: The rate at which the M2 receptor system equilibrates depends on the order in which orthosteric and allosteric ligands are added, consistent with a kinetically defined capping model.

Such an arrangement would allow an allosteric ligand to bind with high affinity to protomers with a vacant orthosteric site and thereby to increase the binding of an orthosteric ligand to linked protomers with a vacant allosteric site.

fact: Confocal imaging of intact CHO cells was performed using a 63× oil-immersion objective with excitation at 488 nm to capture fluorescence emission spectra.
source_span: Confocal imaging of intact CHO cells was performed on a Zeiss microscope ( model LSM710 ) using a Plan-Apochromat oil-immersion objective lens ( 63× , 1 . 4 NA ) . Samples were irradiated at 488 nm and a power of 0 . 37 μW . An area of 134 . 7 × 134 . 7 μm2 was captured through a pinhole of 1 Airy unit , and each pixel in the image represented 0 . 26 μm2 according to the Nyquist theorem . A stack of 30 images was acquired at 5 nm intervals from 495 nm to 640 nm , and the data were processed through custom-written software in Matlab to obtain the emission spectrum corrected for background .

In the case of kA , the fitted value from Equation 10 or 11 was reduced by 6% to compensate for the direct excitation of mCherry at 498 nm .

source_span: Time-dependent binding of an orthosteric ligand ( L ) to a monomeric receptor ( R ) was simulated according to Figure 6 , in which access to and egress from the orthosteric site is precluded by an allosteric ligand ( A ) . The system is defined by four ordinary differential equations ( Equation 13 ) , which were solved numerically to obtain the amount of bound orthosteric ligand at different times ( i . e . , [RL] + [ARL] ) .

source_span: The rate constants in Equation 13 were computed from the affinity constants according to Equations 14–16 , as described previously ( Shivnaraine et al . , 2012 ) . Values of the cooperativity factor α were partitioned between the rate constants for association and dissociation according to Equation 17 .

fact: Molecular dynamics simulations were performed in an isothermal-isobaric ensemble with a 2 fs timestep to study the system at atomic resolution.
source_span: Simulations were performed in the isothermal-isobaric ( NPT ) ensemble according to the Nosé-Poincaré-Andersen ( NPA ) equations of motion with a time-step of 2 fs . A cut-off of 10 Å was applied to non-bonding interactions . Equilibration was for 1 ns ( 300 K , harmonic restraints of 0 . 5 kcal mol-1 Å-2 applied to non-hydrogen atoms ) , and production continued for 30 ns ( 300 K , no restraints ) .

fact: An ENU mouse mutant with the Rasgrp1Anaef variant displays elevated frequencies of CD44hi CD4+ cells and antinuclear antibodies with a homogeneous nuclear pattern.
source_span: As part of a mouse genome-wide screen for immune phenotypes induced by ENU mutagenesis ( Nelms and Goodnow , 2001 ) , we identified a variant C57BL/6 ( B6 ) pedigree displaying elevated frequencies of CD44hi CD4+ cells ( Figure 1A ) , elevated CD44 expression on naïve FOXP3− CD44lo CD4+ cells ( Figure 1B ) and antinuclear antibodies ( ANAs ) staining with a homogeneous nuclear pattern ( Figure 1C , D ) .

source_span: Since heterozygous Rasgrp1+/− thymocytes express half the Rasgrp1 dosage but do not display an abnormal immune phenotype, whereas heterozygous Rasgrp1Anaef/+ mice do exhibit abnormal immune phenotypes, we conclude that the immune dysregulation in mice bearing the Rasgrp1Anaef allele is caused by the specific R519G alteration and not simply by a reduction of Rasgrp1 protein levels.

fact: RNA sequencing was performed on sorted pancreatic cells to analyze gene expression changes using established bioinformatics pipelines.
source_span: Each sample was used for either RNAseq or ATAC-seq . Total RNA was isolated from cells sorted into TRIzolLS and assessed using a BioAnalyzer ( Agilent ) . Sequencing and library preparation was performed at the Integrated Genomics Operation ( IGO ) at MSKCC . Ribosomal RNA was depleted using RiboZero ( Illumina ) and stranded KAPA RNA libraries were prepared from 1 ug RNA . Approximately 40 million paired-end 50 bp reads were sequenced per replicate on a HiSeq 2000 . Resulting RNA-Seq data was analyzed by removing adaptor sequences using Trimmomatic ( Bolger et al . , 2014 ) . Reads were then aligned to the mouse genome ( NCBI37/mm9 ) using STAR aligner ( Dobin et al . , 2013 ) and transcript counting was performed by HTseq ( Anders et al . , 2015 ) . Differential expression analysis was performed using the Limma and Voom R/Bioconductor packages with an FDR cutoff of 0 . 05 ( Law et al . , 2014; Ritchie et al . , 2015 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a key method used to identify gene expression changes, central to the study's main findings.

selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key analytical step to interpret gene expression data, relevant to principal findings and significance.

fact: ATAC-seq was performed on sorted pancreatic cells to assess chromatin accessibility changes between conditions.
source_span: 50 , 000 mKate2+ cells isolated by FACS were lysed in 50 ul lysis buffer ( Buenrostro et al . , 2015 ) and subjected to transposition with Nextera Tn5 transposase according to manufacturer’s instructions ( Illumina FC-121–1030 ) . DNA was eluted from a MinElute column in 11 . 5 ul elution buffer ( Qiagen ) . ATAC libraries were constructed using the NEBNext High-Fidelity 2x PCR Master Mix ( NEB M0541 ) as in Buenrostro et al with the following modifications: DNA was PCR-amplified for 1 cycle of 5’ at 72°C and 30’ at 98°C followed by 12 cycles of 10’ at 98°C , 30’ at 63°C and 1’ at 72°C . Amplified DNA was purified on a Qiagen MinElute column and eluted in 22 ul of Qiagen elution buffer . Purified libraries were assessed using a Bioanalyzer High-Sensitivity DNA Analysis kit ( Agilent ) . Paired-end 50 bp reads were sequenced with the Center for Epigenetics Research at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center .

fact: Mean squared displacement (MSD) analysis shows that CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites have significantly reduced displacement slopes compared to wild-type, indicating impaired motility.
source_span: The visibly reduced dispersal of mutant sporozoites was reflected in a decreased slope obtained from linear regression fitting of the MSD plot... slopeCSΔN = 1190 and slopeTRAP-VAL = 740 compared to slopeWT = 2370.
selection_reasoning: This provides quantitative evidence of motility impairment supporting the functional conclusions.

fact: Sporozoites glide alongside dermal vascular endothelia and frequently circle extensively around blood vessels in the skin.
source_span: Visualization of sporozoites and dermal blood vessels shows that sporozoites glide alongside dermal vascular endothelia and frequently circle extensively around the vessel
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the natural behavior of sporozoites in the dermis, which is central to understanding their interaction with blood vessels.

fact: Wild-type sporozoites spend about 28% of their motile time gliding in close proximity to blood vessels in the dermis.
source_span: compared to wild-type control sporozoites, which spend 28% of their motile time gliding in close proximity to blood vessels
selection_reasoning: This baseline measurement is necessary to compare mutant sporozoite behavior and understand the significance of changes.

fact: CSΔN mutant sporozoites spend significantly more time, about 40.7% of their motile time, gliding close to dermal blood vessels compared to wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: CSΔN sporozoites spend significantly more time in association with dermal vascular endothelia; an average of 40.7% of their motile time is spent close to blood vessels
selection_reasoning: This key finding highlights altered behavior of the CSΔN mutant relevant to sporozoite interaction with blood vessels.

fact: TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites spend the same proportion of their motile time gliding close to blood vessels as wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend the same proportion of their motile time gliding close to blood vessels as wild-type control parasites
selection_reasoning: This comparison shows that the TRAP-VAL mutation does not affect sporozoite association time with blood vessels, an important contrast to CSΔN.

fact: Both CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites show decreased dispersal and displacement in the dermis compared to wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: revealing a decreased dispersal of mutant sporozoites ... MSD plot shows decrease in displacement of mutant sporozoite tracks
selection_reasoning: Decreased dispersal is a principal finding indicating altered motility of mutant sporozoites in the skin.

fact: The gliding speed of CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites decreases significantly when they approach blood vessels, similar to wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: These data reveal a significant decrease in gliding speed of CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites, once the sporozoite is approaching vasculature, similar to wild-type control sporozoites
selection_reasoning: This finding shows that mutant sporozoites retain a key motility characteristic near blood vessels, relevant to their invasive behavior.

fact: The rates of blood and lymphatic vessel invasion by CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites are dramatically reduced compared to wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: In the duration of the acquired 4 min videos, 2.38% and 2.06% of WT sporozoites invaded blood vessels and lymphatic vessels, respectively. This was in sharp contrast to the blood and lymphatic vessel invasion rates of CSΔN (0.23% and 0.26%) and TRAP-VAL (0.05% and 0%)
selection_reasoning: This principal finding demonstrates impaired vascular invasion by mutant sporozoites, a key functional consequence.

fact: Blood vessel invasion is characterized by a sudden increase in speed or visual entry into the blood vessel followed by disappearance from the field of view.
source_span: blood vessel invasion being defined by a sudden increase in speed or visual entry of the blood vessel and disappearance out of the field of view
selection_reasoning: This definition clarifies how invasion events were identified, important for interpreting invasion data.

fact: Lymphatic vessel invasion is characterized by a switch from directed forward movement to sideward drifting with low velocity.
source_span: Lymphatic invasion was characterized by the switch from directed forward movement to sideward drifting with a low velocity
selection_reasoning: This definition explains the criteria for lymphatic invasion, supporting the invasion rate findings.

fact: Plasmodium sporozoites switch from 'avascular motility' to 'perivascular motility' when approaching blood vessels in the dermis.
source_span: MSD analysis of the two tracking sets revealed that similar to wild-type control sporozoites, perivascular CSΔN tracks have a decreased MSD and gliding speed, indicating that while CSΔN sporozoites spend more time gliding in proximity to vasculature, the switch from ‘avascular’ to ‘perivascular motility’ appears normal.
selection_reasoning: This motility switch is a key biological behavior relevant to how sporozoites interact with blood vessels, central to understanding their invasion process.

fact: Mutant sporozoites CSΔN and TRAP-VAL show dramatically reduced blood vessel invasion compared to wild-type sporozoites after intradermal inoculation.
source_span: Blood vessel invasion of the CSΔN mutant is reduced to 0.23% and only 0.05% of TRAP-VAL sporozoites is seen to enter into blood vessels, which is consistent with the decrease in infectivity of these mutants upon intradermal inoculation.
selection_reasoning: Reduced blood vessel invasion by mutants is a principal finding linking molecular mutations to impaired infectivity.

fact: CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutant sporozoites also show reduced or absent invasion of the lymphatic system compared to wild-type sporozoites.
source_span: Invasion of the lymphatic system by CSΔN sporozoites is reduced to 0.26% and not detected at all in the case of TRAP-VAL sporozoites.
selection_reasoning: Lymphatic invasion is an important route for sporozoite dissemination, so its reduction in mutants is a key finding.

fact: The decreased blood vessel invasion by CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutants is not fully explained by reduced motility or time spent near vessels, indicating an additional defect in vessel entry.
source_span: TRAP-VAL sporozoites spend on average 40% less time on vessels due to many non-motile sporozoites, yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 97%, suggesting that even when TRAP-VAL sporozoites do contact vessels they cannot invade them. CSΔN mutants spend approximately the same total time on vessels as wild-type sporozoites, yet blood vessel entry events were reduced by 90%.
selection_reasoning: This highlights a mechanistic insight that the mutants have impaired vessel entry beyond motility defects.

fact: Mutations in CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites cause increased surface exposure of cell-adhesion domains, which likely impairs their ability to invade blood vessels.
source_span: Both CSΔN and TRAP-VAL mutations result in the increased surface exposure of cell-adhesion domains: in CSΔN sporozoites, the absence of the N-terminus leads to constitutive exposure of the cell-adhesive type I thrombospondin domain; in TRAP-VAL sporozoites, the altered proteolytic cleavage site leads to retention of TRAP molecules on the surface.
selection_reasoning: This molecular mechanism explains the impaired invasion phenotype and is central to the study's conclusions.

fact: Gliding motility of Plasmodium sporozoites in the dermis is essential for their infectivity and changes significantly over the first 120 minutes after inoculation.
source_span: The gliding motility of Plasmodium sporozoites is essential for their infectivity. Intravital imaging of sporozoites over the first 120 min after inoculation highlights significant changes in their motility in this time frame.
selection_reasoning: This background and temporal characterization of motility sets the stage for understanding sporozoite behavior relevant to infection.

fact: Intravital microscopy with fluorescently labeled dermal vascular endothelia was used to track and quantify blood and lymphatic vessel invasion by wild-type and mutant sporozoites.
source_span: Intravital microscopy of mutant CSΔN and TRAP-VAL sporozoites in conjunction with fluorescently labeled dermal vascular endothelia was performed, and invasion events were manually quantified.
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is important to understand how invasion events were measured.

fact: CD31-labeling of blood vessels does not interfere with sporozoite entry into dermal blood or lymphatic vessels or parasite dispersal.
source_span: Importantly, CD31-labeling is not interfering with entry into dermal blood or lymphatic vessels or parasite dispersal, as vessel invasion rates, as well as sporozoite MSDs, are comparable in videos acquired in mice with and without labeled blood vessels.
selection_reasoning: This validates the experimental approach and supports the reliability of invasion measurements.

fact: The gliding motility of Plasmodium sporozoites is essential for their infectivity.
source_span: The gliding motility of Plasmodium sporozoites is essential for their infectivity.
selection_reasoning: This establishes the biological importance of sporozoite motility, a key background fact for understanding the study.

fact: Sporozoites initially move rapidly and with minimal constraint in the dermis within the first 20 minutes after inoculation, likely maximizing tissue exploration.
source_span: Within the first 20 min after intradermal inoculation , sporozoites displace with high speed and minimal constraint , which likely maximizes the volume of tissue that is explored by the population of sporozoites .
selection_reasoning: Describes the early motility pattern critical to understanding sporozoite behavior and infection strategy.

fact: Starting 20 minutes after inoculation, sporozoite motility becomes increasingly confined and many sporozoites engage in continuous circular motility near blood vessels.
source_span: Most significantly starting 20 min after inoculation , the migratory pattern of sporozoites becomes increasingly confined , and a growing number of sporozoites engage in continuous circular motility .
selection_reasoning: Identifies a key change in motility pattern linked to blood vessel interaction, central to the study's findings.

fact: Sporozoites slow down and many stop moving by 2 hours after inoculation, with about 70% becoming non-motile.
source_span: 1 hr after inoculation , sporozoites begin to slow down and a significant proportion stop moving with the proportion of non-motile sporozoites increasing to 70% by 2 hr .
selection_reasoning: Describes a late-phase motility change important for understanding sporozoite behavior over time.

fact: Sporozoite migration in the dermis is not random Brownian motion but is biased by internal or host–pathogen interactions.
source_span: Our data show that distribution of displacements of migrating sporozoites is not Gaussian , which would be expected if sporozoites migrated in a pattern similar to a Brownian walk ... This suggests that internal components or external host–pathogen interactions bias the directionality of sporozoite movement away from Brownian motion .
selection_reasoning: Challenges previous assumptions and highlights a key mechanistic insight into sporozoite motility.

fact: Sporozoites switch from linear motility to more curved and confined motility upon approaching blood vessels, indicating specific host–parasite interactions.
source_span: We found that once the sporozoite approaches a blood vessel , the more linear type of motility is lost and the sporozoite switches to a more curved and confined motility .
selection_reasoning: Identifies a critical behavioral adaptation linked to blood vessel recognition.

fact: Sporozoites exhibit two types of motility: avascular motility that optimizes dispersal and perivascular motility characterized by confined, curved trajectories near blood vessels.
source_span: Sporozoites appear to engage in two types of motility: ‘avascular motility’ which is likely to optimize dispersal , and ‘perivascular motility’ defined by more confined trajectories with increased curvature .
selection_reasoning: Defines key motility modes central to the study's conceptual framework.

fact: Perivascular motility enhances sporozoite contact with capillaries rather than larger blood vessels.
source_span: Our analysis of track curvature reveals that sporozoites gliding in the proximity of blood vessels describe trajectories with local curvatures that interestingly relate to the curvature of the capillary vessel ... This suggests that ‘perivascular motility’ enhances contact with capillaries , rather than the larger dermal terminal arterioles or post-capillary venules .
selection_reasoning: Links motility behavior to specific vascular structures relevant for infection.

fact: Sporozoites decrease their speed when near blood vessels compared to other dermal locations.
source_span: In addition to the change in sporozoite trajectories , we found that they also had a significant decrease in speed when in the vicinity of blood vessels .
selection_reasoning: Describes a key kinetic change associated with blood vessel interaction.

fact: Mutant TRAP-VAL sporozoites move at less than half the speed of wild-type sporozoites in the dermis, reducing tissue exploration and blood vessel invasion, which explains their reduced infectivity.
source_span: The importance of high sporozoite gliding speed is highlighted by the behavior of the TRAP-VAL mutant that moves with less than half the motile speed of wild-type control parasites in the dermis ... Consequently , TRAP-VAL sporozoites have a significantly decreased chance to encounter and invade a blood vessel , which together with the increase in number of non-motile TRAP-VAL sporozoites , largely explains their reduced infectivity .
selection_reasoning: Connects motility defects to functional infectivity outcomes, a principal finding.

fact: Wild-type sporozoites rapidly disperse from the skin, possibly to escape phagocytic host cells.
source_span: Although there is no evidence for an innate host immune response that may impair the exit of sporozoites from the dermis , the observed rapid dispersal of wild-type control sporozoites suggests that the parasite has evolved to leave the skin quickly , possibly as a means to escape from phagocytic host cells .
selection_reasoning: Provides biological significance and evolutionary rationale for rapid sporozoite dispersal.

fact: CSΔN mutant sporozoites show normal avascular and perivascular motility but have increased association with dermal vascular endothelia and somewhat decreased gliding speed, leading to reduced dispersal.
source_span: CSΔN sporozoites engage in a pattern of ‘avascular’ and ‘perivascular motility’ comparable to that of wild-type sporozoites ... Of particular interest was the observed increase in the association of CSΔN sporozoites with dermal vascular endothelia ... this , together with the somewhat decreased gliding speed , explains the overall decrease in dispersal of this mutant .
selection_reasoning: Describes mutant phenotype linking molecular changes to altered motility and dispersal.

fact: The N-terminal portion of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) masks the cell-adhesive TSR domain during sporozoite migration through the skin, and controlled proteolytic processing regulates TSR exposure.
source_span: It was previously proposed that the function of the N-terminal portion of CSP is to mask the cell-adhesive TSR domain as sporozoites migrate through the skin and controlled proteolytic processing of CSP by a parasite protease regulates the exposure of the TSR .
selection_reasoning: Provides mechanistic background relevant to mutant phenotypes and sporozoite adhesion.

fact: Constitutive exposure of the TSR domain on CSΔN sporozoites leads to increased time spent on vascular endothelia.
source_span: We find that the constitutively exposed TSR on the surface of CSΔN sporozoites leads to increased time spent on vascular endothelia .
selection_reasoning: Links molecular alteration to altered host interaction, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: The N-terminal portion of the circumsporozoite protein (CSP) masks the cell-adhesive TSR domain during sporozoite migration through the skin, and controlled proteolytic processing regulates exposure of the TSR.
source_span: It was previously proposed that the function of the N-terminal portion of CSP is to mask the cell-adhesive TSR domain as sporozoites migrate through the skin and controlled proteolytic processing of CSP by a parasite protease regulates the exposure of the TSR ( Coppi et al . , 2005 , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the molecular mechanism regulating sporozoite adhesion during skin migration, which is central to the study's focus.

fact: Constitutive exposure of the TSR domain on CSΔN mutant sporozoites leads to increased time spent adhering to vascular endothelia in the dermis.
source_span: We find that the constitutively exposed TSR on the surface of CSΔN sporozoites leads to increased time spent on vascular endothelia .
selection_reasoning: This key finding links the mutation to altered sporozoite behavior relevant to dermal migration and vascular interaction.

fact: Dynamic regulation of TSR exposure is hypothesized to be necessary for sporozoites to migrate through the dermis and locate suitable blood vessel entry sites.
source_span: We therefore hypothesize that the ability of the sporozoite to dynamically regulate exposure of the TSR is necessary for continued migration through the dermis , which may be crucial for the sporozoite to locate the areas of the vasculature that allow for blood vessel entry or for blood vessel entry itself .
selection_reasoning: This hypothesis addresses the biological significance of TSR regulation in sporozoite infectivity and migration.

fact: Mutant sporozoites with altered motility patterns or speed show dramatic decreases in blood vessel invasion and infectivity.
source_span: Mutant sporozoites that display modest changes in motility pattern or speed have dramatic decreases in blood vessel invasion and infectivity .
selection_reasoning: This principal finding highlights the importance of sporozoite motility regulation for successful infection.

fact: Wild-type sporozoites spend over a quarter of their time engaging with blood vessels but often fail to enter the blood circulation, suggesting only certain vascular areas are suitable for sporozoite entry.
source_span: We show that wild-type control sporozoites spend over a quarter of their time engaging with blood vessels , frequently without successful entry into the blood circulation . This suggests that only certain areas of the vasculature are suitable for sporozoite entry .
selection_reasoning: This observation refines understanding of sporozoite vascular entry and the challenges they face in the dermis.

fact: The abluminal surface of dermal capillaries is heterogeneous, with gaps in the basement membrane where pericytes form tight junctions with endothelial cells, potentially creating preferential sites for sporozoite invasion.
source_span: It is known that the abluminal surface of dermal capillaries is not uniform; for example , the basement membrane surrounding the capillary bed is not continuous and through its gaps , pericytes form tight junctions with the underlying endothelial cell ( Braverman , 1997 ) . Thus , there may be certain areas of the vasculature that are preferentially invaded by sporozoites .
selection_reasoning: This background fact provides biological context for the spatial selectivity of sporozoite vascular entry.

fact: Exit from the dermal inoculation site is an important barrier for sporozoites and represents a promising target for malaria intervention strategies.
source_span: These data suggest that exit from the inoculation site presents an important barrier for the sporozoite and is therefore an opportune time to intervene .
selection_reasoning: This implication connects the study findings to potential translational and therapeutic relevance.

fact: The partial efficacy of the RTS,S malaria vaccine may result from antibodies targeting sporozoites in the dermis.
source_span: Indeed , the partial success of RTS , S , the only malaria vaccine candidate in Phase III clinical trials , may result from antibodies that target sporozoites in the dermis ( Foquet et al . , 2014 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the study to clinical vaccine development and highlights the dermis as a key site of immune targeting.

fact: Future malaria vaccine strategies should consider including antigens critical for sporozoite exit from the dermis to improve efficacy.
source_span: As we build upon RTS , S , it will be important to consider expanding the antigen repertoire to include proteins critical for dermal exit .
selection_reasoning: This recommendation is a significant translational implication derived from the study.

fact: Analyzing dermal sporozoite motility could be used to evaluate and predict the efficiency of new malaria vaccine targets.
source_span: Additionally , our data suggest that an analysis of dermal sporozoite motility could be incorporated in the evaluation of future vaccine strategies to predict efficiency of new vaccine targets .
selection_reasoning: This methodological implication suggests a novel approach to vaccine assessment based on sporozoite behavior.

fact: Cells are organized by functional modules that contain components whose removal severely compromises the module's function.
source_span: Cells are organized by functional modules , which typically contain components whose removal severely compromises the module's function .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological context and importance of functional modules, setting up the study's focus on module robustness.

fact: Components essential for a functional module in some organisms can be absent in evolutionarily distant organisms, suggesting that cells can evolve to perform the same biological functions with different proteins.
source_span: Despite their importance , these components are not absolutely conserved between parts of the tree of life , suggesting that cells can evolve to perform the same biological functions with different proteins .
selection_reasoning: This motivates the study by highlighting evolutionary flexibility in essential cellular functions.

fact: The study evolved Saccharomyces cerevisiae for 1000 generations without the important polarity gene BEM1 to investigate evolutionary adaptation.
source_span: We evolved Saccharomyces cerevisiae for 1000 generations without the important polarity gene BEM1 .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to study evolutionary recovery after gene deletion.

fact: Deleting the polarity gene BEM1 initially caused a rapid increase in fitness in bem1∆ lineages, which then slowly reached over 90% of the fitness of their BEM1 ancestors after evolution.
source_span: Initially the bem1∆ lineages rapidly increase in fitness and then slowly reach >90% of the fitness of their BEM1 ancestors at the end of the evolution .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing evolutionary recovery of fitness after gene deletion.

fact: Sequencing genomes and monitoring polarization revealed a common evolutionary trajectory with a fixed sequence of adaptive mutations that improve cell polarization by inactivating proteins.
source_span: Sequencing their genomes and monitoring polarization reveals a common evolutionary trajectory , with a fixed sequence of adaptive mutations , each improving cell polarization by inactivating proteins .
selection_reasoning: This key result identifies the genetic basis and order of adaptive changes underlying recovery.

fact: Organisms can be evolutionarily robust to physiologically destructive perturbations, and recovery by gene inactivation can lead to rapid divergence in the components used for important cellular functions.
source_span: Our results show that organisms can be evolutionarily robust to physiologically destructive perturbations and suggest that recovery by gene inactivation can lead to rapid divergence in the parts list for cell biologically important functions .
selection_reasoning: This is a major conclusion about evolutionary robustness and functional module plasticity.

fact: Cell polarization in budding yeast involves selection of a polarity axis followed by asymmetric organization of cytoskeletal elements and cell growth along this axis.
source_span: Polarization involves selection of an axis of polarity , followed by the asymmetric organization of cytoskeletal elements and membranous organelles and cell wall growth along this axis .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological process studied and why BEM1 is important.

fact: Yeast cells polarize and bud by localizing and activating the small GTPase Cdc42 at a single site on the plasma membrane.
source_span: Yeast cells polarize and bud by localizing and activating the small GTPase , Cdc42 , at a single site ( Slaughter et al . , 2009b; Wu and Lew , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides necessary biological context for understanding the role of BEM1 in polarization.

fact: Deleting Bem1, a regulator of Cdc42, causes profound defects in cell polarization and proliferation in yeast.
source_span: Deleting Bem1 led to profound defects in cell polarization and proliferation , but cells recovered to nearly wild-type growth rates over 1000 generations .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the immediate impact of the gene deletion, central to the study's question.

fact: The recovery of polarization and growth after Bem1 deletion followed a reproducible evolutionary trajectory involving inactivation of the same polarization-regulating genes in the same order.
source_span: Genetic analysis revealed that this recovery followed a reproducible trajectory in which the same genes , which regulate polarization , were inactivated in the same order .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the predictability and mechanistic insight into the evolutionary adaptation process.

fact: The study used experimental microbial evolution combined with genome sequencing and genetic analysis to identify mutations responsible for adaptation after deleting an important gene.
source_span: Experimental microbial evolution circumvents these problems: sequencing and genetic analysis identifies the mutations responsible for the selected phenotype and storing and analyzing intermediate steps reveals the order in which mutations occurred ( Lenski and Travisano , 1994; Lang et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the high-level methodological approach enabling the study's findings.

fact: Bem1 recruits the guanine exchange factor Cdc24 and Cdc42 to the membrane, where Cdc24 activates membrane-bound Cdc42, playing a key role in yeast cell polarization.
source_span: We strongly perturbed yeast polarization by removing Bem1 , a regulator of Cdc42 , which recruits the guanine exchange factor ( GEF ) Cdc24 as well as Cdc42 to the membrane where Cdc24 activates membrane-bound Cdc42 .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the molecular role of Bem1, clarifying why its deletion disrupts polarization.

fact: Bem1 is a relatively young component in polarity establishment that had a different role in ancestral fungi, suggesting alternative, more ancient polarization modules exist.
source_span: We decided to delete Bem1 because previous research suggests that this protein is a relatively young component in polarity establishment that had a different role in ancestral fungi ( Semighini and Harris , 2008 ) .
selection_reasoning: This motivates the choice of Bem1 deletion to reveal alternative evolutionary solutions.

fact: Deleting the BEM1 gene in yeast cells caused severe defects in cell polarization and proliferation.
source_span: Deleting Bem1 led to profound defects in cell polarization and proliferation
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the initial problem that motivated the study.

fact: Yeast cells lacking BEM1 recovered to nearly wild-type growth rates after evolving for 1000 generations.
source_span: cells recovered to nearly wild-type growth rates over 1000 generations
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing evolutionary adaptation over time.

fact: The recovery of polarization and growth in bem1∆ cells followed a reproducible genetic trajectory involving inactivation of the same polarization-regulating genes in the same order.
source_span: Genetic analysis revealed that this recovery followed a reproducible trajectory in which the same genes, which regulate polarization, were inactivated in the same order.
selection_reasoning: This key genetic insight explains the mechanism behind the observed adaptation.

fact: Epistatic interactions between mutated genes explained the evolutionary trajectory that gradually improved cell polarization in bem1∆ yeast cells.
source_span: Systematic analysis of the interactions between the mutated genes revealed epistatic interactions that explained the evolutionary trajectory that gradually improved cell polarization.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the genetic interactions underlying the adaptation process.

fact: Yeast cells lacking BEM1 had a much lower initial colony formation frequency and slower growth rates compared to wild-type cells.
source_span: bem1∆ spores formed colonies at a frequency of 6 ± 0.4 × 10−5 ... while wild-type (BEM1) spores formed colonies at a frequency of 0.95 ... The initial growth rate of the bem1∆ lineages was approximately 12 times lower than the wild-type growth rate.
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the initial fitness defect caused by BEM1 deletion, motivating the evolution experiment.

fact: Most bem1∆ cells failed to polarize within 500 minutes and grew isotropically into large cells that often lysed, unlike wild-type cells which always polarized successfully.
source_span: The majority of bem1∆ cells (28/35 vs 0/41 for wild-type cells) did not polarize within 500 min but grew isotropically resulting in very large cells ... that often lysed (16/35) ... wild-type cells ... always eventually polarize successfully
selection_reasoning: This describes the cellular phenotype caused by BEM1 deletion, important for understanding the defect.

fact: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize did so quickly, in contrast to wild-type cells which showed a wider distribution of polarization times.
source_span: The bem1∆ cells that did polarize ... polarize fast, in contrast to wild-type cells, which show a wider distribution of polarization times
selection_reasoning: This nuanced observation about polarization timing is relevant to the cellular mechanism.

fact: Experimental evolution was performed by serially diluting and growing multiple independent bem1∆ and wild-type yeast cultures for 1000 generations.
source_span: From both colonies, we started with 10 wild-type and 10 bem1∆ cultures, which we evolved for one thousand generations by serial dilutions
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is essential to understand how adaptation was studied.

fact: By the end of the evolution experiment, bem1∆ cells had growth rates close to, but still significantly lower than, wild-type cells.
source_span: By the end of the experiment, however, the bem1∆ cells grew at almost the rate of their wild-type ancestors ... growth rates of bem1∆ cells are close to, but in aggregate significantly lower (t-test, p-value < 1e−5) than the growth rate of wild-type cells at the end of the evolution experiment
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the extent of recovery and remaining difference after evolution.

fact: Cell size distributions in bem1∆ populations shifted during evolution from larger and more variable sizes toward wild-type size and variability, indicating improved polarization dynamics.
source_span: At the beginning of the experiment, bem1∆ cells were larger and showed a wider distribution than the wild-type ancestor ... At the end of the experiment, however, both the mode and the standard deviation in bem1∆ cells adapted to wild-type cell size ... suggesting a properly functioning polarization machinery.
selection_reasoning: This links phenotypic changes to improved cellular function, supporting the main findings.

fact: Cell size was used as a proxy for polarization dynamics because yeast cells continue to grow during polarity establishment, so longer polarization times result in larger cells.
source_span: We examined how the cell size distribution ... changed during the experiment: cells that take longer to polarize are on average larger than cells that polarize fast because yeast cells continue to grow during polarity establishment
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the rationale for measuring cell size as an indicator of polarization.

fact: The study discusses the role of loss-of-function mutations in the evolution of populations outside the laboratory.
source_span: We discuss the role of loss-of-function mutations in the evolution of populations outside the laboratory.
selection_reasoning: This highlights the broader significance and relevance of the findings.

fact: Deletion of the BEM1 gene in yeast cells causes severe growth defects that can be partially compensated by additional mutations.
source_span: cells from the original colony ( Video 3 ) showed the same severe growth defects as freshly germinated bem1∆ spores , whereas engineered bem1∆ bem3∆ cells had a much less severe defect .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the main genetic perturbation studied and its impact on growth, which is central to the study's motivation and findings.

fact: Evolved yeast lines lacking BEM1 acquired recurrent mutations in three genes: BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2, which are specific adaptations to the deletion of BEM1.
source_span: We found three genes that were mutated at least three times: BEM3 ( 10/10 ) , NRP1 ( 5/10 ) , and BEM2 ( 3/10 ) . Mutations in these genes were not reported in a variety of other yeast evolution experiments ... suggesting that they are specific for the deletion of BEM1 .
selection_reasoning: Identifying specific adaptive mutations is a principal finding explaining how cells compensate for BEM1 deletion.

fact: Wild-type yeast lines evolved under the same conditions showed diverse mutations, with ECM21 being the only gene mutated more than once, indicating different adaptation pathways compared to bem1∆ lines.
source_span: In the control , wild-type lines we found a diverse set of mutations ... with only one gene , ECM21 , being mutated twice . ECM21 was also the only mutated gene ... that was also found in either of two other large scale evolution experiments ... suggesting that adaptation in our control experiments involves similar mutations to those in other studies ...
selection_reasoning: This background fact contrasts the bem1∆ adaptation with wild-type adaptation, highlighting the specificity of the observed mutations.

fact: Cell size increases and variability change during evolution in both wild-type and bem1∆ yeast lines, and cell size correlates linearly with polarization time.
source_span: Data from Figure 2 , Figure 3 , and Figure 4 are combined to show that cell size is a reasonable approximation for polarization time ... The plot indeed suggests a linear relation between cell size and polarization time .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic relationship links a measurable phenotype (cell size) to a key cellular process (polarization), relevant to understanding adaptation.

fact: The study sequenced whole genomes of multiple evolved yeast lines to identify mutations responsible for changes in growth rate and cell size.
source_span: We sequenced the whole genomes of several evolved lines: from the seven wild-type lines ... we sequenced five lines . We sequenced a total of 10 bem1∆ lines ...
selection_reasoning: This high-level method is central to discovering the genetic basis of adaptation.

fact: Mutations in IRA1 found in one bem1∆ evolved line are common in other yeast evolution experiments and are not specific to BEM1 deletion.
source_span: Only one of these mutations , the mutation in IRA1 , in line T3 , is also commonly found in other yeast evolution experiments suggesting that it is not specific for the deletion of BEM1 .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies which mutations are specific adaptations versus general evolutionary changes.

fact: The adaptive mutations in BEM3 in different bem1∆ lines are early stop mutations that arose independently.
source_span: The A-lines shared the same early stop mutation in BEM3 , but lines T2 and T3 independently acquired different early stop mutations in BEM3 .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the convergent nature of adaptation at the genetic level.

fact: Reconstructed yeast strains combining mutations in BEM3, NRP1, and BEM2 show improved growth rates compared to bem1∆ strains without these mutations.
source_span: The log phase growth rate in bulk ... is measured for the reconstructed intermediates of bem1∆ cells in line A1 and A2 ...
selection_reasoning: This experimental result demonstrates the functional significance of the identified mutations.

fact: The study investigated neural mechanisms accompanying commitment (acceptance, rejection) and deferral (failure to accept or reject) during economic choice using a multi-alternative choice task with irreversible financial consequences.

fact: In the task, participants chose between accepting and deferring acceptance in some blocks, and between rejecting and deferring rejection in other blocks, allowing probing of value encoding as a function of preference and commitment timing.
source_span: In half of the blocks , participants had to choose between accepting ( inclusion by commitment ) and deferring acceptance of a prospect ( exclusion by deferral ) . In the other half of the blocks , participants chose between rejecting ( exclusion by commitment ) and deferring rejection ( inclusion by deferral ) . Therefore , preference for a bandit would be implied by commitment in rule-in and deferral in rule-out . Our task , thus , allowed us to probe value encoding in the prefrontal cortex as a function of whether a stimulus was preferred ( i . e . , included or excluded ) and whether commitment was made now or deferred until later .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the key task design that enables testing how preference and commitment affect neural value encoding.

fact: Participants performed the task in an fMRI scanner, viewing spirals of variable length associated with four options (bandits), with each spiral length drawn from a Gaussian distribution with a fixed mean per bandit during a block.

fact: In rule-in blocks, participants started with an empty asset pool and per-trial yield was the average payoff of all accepted bandits; in rule-out blocks, participants started with all bandits in the asset pool and per-trial yield was the average payoff of all bandits not yet rejected.
source_span: On rule-in blocks , participants began the block with an empty pool of assets and the per-trial momentary yield was determined by the average payoff of all bandits committed to ( accepted ) thus far ( Figure 1A: upper panel and ‘Materials and methods’ ) . On rule-out blocks , participants' asset pool initially included all four alternatives and the per-trial yield was the average of the payoff of all bandits not yet committed to ( not yet rejected , Figure 1A: lower panel ) .
