fact: Ci variants that cannot be processed still supported normal graded activation of Hedgehog target genes and normal adult wing development when combined with a constitutive Ci repressor.
source_span: Ci variants that cannot be processed supported a normal pattern of graded target gene activation and the development of adults with normal wing morphology , when supplemented by constitutive Ci repressor , showing that Hh can signal normally in the absence of regulated processing .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding demonstrating that regulated Ci processing is not essential for normal Hh signaling and development.

fact: Processing-resistant Ci variants were significantly activated even without Hedgehog by eliminating Cos2 or PKA, revealing that Cos2 and PKA have separate inhibitory roles beyond promoting Ci processing.
source_span: The processing-resistant Ci variants were also significantly activated in the absence of Hh by elimination of Cos2 , likely acting through binding the CORD domain of Ci , or PKA , revealing separate inhibitory roles of these two components in addition to their well-established roles in promoting Ci processing .
selection_reasoning: This finding identifies additional regulatory roles of Cos2 and PKA in Ci activity, important for understanding Hh pathway regulation.

fact: Hedgehog signaling proteins are essential for development and adult tissue maintenance in both invertebrates and vertebrates.
source_span: Hedgehog ( Hh ) signaling proteins guide development and help maintain adult tissue homeostasis in both invertebrates and vertebrates ( Hui and Angers , 2011; Ingham and McMahon , 2001; Petrova and Joyner , 2014 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological importance of Hh signaling.

fact: Abnormal Hedgehog protein production, distribution, or response causes developmental birth defects and cancers such as holoprosencephaly, limb abnormalities, medulloblastoma, and basal cell carcinoma.
source_span: Aberrant Hh protein production , distribution , and responses are common causes of developmental birth defects and cancer , including holoprosencephaly , limb and digit abnormalities , medulloblastoma , and basal cell carcinoma ( Anderson et al . , 2012; Cortes et al . , 2019; Ng and Curran , 2011; Pak and Segal , 2016; Petrova and Joyner , 2014; Sasai et al . , 2019 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the clinical relevance and motivation for studying Hh signaling mechanisms.

fact: Many Hedgehog pathway components were first identified in Drosophila and later found to have mammalian counterparts, including Smoothened, which is targeted by anticancer drugs.
source_span: Many conserved Hh components were initially identified in Drosophila melanogaster and then found to have a mammalian ortholog , including the key transducing protein Smoothened ( Smo ) , which is now the target of several anticancer drugs ( Cortes et al . , 2019; Ng and Curran , 2011; Pak and Segal , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact justifies the use of Drosophila as a model and links the pathway to therapeutic applications.

fact: Drosophila is well suited for precise genetic tests under physiological conditions to understand fundamental Hedgehog signaling mechanisms.
source_span: It is therefore important to understand the fundamental molecular mechanisms involved in the pathway in Drosophila which is well suited to precise and detailed genetic tests conducted under physiological conditions .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the rationale for using Drosophila to study Hh signaling.

fact: In Drosophila wing discs, Hedgehog is produced in posterior cells and signals to anterior cells expressing Ci, creating a gradient of signaling activity across the anterior-posterior border.
source_span: In third instar larval Drosophila wing discs , Hh is expressed in posterior compartment cells and Ci is expressed only in anterior cells , so that Hh signals to a band of anterior cells at the anterior-posterior ( AP ) border with declining strength from posterior to anterior ( Blair , 2003; Lawrence and Struhl , 1996 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential biological context for the spatial pattern of Hh signaling studied.

fact: Ci regulates different Hedgehog target genes in a spatially graded manner within the wing disc, inducing decapentaplegic broadly, patched in a gradient, and engrailed only near the Hh source.
source_span: Within this AP border territory , Ci induces decapentaplegic ( dpp ) in a broad region , patched ( ptc or a ptc-lacZ transcriptional reporter ) in a gradient within a narrower domain , and engrailed ( en ) only in the cells closest to the source of Hh ( see Figure 8; Blair , 2003; Vervoort , 2000 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the graded gene expression outputs of Hh signaling via Ci.

fact: In the absence of Hedgehog, the receptor Patched inhibits Smoothened, keeping Smoothened levels low and mainly in internal vesicles.
source_span: In the absence of Hh , the ligand-free receptor , Patched ( Ptc ) , actively inhibits the actions of another transmembrane protein Smoothened ( Smo ) , which is present under these conditions at relatively low levels and mainly associated with internal vesicles ( Denef et al . , 2000; Nakano et al . , 2004; Strigini and Cohen , 1997; Zhao et al . , 2007 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key regulatory step in the Hh pathway relevant to Ci regulation.

fact: Costal2 (Cos2) acts as a scaffold to bring kinases including Protein Kinase A (PKA), GSK3, and CK1 to Ci-155, facilitating its phosphorylation and subsequent processing into a repressor form.
source_span: Costal2 ( Cos2 ) , a kinesin-family protein , complexed to Fused ( Fu ) , acts as a scaffold to bring Protein Kinase A ( PKA ) , Glycogen Synthase Kinase-3 ( GSK3 ) , and Casein Kinase-1 ( CK1 ) to C-155 and facilitate phosphorylation of Ci-155 at a series of clustered PKA , CK1 and GSK3 sites ( Ranieri et al . , 2014; Zhang et al . , 2005 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the molecular mechanism of Ci processing regulation.

fact: Phosphorylated Ci-155 is ubiquitinated by a Cul1-SCF ubiquitin ligase complex and partially degraded by the proteasome to form Ci-75, a transcriptional repressor.
source_span: This creates a binding site for Slimb , the substrate recognition component of a Cul1-SCF ubiquitin ligase complex , which promotes Ci-155 ubiquitination and subsequent partial proteolysis ( ‘processing’ ) by the proteasome to a repressor form ( Ci-75 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact details the processing step that converts Ci into its repressor form, central to pathway regulation.

fact: Ci-75 represses transcription of Hedgehog target genes such as decapentaplegic and hedgehog itself in anterior wing disc cells.
source_span: Ci-75 has a critical role in anterior wing disc cells , silencing transcription of dpp and hh ( Domínguez et al . , 1996 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the functional consequence of Ci processing in gene regulation.

fact: Hedgehog binding to Patched activates Smoothened through phosphorylation and plasma membrane accumulation, leading to inhibition of Ci-155 processing and activation of Ci-155.
source_span: Hh binding to Ptc leads to Smo activation in a process that involves Smo phosphorylation by PKA , CK1 , and G-protein-coupled receptor kinase 2 ( Gprk2 ) , Smo accumulation at the plasma membrane and a change in Smo conformation or oligomerization ( Kalderon , 2008; Maier et al . , 2014; Zhao et al . , 2007 ) . Activation enhances and likely alters the nature of binding of Smo to Cos2-Fu complexes , with two important consequences . First , Ci-155 processing is inhibited , due to titration of Cos2 complexes away from Ci-155 and perhaps also to partial dissociation of PKA , CK1 or GSK3 from Cos2/Fu complexes ( Li et al . , 2014; Ranieri et al . , 2014; Zhang et al . , 2005 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes how Hh signaling leads to Ci activation, a key pathway step.

fact: Activated Fused (Fu) kinase is essential for full activation of Ci-155 after Hedgehog signaling.
source_span: Second , Cos2-associated Fu molecules are brought together to cross-phosphorylate activation loop residues , leading to full activation of Fu protein kinase activity ( Shi et al . , 2011; Zhang et al . , 2011; Zhou and Kalderon , 2011 ) . Activated Fu protein kinase is critical for the full activation of Ci-155 .
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a critical kinase activity required for Ci activation downstream of Hh.

fact: If Ci-155 processing is blocked but Fu kinase activity is absent, Ci-155 remains inactive in the cytoplasm through association with Suppressor of fused (Su(fu)) and Cos2.
source_span: If Ci-155 processing is blocked but there is no Fu kinase activity , Ci-155 is largely maintained in an inactive cytoplasmic form through direct associations with Suppressor of fused ( Su ( fu ) ) and Cos2 ( Forbes et al . , 1993; Ohlmeyer and Kalderon , 1998; Préat et al . , 1993 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the necessity of Fu kinase for Ci activation beyond processing inhibition.

fact: Activated Fu protein kinase is critical for the full activation of Ci-155 in the Hedgehog signaling pathway.

fact: The effect of serotype 19F on carriage duration is independent of bacterial genetic background.
source_span: The covariance test found that 19F , erythromycin resistance and being non-typable had significant effects on the model ( in that order ) . As these terms enter the model before any lineage specific effect , this suggested these serotypes and resistances are associated with variation in carriage duration independent of background genotype ... only serotype 19F reached genome-wide significance ( p=3 . 8×10−7 ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a key locus effect, showing that serotype 19F influences carriage duration beyond lineage effects.

fact: No significant difference in carriage duration was observed between isolates with or without capsule within the same lineage, suggesting capsule presence alone does not explain variation in carriage duration within lineages.
source_span: No significant difference in duration was seen between isolates with or without capsule within the same lineage ( p=0 . 39; Figure 4 ) .
selection_reasoning: This result tests and limits the role of capsule gain/loss events, refining understanding of serotype effects.

fact: The main bacterial lineage effect on pneumococcal carriage duration in infants is determined by serotype, with serotype 19F showing a significant association independent of genetic background.
source_span: The predictors had the same order of significance , but only serotype 19F reached genome-wide significance ( p=3 . 8×10−7 ) . Together , this suggests that the main lineage effect on carriage duration is the serotype , but only some serotypes ( 19F ) have an association independent of genetic background .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the key bacterial factor influencing carriage duration, a principal finding central to the study.

fact: Erythromycin resistance in Streptococcus pneumoniae is significantly associated with increased carriage duration in infants.
source_span: We also found that erythromycin resistance may be significantly associated with an increased carriage duration . While being a relatively uncommon treatment in this setting ( 3% of treatments captured ) , we did not find that other antibiotics were associated .
selection_reasoning: This highlights an important antibiotic resistance factor affecting carriage duration, relevant for clinical and epidemiological implications.

fact: Common pneumococcal serotypes 19F, 23F, and 14 are carried the longest in infants, while non-typeable pneumococci are carried for the shortest duration.
source_span: The results show 19F , 23F and 14 were carried the longest , 6A/C and 6B for intermediate lengths , and NT the shortest .
selection_reasoning: This provides a clear summary of serotype-specific carriage durations, a key descriptive finding.

fact: Infants typically experience one or two long carriage episodes (over 90 days) of common pneumococcal serotypes and around two short carriage episodes (under a month) of non-typeable Streptococcus pneumoniae in their first two years.
source_span: The overall picture of the first two years of infant carriage is one containing one or two long ( over 90 day ) carriage episodes of a common serotype ( 6A/C , 6B , 14 , 19F , 23F ) and around two short ( under a month ) carriage episodes of non-typable S . pneumoniae .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the typical pattern of pneumococcal carriage in infants, important for understanding disease dynamics.

fact: Some rarer pneumococcal serotypes are carried for shorter durations, possibly due to competitive exclusion by fitter serotypes.
source_span: Colonisation by other serotypes seem to cause slightly shorter carriage episodes , though the relative rarity of these events naturally limits the confidence in this inference . That some serotypes are rarer and carried for shorter time periods may be evidence of competitive exclusion ( Hardin , 1960; Trzciński et al . , 2015 ) , as fitter serotypes quickly replace less fit serotypes thus leading to reduced carriage duration .
selection_reasoning: This provides a biological explanation for variation in carriage duration, relevant to the study's interpretation.

fact: Genome-wide association analysis identified a significant locus in the prophage replication module associated with pneumococcal carriage duration.
source_span: The only genome-wide significant SNP hits are synonymous changes ( MAF = 1% ) in the replication module of the prophage in the ATCC 700669 genome ( Croucher et al . , 2009 ) , a highly variable component of the pneumococcal genome ( Croucher et al . , 2014a ) ( Figure 5 ) .
selection_reasoning: This identifies a novel genetic locus linked to carriage duration, a principal genetic finding.

fact: Presence of specific prophage sequences in Streptococcus pneumoniae is associated with a slight decrease in carriage duration in infants.
source_span: These results are therefore evidence that infection with a specific phage sequence is associated with a slight decrease in carriage duration .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a novel mechanism by which mobile genetic elements influence bacterial carriage, important for understanding pathogen dynamics.

fact: The study used linear mixed models incorporating bacterial relatedness to control for population structure when analyzing genetic associations with carriage duration.
source_span: To fully account for the effect of the bacterial genome rather than relying on discrete clusters as covariates in the regression , we performed regression of these lineage effects under an LMM where the relatedness between strains was instead included as a random effect .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key methodological approach enabling robust genetic association analysis.

fact: Heritability estimates of pneumococcal carriage duration are consistent with previous studies and suggest that serotype effects on carriage duration may be generalizable across populations.
source_span: While our heritability estimates are specific to this population due to differences in host , vaccine deployment and transmission dynamics , the similarity of the estimates of serotype effect to those from different study populations suggests our results may be somewhat generalisable .
selection_reasoning: This supports the broader relevance and significance of the findings.

fact: Infection with a specific phage sequence is associated with a slight decrease in Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage duration.
source_span: These results are therefore evidence that infection with a specific phage sequence is associated with a slight decrease in carriage duration.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking phage presence to a key phenotype relevant to bacterial carriage.

fact: Previous studies have shown that phage elements can reduce the fitness of Streptococcus pneumoniae during carriage in vivo.
source_span: Additionally, previous in vivo tests have shown phage elements to cause a fitness decrease of S. pneumoniae during carriage (DeBardeleben et al., 2014).
selection_reasoning: This background supports the biological relevance of phage effects on bacterial carriage.

fact: Genetic polymorphisms in the prophage replication module are associated with changes in carriage duration in about 2% of viral sequences.
source_span: The genetic polymorphisms in the prophage associated with changes in carriage duration, found in 2% of viral sequences, are found within coding sequences inside the phage replication module (Romero et al., 2009).
selection_reasoning: This identifies a specific genetic region linked to the observed phenotype.

fact: Prophage frequently insert into the comYC gene in Streptococcus pneumoniae, disrupting its function and preventing bacterial transformation.
source_span: Pneumococcal prophage frequently insert into comYC, thereby preventing the host cell undergoing transformation (Croucher et al., 2011; Croucher et al., 2014b).
selection_reasoning: This mechanism explains how prophage can alter bacterial phenotype relevant to carriage.

fact: Having an intact comYC gene is significantly associated with increased carriage duration in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source_span: We found that having an intact comYC gene (23% of isolates) was significantly associated with an increased carriage duration using the LMM (β=0.29; p=1.4×10−44).
selection_reasoning: This is a key genetic factor influencing carriage duration, central to the study's findings.

fact: The effect of phage-associated genetic variants on carriage duration may be mediated through disruption of the comYC gene.
source_span: An interpretation consistent with these findings would be that the effect of phage k-mers is actually through interrupting comYC.
selection_reasoning: This links phage genetic variation to a known functional gene affecting carriage.

fact: Phage structural protein PblB can mediate bacterial adhesion to human cells and may influence bacterial carriage duration.
source_span: One phage protein that has been found to alter the bacterial phenotype is PblB, a phage structural protein that can also mediate bacterial adhesion to human cells (Loeffler and Fischetti, 2006).
selection_reasoning: This identifies a specific phage protein with potential relevance to bacterial colonization.

fact: Penicillin resistance genes pbp1a and pbp2b show suggestive association with increased carriage duration in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source_span: Signals at the suggestive level include pbp1a and pbp2b, which suggest as above that penicillin resistance may slightly increase carriage duration.
selection_reasoning: This highlights a possible link between antibiotic resistance and carriage duration.

fact: K-mers from erythromycin resistance genes (ermB, mel, mef) did not reach significance for association with carriage duration in this study.
source_span: K-mers from erythromycin resistance genes (ermB, mel, mef) were expected to reach significance from the above analysis, but did not.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies which resistance genes were not strongly linked to carriage duration, refining the study's conclusions.

fact: The study used linear mixed models and association tests correcting for population structure to identify genetic variants associated with carriage duration.
source_span: Using a monthly swabbing approach, it was only possible to robustly infer changes in the carriage duration of genotypes that colonise hosts for long periods... To search for candidate regions which may be independently associated with both a lineage and increased carriage duration, we ran an association test using a set number of fixed effects as the population structure correction.
selection_reasoning: This describes the high-level methodological approach relevant to the main findings.

fact: The serotype 19F, predominantly the β-lactam resistant PMEN14 lineage, is most associated with increased carriage duration.
source_span: As 19F, the serotype most associated with carriage duration, is predominantly the β-lactam resistant PMEN14 lineage the pbp association may be driven through strong LD between with this serotype.
selection_reasoning: This links a specific bacterial serotype and lineage to the phenotype studied.

fact: Additional genes associated with carriage duration include recA, bgaA, phoH-like protein, ftsZ, groEL, dnaB, phtD, mraY, tlyA, zinT, adcA, and recJ.
source_span: The most highly associated SNPs were in all three pbp regions... recA (DNA repair and homologous recombination), bgaA (beta-galactosidase), phoH-like protein (phosphate starvation-inducible protein), ftsZ (cell division protein) and groEL (chaperonin)... dnaB (DNA replication)... Associated k-mers were also found in phtD (host cell surface adhesion), mraY (cell wall biosynthesis), tlyA (rRNA methylase), zinT (zinc recruitment), adcA (zinc recruitment) and recJ (DNA repair).
selection_reasoning: This summarizes other genetic loci implicated in carriage duration, broadening the study's scope.

fact: Bacteriocin blpZ and immunity protein pncM k-mers are associated with variability in carriage duration.
source_span: Additionally we found k-mers in the bacteriocin blpZ and immunity protein pncM (Bogaardt et al., 2015) to be associated with variability in carriage.
selection_reasoning: This identifies additional genetic elements potentially influencing bacterial carriage.

fact: The genetic variation of the pneumococcal genome explains most of the variability in carriage duration of Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source_span: By developing models for longitudinal swab data and combining the results with whole genome sequence data we have quantified and mapped the genetic contribution to the carriage duration of S . pneumoniae . We found that despite a range of other factors such as host age which are known to cause carriage duration to differ , sequence variation of the pneumococcal genome explains most of this variability ( 63% ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding quantifying the genetic contribution to carriage duration, central to the study's main question and significance.

fact: Common pneumococcal serotypes and resistance to erythromycin explain part of the variation in carriage duration.
source_span: Common serotypes and resistance to erythromycin cause some of this effect ( 19% total ) , as does the presence or absence of particular prophage sequence in the genome .
selection_reasoning: Identifying serotype and antibiotic resistance as contributors to carriage duration variation is a key mechanistic and clinically relevant finding.

fact: The presence or absence of particular prophage sequences in the pneumococcal genome is significantly associated with variation in carriage duration.
source_span: Common serotypes and resistance to erythromycin cause some of this effect ( 19% total ) , as does the presence or absence of particular prophage sequence in the genome .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a novel genetic factor influencing carriage duration, important for understanding pneumococcal biology and evolution.

fact: Having an intact comYC gene, which can be disrupted by prophage insertion, is associated with increased carriage duration in Streptococcus pneumoniae.
source_span: Investigating a mechanism for the prophage association , we found that having an intact comYC gene , which is frequently interrupted by prophage causing loss of function of the competence system , was associated with increased carriage duration .
selection_reasoning: This provides a mechanistic insight linking prophage disruption to carriage duration, relevant for the study's biological conclusions.

fact: Increasing child age contributes to a decrease in the duration of pneumococcal carriage episodes.
source_span: As found previously , increasing child age contributes to a decrease in the duration of carriage episodes . From a mean of 68 days long , we calculated a drop of 19 days after a year , and 32 days after two years .
selection_reasoning: This environmental factor is a known contributor to carriage duration variance and is important background and covariate information.

fact: Previous carriage of any pneumococcal serotype is associated with an increase in the duration of future carriage episodes.
source_span: Previous carriage of any serotype was estimated to cause an increase in the duration of future carriage episodes , though previous studies have found no overall effect ( Weinberger et al . , 2008 ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding about prior exposure is relevant to understanding host factors influencing carriage duration.

fact: Antigenic variation in known pneumococcal regions such as pspA, pspC, zmpA, or zmpB was not associated with changes in carriage duration.
source_span: Antigenic variation in known regions ( of pspA , pspC , zmpA or zmpB ) may be expected to cause a change in carriage duration ( Lipsitch and O'Hagan , 2007 ) , however we found none of these to be associated with a change in carriage duration .
selection_reasoning: This negative result clarifies which genetic factors do not influence carriage duration, refining the study's conclusions.

fact: Intra-strain competition within the host may occur via bacteriocin and immunity proteins such as blpZ and pncM, which are associated with variability in carriage duration.
source_span: Additionally we found k-mers in the bacteriocin blpZ and immunity protein pncM ( Bogaardt et al . , 2015 ) to be associated with variability in carriage duration . This could be evidence that intra-strain competition occurs within host via this mechanism , consistent with previous in vitro mouse models ( Dawid et al . , 2007 ) .
selection_reasoning: This suggests a biological mechanism potentially affecting carriage duration, important for understanding pneumococcal ecology.

fact: The study used longitudinal swab data combined with whole genome sequencing to quantify genetic contributions to pneumococcal carriage duration.
source_span: By developing models for longitudinal swab data and combining the results with whole genome sequence data we have quantified and mapped the genetic contribution to the carriage duration of S . pneumoniae .
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is essential to understand how the main findings were obtained.

fact: Variants other than serotype exist in the pneumococcal genome that affect carriage duration, consistent with recent theoretical predictions.
source_span: Importantly , our analysis of heritability shows that variants other than serotype affect carriage duration , consistent with recent theoretical work ( Lehtinen et al . , 2017 ) . Here we have shown that these alleles do exist in a natural population , and also identified candidates for the loci which fulfil this role .
selection_reasoning: This confirms a key conceptual advance that genetic factors beyond serotype influence carriage duration.

fact: Variants other than pneumococcal serotype affect the duration of bacterial carriage in the nasopharynx.
source_span: Importantly , our analysis of heritability shows that variants other than serotype affect carriage duration , consistent with recent theoretical work ( Lehtinen et al . , 2017 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a core finding linking genetic variation beyond serotype to carriage duration, central to the study's main scientific claim.

fact: Specific genetic loci in the pneumococcal genome have been identified as candidates influencing carriage duration in a natural population.
source_span: Here we have shown that these alleles do exist in a natural population , and also identified candidates for the loci which fulfil this role .
selection_reasoning: Identifying candidate loci is a principal result supporting the genetic basis of carriage duration variation.

fact: Variation in pneumococcal carriage duration is linked to antibiotic resistance.
source_span: Together these studies suggest that variants exist in the pneumococcal genome which alter carriage duration , which in turn is linked to antibiotic resistance .
selection_reasoning: This relationship has clinical and public health significance, connecting carriage duration to resistance.

fact: The study used genome-wide association study (GWAS) methods to investigate the complex phenotype of pneumococcal carriage duration in a natural infant population.
source_span: By instead using genome-wide association study methods we have been able to quantitatively investigate a complex phenotype in a natural population .
selection_reasoning: This high-level methodological approach is key to understanding how the findings were obtained.

fact: The study population consisted of infants from the Maela longitudinal birth cohort who were swabbed regularly to measure pneumococcal carriage over time.
source_span: The study population was a subset of infants from the Maela longitudinal birth cohort ( Turner et al . , 2013a ) , and was split into two cohorts . In the ‘routine’ cohort , 364 infants were swabbed monthly from birth , 24 times in total .
selection_reasoning: Describing the study population and sampling frequency provides essential context for the study design.

fact: Carriage duration was inferred using a continuous-time hidden Markov model applied to longitudinal swab data.
source_span: We modelled the time series of swab data using a continuous-time HMM , as implemented in the R package msm ( RRID:SCR_015500 ) ( Jackson , 2011 ) . Unobserved ( true ) states correspond to whether the child is carrying bacteria in their nasopharynx , and observed ( emitted ) states correspond to whether a positive swab was seen at each point .
selection_reasoning: This modeling approach is a key methodological innovation enabling estimation of carriage duration from swab data.

fact: Environmental factors such as host immune response variation and co-infections may also influence pneumococcal carriage duration but were not fully accounted for in this study.
source_span: Additional environmental factors that explain some of the remainder of the variance may include the variation of the host immune response and interaction with other infections or co-colonisation .
selection_reasoning: Acknowledging environmental influences highlights limitations and complexity relevant to interpreting the findings.

fact: Co-infection with influenza A virus is known to affect pneumococcal population dynamics in the nasopharynx but was not recorded in this study.
source_span: In particular , co-infection with influenza A was not recorded but is known to affect population dynamics within the nasopharynx ( Kono et al . , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background on factors influencing carriage dynamics and study limitations.

fact: The heritability of pneumococcal carriage duration could not be fully explained due to the close association of the phenotype with bacterial lineage and limited power to fine-map variants.
source_span: We were not able to fully explain the basis for heritability of carriage duration for a number of reasons . The close association of the phenotype with lineage limited our power to fine-map lineage associated variants other than capsule type which may affect carriage duration .
selection_reasoning: This limitation is critical for understanding the scope and interpretation of genetic findings.

fact: Meta-analysis combining larger studies with higher resolution data may help resolve the genetic basis of pneumococcal carriage duration.
source_span: Meta-analysis with more large studies with higher resolution may help to resolve these issues: we are conducting a similar study in Cape Town , South Africa which will combine sequence data with two-weekly swabs and will be compared to these results in future .
selection_reasoning: This points to future research directions and the significance of the current study as a foundation.

fact: The study's analysis of heritability and variance explained in pneumococcal carriage duration demonstrates the utility of such approaches for investigating complex bacterial traits.
source_span: We believe that the analysis of heritability and variance explained in a phenotype of interest , as presented here , will be an important part analysis of complex bacterial traits in future studies .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the broader significance and methodological contribution of the study.

fact: The carriage duration phenotype distribution was positively skewed and approximately exponential, requiring a logarithmic transformation to better fit linear regression assumptions.
source_span: The phenotype distribution was positively skewed , with an approximately exponential distribution ( Figure 3 ) . Residuals were therefore non-normally distributed , potentially reducing power ( McCulloch , 2003 ) . In the regression setting , a monotonic function can be applied to transform the response variable to avoid this problem . We took the natural logarithm of the carriage duration𝐲^=ln⁢ ( 𝐲 ) which led to the residuals being much closer to being normally distributed ( Figure 3 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background and data transformation step is critical to understanding the modeling approach and validity of the genetic association analyses.

fact: Broad sense heritability of carriage duration was estimated using the ANOVA-CPP method with a patristic distance cutoff of 0.04.
source_span: We estimated broad sense heritability H2 with the ANOVA-CPP method in the patherit R package ( Mitov and Stadler , 2016 ) , using a patristic distance cutoff of 0 . 04 ( Figure 4 ) .
selection_reasoning: Estimating heritability is a key step to quantify the genetic contribution to carriage duration.

fact: An Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model was used to test the effect of lineage genetics on carriage duration by fitting the trait along the phylogeny and comparing model likelihoods.
source_span: To test the effect of lineage genetics we used the patherit package to fit an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model of the warped carriage duration along the phylogeny . We compared the likelihood of the full fit to that with no genetic effect on the trait ( σG2=0 ) using a likelihood ratio test ( LRT ) with one degree of freedom .
selection_reasoning: This method assesses how much lineage-related genetic variation influences carriage duration, a principal question of the study.

fact: SNP-based heritability of carriage duration was estimated using a linear mixed model implemented in warped-lmm, which learns a monotonic transform to ensure normal residuals.
source_span: To estimate the SNP-based heritability hSNP2 we applied a linear mixed model , which uses the genomic relatedness matrix ( as calculated from SNPs passing filtering ) as random effects . We used the implementation in warped-lmm ( RRID:SCR_015503 ) ( Fusi et al . , 2014 ) , which learns a monotonic transform as it fits the model to the data to ensure residuals are normally distributed ( Figure 3 ) .
selection_reasoning: Estimating SNP-based heritability quantifies the proportion of variance explained by common genetic variants, a key finding.

fact: Child age and previous carriage status were included as covariates in the heritability and association analyses.
source_span: Child age and whether previous carriage had occurred were included as covariates .
selection_reasoning: Including these covariates controls for important non-genetic factors influencing carriage duration.

fact: Serotype and antibiotic resistance were encoded as dummy variables and included as predictors in regression models to explain variation in carriage duration.
source_span: We encoded all 56 observed serotypes ( including non-typables ) and resistance to the six antibiotics as dummy variables . We used 6A/C as the reference level , as this had a mean carriage duration close to the grand mean in previous analysis . Orthogonal polynomial coding was used for the latter four antibiotics , where resistance could be intermediate or full . We then regressed this design matrix X was against the transformed carriage duration 𝐲^ .
selection_reasoning: Serotype and resistance are key biological factors hypothesized to influence carriage duration.

fact: Variable selection using lasso regression identified 20 predictors with non-zero coefficients that explained a significant proportion of variance in carriage duration.
source_span: We performed variable selection using lasso regression ( Efron et al . , 2004 ) , implemented in the R package glmnet ( RRID:SCR_015505 ) ( Friedman et al . , 2010 ) . We used leave-one-out cross-validation to choose a value for the ℓ1 penalty; the value one standard error above the minimum cross-validated error ( Tibshirani et al . , 2001 ) was selected ( λ=0 . 033; Figure 4 ) . The 20 predictors with non-zero coefficients in the model at this value of λ ( Table 2 ) were used in a linear regression to calculate the multiple R2 , which corresponds to the proportion of variance explained by these predictors .
selection_reasoning: This identifies key genetic and phenotypic predictors of carriage duration, a principal finding.

fact: Genomic partitioning was used to estimate the variance in carriage duration explained separately by serotype variation and antibiotic resistance loci.
source_span: To estimate the variance components from serotype and resistance we used genomic partitioning ( Yang et al . , 2011 ) , as implemented in LDAK . We used SNPs in the capsule locus to calculate a kinship matrix approximating the contribution from serotype variation . For antibiotic resistance we used SNPs in the pbp genes , dyr gene and ICE transposon to calculate a kinship matrix . Restricted maximum likelihood was used to estimate the variance explained by each of these components .
selection_reasoning: Partitioning variance by genetic components clarifies the relative contribution of serotype and resistance to carriage duration.

fact: Capsule switch events were identified by reconstructing ancestral serotype states and analyzing carriage duration of unencapsulated children to assess the effect of recent capsule gain.
source_span: Capsule switch events had been previously identified by first reconstructing of the ancestral state of the serotype at each node through maximum parsimony ( Chewapreecha et al . , 2014a ) . For each node involving loss or gain of the capsule , those with at least one child being a tip were selected to find recent switches ( all were capsule gain ) . The carriage duration of all unencapsulated children of the identified node were used as the null distribution to calculate an empirical p-value for the switched isolate .
selection_reasoning: This analysis addresses the impact of capsule switching on carriage duration, a key biological mechanism.

fact: A linear mixed model implemented in fast-lmm was used to associate genetic variants with carriage duration while controlling for lineage effects and covariates.
source_span: We used the linear mixed model implemented in fast-lmm ( RRID:SCR_015506 ) ( Lippert et al . , 2011 ) to associate genetic elements with carriage duration , independent of overall lineage effects . We used the warped phenotype as the response , the kinship matrix ( calculated from SNPs ) as random effects , and variant presence , child age and previous carriage as fixed effects .
selection_reasoning: This method is central to identifying genetic variants associated with carriage duration beyond lineage structure.

fact: Genome-wide significance thresholds were set using Bonferroni correction based on the number of phylogenetically independent SNPs and k-mers tested.
source_span: For SNPs we used a Bonferroni correction with α<0 . 05 and an N of 92487 phylogenetically independent sites to derive a genome-wide significance cutoff of p<5 . 4×10-7 , and a suggestive significance cutoff ( Lander and Kruglyak , 1995; Stranger et al . , 2011 ) of p=1 . 1×10-4 . ... For k-mers we counted 5254876 phylogenetically independent sites , giving a genome wide significance cutoff of 9 . 5×10-9 .
selection_reasoning: Defining significance thresholds is essential for interpreting association results.

fact: Significant k-mers associated with carriage duration were mapped to multiple reference genomes and known transposon sequences to identify their genomic context.
source_span: We used blastn ( RRID:SCR_001598 ) with default settings to map the significant k-mers to seven reference genomes ( ATCC 700669 , INV104B , OXC141 , SPNA45 , Taiwan19F , TIGR4 and NT_110_58 ) , and the possible Tn916 sequences ( Croucher et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: Mapping significant variants to reference genomes helps interpret their biological relevance.

fact: Population structure was corrected in association tests using patristic distances projected into 30 dimensions as covariates in SEER’s linear regression.
source_span: To correct for population structure we used the patristic distances from the phylogenetic tree as the kinship matrix , which we then projected into 30 dimensions using metric multidimensional scaling . The coordinates of the samples in this space were used as covariates in SEER’s linear regression .
selection_reasoning: Correcting for population structure is critical to avoid confounding in genetic association studies.

fact: Association tests on SNPs and k-mers with minor allele frequency greater than 1% were performed using multiple linear regression, reporting top hits with p-values less than 10^-14.
source_span: We performed association tests on SNPs and k-mers with MAF > 1% using multiple linear regression , and report the top hits with p<10-14 .
selection_reasoning: This describes the main association testing approach and significance criteria.

fact: Much of the molecular motion in the cytoplasm is diffusive, which may limit the speed of cellular processes.
source_span: Much of the molecular motion in the cytoplasm is diffusive , which possibly limits the tempo of processes .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why studying diffusion in cells is important for understanding cellular function.

fact: Protein mobility in the cytoplasm depends on protein surface properties and ionic strength.
source_span: We studied the dependence of protein mobility on protein surface properties and ionic strength .
selection_reasoning: This states the main research question and focus of the study.

fact: The study measured translational diffusion coefficients of surface-modified fluorescent proteins in the cytoplasm of Escherichia coli, Lactococcus lactis, and Haloferax volcanii.
source_span: We used surface-modified fluorescent proteins ( FPs ) and determined their translational diffusion coefficients ( D ) in the cytoplasm of Escherichia coli , Lactococcus lactis and Haloferax volcanii .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental approach and model organisms used.

fact: In Escherichia coli, the diffusion coefficient depends on the net charge and its distribution on the protein surface, with positively charged proteins diffusing up to 100-fold slower than negatively charged ones.
source_span: We find that in E . coli D depends on the net charge and its distribution over the protein , with positive proteins diffusing up to 100-fold slower than negative ones .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about how protein charge affects diffusion in E. coli.

fact: The effect of protein charge on diffusion is weaker in Lactococcus lactis and Haloferax volcanii due to electrostatic screening caused by higher ionic strength.
source_span: This effect is weaker in L . lactis and Hfx . volcanii due to electrostatic screening .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights how ionic strength modulates protein diffusion effects across species.

fact: The decreased mobility of positively charged fluorescent proteins is likely caused by their interaction with ribosomes.
source_span: The decrease in mobility is probably caused by interaction of positive FPs with ribosomes as shown in in vivo diffusion measurements and confirmed in vitro with purified ribosomes .
selection_reasoning: This identifies a key mechanism underlying the observed diffusion differences.

fact: Ribosome surface properties may limit the composition of the cytoplasmic proteome by affecting protein diffusion.
source_span: Ribosome surface properties may thus limit the composition of the cytoplasmic proteome .
selection_reasoning: This implication connects molecular diffusion to broader cellular proteome organization.

fact: Diffusion is especially important in prokaryotes because they lack active mechanisms for cytoplasmic transport.
source_span: This is especially important in prokaryotes because of the virtual absence of active mechanisms of cytoplasmic transport .
selection_reasoning: This background explains why diffusion rates matter particularly in prokaryotic cells.

fact: The rate of diffusion, characterized by the diffusion coefficient, is critical for processes that are diffusion limited, such as binding of tRNA complexes to the ribosome.
source_span: For Brownian diffusion the rate of movement is characterized entirely by the diffusion coefficient , D . The exact value of the diffusion coefficient is important to the rate of a process only if it is diffusion limited , e . g . if the necessary conformational changes in an enzyme are faster than the diffusion of reactants . Examples of diffusion-limited processes are binding of tRNA complexes to the ribosome , which leads to limitation in cell growth ...
selection_reasoning: This explains the biological significance of diffusion coefficients for cellular processes.

fact: The cytoplasm is crowded with macromolecules including nucleic acids and over 1000 types of proteins, with 50 protein types making up 85% of the E. coli cytoplasmic proteome.
source_span: The cytoplasm of cells is not only crowded with macromolecules ... but also consists of various types of nucleic acids and >1000 types of protein ... though only 50 protein types make up 85% of the cytoplasmic proteome of E . coli ...
selection_reasoning: This background contextualizes the complexity of the cellular environment affecting diffusion.

fact: Weak and nonspecific interactions between proteins are common in the E. coli cytoplasm and influence protein diffusion.
source_span: Various studies report on the presence of weak and nonspecific interactions between these components . NMR studies on proteins , either in the E . coli cytoplasm ... reveal that there are weak interactions between E . coli proteins and proteins cytochrome c , ubiquitin , and calmodulin .
selection_reasoning: This supports the study’s focus on how surface properties affect diffusion via interactions.

fact: Highly expressed proteins in E. coli are evolutionarily constrained to be less sticky, suggesting nonspecific interactions are consequential for protein diffusion.
source_span: In a computational study on protein interactions it was found that in E . coli more highly expressed proteins are constrained in evolution to be less sticky ... suggesting that nonspecific interactions are common and consequential .
selection_reasoning: This provides evolutionary context for the importance of protein surface properties.

fact: The study used GFP variants with net charges ranging from −30 to +25 and two +11 charge variants differing in charge distribution to probe diffusion dependence on surface charge.
source_span: Here , we use a set of GFP variants with a net charge that ranges from −30 to +25; we also studied two variants of +11 GFP that differ in the distribution of the charge over the surface .
selection_reasoning: This describes the experimental design to test the effect of charge and charge distribution.

fact: The three organisms studied differ in cytoplasmic ionic strength, with potassium ion concentrations of approximately 0.2 M in E. coli, 0.8 M in L. lactis, and 2.1 M in Hfx. volcanii.

fact: Whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing of MMR-deficient tumors reveals a hypermutator phenotype with approximately 50 times more somatic mutations than MMR-proficient tumors.

fact: The study used whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing of tumor-normal pairs from endometrial tumors with confirmed MMR deficiency to characterize mutation spectra.

fact: Mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient tumors have a higher frequency of insertions and deletions (indels) than single basepair substitutions.

selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the mutation spectrum in MMR-deficient tumors, central to understanding their mutational profile.

fact: Indels in MMR-deficient tumors predominantly affect homopolymers, with a 40-fold enrichment over expected by chance.
source_span: Indels predominantly affected homopolymers ( 40-fold enrichment over expected by chance ) and to a lesser extent also microsatellites ( 2 . 3-fold enrichment; Figure 1B , Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This key mechanistic detail explains the mutation pattern characteristic of MMR deficiency.

fact: Substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors are only slightly enriched in homopolymers and microsatellites.
source_span: Substitutions were only slightly enriched in homopolymers and microsatellites ( 3- and 1 . 5-fold enrichment , respectively; Figure 1B ) .
selection_reasoning: This contrasts with the indel enrichment and helps define the mutation spectrum in MMR-deficient tumors.

fact: Mutations in MMR-deficient tumors occur as frequently in introns as in the rest of the genome but are clearly less frequent in exons.
source_span: Mutations occurred as frequently in introns as in the rest of the genome , but were clearly less frequent in exons ( excluding 5′ and 3′ untranslated regions [UTRs] ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights regional variation in mutation frequency relevant to tumor biology.

fact: Indels are 91% less frequent in exons of MMR-deficient tumors compared to other genomic regions.
source_span: This decrease was caused by indels that were 91% less frequent in exons ( Figure 1C , D ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a key observation suggesting selective pressures on mutations in coding regions.

fact: The reduced frequency of exonic indels in MMR-deficient tumors is not fully explained by differences in homopolymer content, length, or base composition.
source_span: Correction for the number of homopolymers , the length of homopolymers or their basepair composition in exons versus other regions weakened this effect , but failed to completely alleviate it ( Figure 1E , Figure 1—figure supplement 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that factors beyond sequence context influence mutation distribution.

fact: Most exonic indels in MMR-deficient tumors (92%) result in frameshift mutations, which have a greater functional impact than substitutions.

selection_reasoning: This fact links mutation type to functional consequences and tumor evolution.

fact: The pattern of fewer exonic indels in MMR-deficient tumors suggests negative clonal selection against frameshift mutations in coding regions during tumorigenesis.
source_span: this suggests that exonic indels are prone to negative clonal selection during tumorigenesis .

fact: Somatic substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors are predominantly transitions, representing 74% of all substitutions.
source_span: When assessing somatic substitutions in MMR-deficient tumors , we observed that 74% of all substitutions represent transitions ( i . e . , purine-to-purine or pyrimidine-to-pyrimidine substitutions ) , which is similar to the patterns observed in the matched germ-line of these tumors ( Figure 2A ) .
selection_reasoning: This characterizes the substitution mutation spectrum, important for understanding mutational processes.

fact: All tumors studied were negative for POLE mutations.
source_span: Notably , all tumors were negative for POLE mutations ( Kandoth et al . , 2013; Palles et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This excludes a confounding mutational process and clarifies the mutation context.

fact: Tumors and matched germ-line samples were whole-genome sequenced using Complete Genomics or Illumina sequencing technology.

selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is relevant to understanding how mutation data were obtained.

fact: Standard diagnostic tests including microsatellite instability (MSI) analysis, immunohistochemistry of MMR proteins, and MLH1 promoter methylation status were performed on tumors.

fact: Somatic mutations arising due to MMR-deficiency mostly involve indels affecting microsatellite sequences and homopolymers.

fact: Seventy-four percent of all somatic substitutions in mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient tumors are transitions, which is similar to the substitution patterns observed in the matched germ-line DNA of these tumors.

selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a key characteristic of MMR-deficient tumor mutation patterns that contrasts with typical tumor genomes and is central to understanding the mutational processes in these tumors.

fact: Tumor genomes from other hypermutator types, such as UV-light-induced melanoma, tobacco smoke-induced small cell lung adenocarcinoma, BRCA1-deficient breast tumors, and MMR-proficient endometrial tumors, display somatic substitution patterns that are clearly dissimilar from their matched germ-line DNA.
source_span: Indeed, when extending these analyses to other hypermutators, that is, UV-light-induced melanoma, tobacco smoke-induced small cell lung adenocarcinoma (SCLC), as well as breast tumors deficient for BRCA1 or EM tumors proficient for MMR, patterns were clearly dissimilar from the matched germ-line.

fact: De novo germ-line substitutions identified through whole-genome sequencing of parent–offspring trios, common genetic variation from the 1000 Genomes Project, and substitutions from human–chimpanzee divergence correlate strongly with the mutation patterns observed in MMR-deficient tumor genomes.

fact: Mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient tumors have mutation patterns that are highly correlated with germ-line genetic variability, suggesting that a considerable fraction of human genetic diversity arises through mismatches escaping MMR.

fact: Somatic insertions and deletions (indels) in MMR-deficient tumors predominantly occur in homopolymers and simple repeats, with deletions being more frequent than insertions.

fact: C:G homopolymers are less likely to accumulate insertions or deletions (indels) in MMR-deficient tumors compared to other homopolymers.

fact: In MMR-deficient tumors and MMR-deficient Caenorhabditis elegans, deletions are more frequent than insertions, with deletions comprising 81% of indels.

selection_reasoning: This finding reveals a fundamental bias in the types of mutations occurring in MMR-deficient contexts, which is central to the study's mutation characterization.

fact: Exome sequencing of 13 MMR-deficient tumors from various tissues revealed a 52-fold increase in somatic mutations compared to MMR-proficient tumors.

fact: Exonic substitutions outnumber exonic indels in MMR-deficient tumors, likely due to negative clonal selection and differences in homopolymer content between exons and other genomic regions.

fact: Most indels in MMR-deficient tumors affect homopolymers rather than microsatellites or non-repeat regions.

fact: Mismatch repair (MMR)-deficient tumors show recurrent indels in homopolymer regions of the genome, with 1.6% of homopolymers affected recurrently across 16 tumors.

fact: Recurrent indels in MMR-deficient tumors occur more frequently in short homopolymers (7–9 nucleotides) predominantly found in coding regions, suggesting positive clonal selection.

fact: The extended Bethesda panel, currently used for microsatellite instability (MSI) testing, has reduced sensitivity due to its limited and difficult-to-analyze markers.

fact: A new panel of 59 recurrent indel markers was developed to improve MSI testing sensitivity, including markers mostly in UTRs and some in coding regions, with homopolymers up to 12 base pairs.
source_span: In an effort to improve MSI testing , we randomly selected 59 recurrent indels affecting ≥6 out of 16 tumors; 50 markers were in 5′ or 3′UTRs and 9 were in coding regions ... selection_reasoning: This describes the key methodological advance aimed at improving MSI detection.

fact: Using a threshold of three positive markers out of 59, the new panel detected MMR-deficiency with approximately 98% sensitivity and over 99% specificity in a discovery set of 236 endometrial tumors.
source_span: This allowed us to determine three positive markers as the threshold with the best Matthew correlation coefficient to detect MMR-deficiency based on IHC and thus to define MSI ... selection_reasoning: This principal finding demonstrates the improved diagnostic performance of the new marker panel.

fact: In a validation set of 114 independent endometrial tumors, the 59-marker panel showed higher sensitivity for detecting MMR-deficiency than the extended Bethesda panel, confirmed by immunohistochemistry.

selection_reasoning: This validates the clinical relevance and superiority of the new MSI testing panel.

fact: A 59-marker panel was developed to detect microsatellite instability (MSI) and showed higher sensitivity than the extended Bethesda panel in identifying MSI-high tumors in endometrial and colorectal cancers.

fact: The 59-marker panel was also able to correctly identify microsatellite instability in ovarian tumors and leukemias.

fact: Mismatch repair-deficient tumors contain numerous frameshift indels in exons and exon/intron boundaries, which are likely loss-of-function mutations.

fact: Each mismatch repair-deficient tumor contains on average approximately 3.3 indels in genes involved in double-strand break repair by homologous recombination.

source_span: Indeed, although stage II or III CRC tumors with MSI are characterized by a modestly improved prognosis, MSI tumors in the advanced setting are generally associated with a more peritoneal metastasis and a worse overall survival independent of the chemotherapy regimen.

fact: The study used whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing on chemo-naive tumor-normal pairs from endometrial, colorectal, and ovarian cancers to identify somatic mutations.

source_span: Germ-line substitutions and indels were eliminated from the list of somatic mutations using the following publicly available datasets: ( i ) common SNPs in dbSNP ( v132 ) with a minor allele frequency of >1% , ( ii ) substitutions identified in the November 2010 release of the 1000 Genomes Project , ( iii ) the Axiom Genotype Data Set containing common SNPs from 1261 HapMap3 individuals in 11 populations , and ( iv ) variant data identified in 46 HapMap individuals ( CG diversity panel ).

fact: Breathing in mice is severely depressed by opioids, and this response is eliminated when the µ-opioid receptor (Oprm1) is globally deleted.
source_span: Like humans , breathing in mice is severely depressed by opioids and this response is eliminated when the µ-Opioid receptor ( Oprm1 ) is globally deleted ( Dahan et al . , 2001 ) .
selection_reasoning: Establishes the mouse model relevance and the role of µ-opioid receptor in OIRD.

source_span: Oprm1 is broadly expressed , in both the central and peripheral nervous systems , including sites that could modulate breathing such as: the cerebral cortex , brainstem respiratory control centers , primary motor neurons , solitary nucleus , and oxygen sensing afferents ( Mansour et al . , 1994; Kirby and McQueen , 1986 ) .
selection_reasoning: Provides biological context for potential sites mediating opioid effects on breathing.

selection_reasoning: States the main knowledge gap motivating the study.

source_span: We find the critical brain site is the preBötzinger Complex , where the breathing rhythm originates , and use genetic tools to reveal that just 70–140 neurons in this region are responsible for its sensitivity to opioids .
selection_reasoning: Identifies the principal brain region responsible for OIRD, a key finding.

fact: Just 70–140 neurons in the preBötzinger Complex are responsible for its sensitivity to opioids.
source_span: We find the critical brain site is the preBötzinger Complex , where the breathing rhythm originates , and use genetic tools to reveal that just 70–140 neurons in this region are responsible for its sensitivity to opioids .
selection_reasoning: Specifies the surprisingly small number of neurons mediating opioid sensitivity, highlighting a precise target.

fact: These opioid-sensitive neurons in the preBötzinger Complex are not required for opioid-induced analgesia, suggesting they could be targeted to prevent respiratory depression without affecting pain relief.
source_span: Importantly , these neurons are not required for opioid-induced analgesia , suggesting a neutral target for developing safer opioids or rescue strategies for opioid overdose .
selection_reasoning: Indicates translational significance for safer opioid therapies.

fact: Morphine administration in awake mice causes a 50–60% decrease in respiratory rate, peak inspiratory airflow, and minute ventilation, modeling opioid-induced respiratory depression.
source_span: Compared to saline , breathing after morphine administration ( in normoxia ) became much slower and inspiratory airflow decreased , each by 60% ( Figure 1B , C ) . This culminated in ~50% decrease in overall minute ventilation ( MV = approximated tidal volume x respiratory rate , Figure 1C ) , demonstrating that 20 mg/kg morphine is , indeed , a suitable dose to model OIRD .
selection_reasoning: Establishes the experimental model and confirms morphine induces respiratory depression.

fact: Morphine prolongs the inspiratory phase and introduces a new pause phase in the breathing cycle of mice, which together contribute to the decreased respiratory rate.
source_span: After morphine , only the inspiratory phase ( measured as inspiratory time , Ti ) became substantially longer ( Figure 1G , H ) . Additionally , hypercapnic breaths showed a new , third phase after the initial expiration ( measured as expiratory time , Te , Figure 1G , H ) that was characterized by prolonged little to no airflow ( <0 . 5 mL/sec . ) preceding hypercapnia induced active expiration ( Pisanski and Pagliardini , 2019 ) . We define this new phase as a pause ( low airflow + active expiration , Figure 1G , Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ) . Such pauses lasted up to several hundred milliseconds ( Figure 1I ) , accounting for about one-third of the average breath length ( Figure 1J ) . Thus , the 50% decrease in respiratory rate after morphine administration is primarily due to prolonging of Ti and pause phases , and the increased prevalence of time spent in pause significantly contributes to the decrease in minute ventilation .
selection_reasoning: Describes the specific breathing pattern changes underlying OIRD, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Opioids cause respiratory depression primarily by decreasing inspiratory airflow and adding a pause phase that delays the initiation of subsequent breaths.
source_span: In summary, opioids cause only two primary changes to the breath, namely, 1) decreased inspiratory airflow and 2) addition of a pause phase that delays initiation of subsequent breaths (Figure 1N).
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the core physiological changes opioids induce in breathing, central to understanding opioid-induced respiratory depression (OIRD).

fact: The preBötzinger Complex (preBötC) in the brainstem is a key site controlling inspiratory airflow and pause phases and is implicated in opioid-induced respiratory depression.
source_span: These two parameters can both be controlled by the breathing central pattern generator, the preBötzinger Complex (preBötC), in the brainstem and suggest that this may be a key locus affected during OIRD (Smith et al., 1991; Feldman et al., 2013; Cui et al., 2016).
selection_reasoning: Identifying the preBötC as a critical brainstem site links the physiological changes to a specific neural substrate relevant for OIRD.

fact: Localized injection of opioids into the preBötC causes respiratory depression, and localized naloxone reverses opioid-induced breathing decreases.
source_span: Indeed, the preBötC has been proposed to play a key role in OIRD since localized injection of opioids results in respiratory depression and localized naloxone reverses decreased breathing after administration of systemic opioids (Montandon et al., 2011; Montandon and Horner, 2014).
selection_reasoning: This supports the functional importance of the preBötC in mediating opioid effects on breathing.

fact: Genetic deletion of the µ-opioid receptor (Oprm1) specifically in preBötC neurons reduces opioid-induced respiratory depression without affecting baseline breathing.
source_span: Deletion of Oprm1 in the preBötC did not affect breathing observed after saline injection (Figure 2D, E), suggesting that in this context, opioids do not exert an endogenous effect. In contrast, breathing was markedly less depressed by morphine administration (Figure 2D, E) compared to the intact control state.
