fact: DNA sequencing data from Primula forbesii and Primula veris were used to identify and compare CYP734A50 gene homologs.
source_span: P . forbesii S-morph DNA-seq data obtained using HiSeq2500 sequencing were assembled using SOAPdenovo2 version 2 . 04 ( Luo et al . , 2012 ) to identify PfoCYP734A50 exons . Close CYP734A50 homologs for both P . veris and P . forbesii were identified by tblastx alignments against the corresponding genome and transcriptome assemblies .
selection_reasoning: Describes the key method and species used to study the gene central to the article.

fact: Gene expression of CYP734A50 was measured in different floral organs of L- and S-morph Primula plants using RNA extraction and quantitative RT-PCR.
source_span: To determine gene expression in different floral organs , recently opened flowers of L- and S-morph plants were manually dissected and the tissue frozen immediately in liquid nitrogen . Total RNA was extracted using RNeasy Plant Mini Kit ( Qiagen ) . Reverse transcription was performed using oligo ( dT ) priming and SuperScript III ( Invitrogen ) . Quantitative RT-PCR was performed using the Bioline SensiMix SYBR Low-ROX kit and a Roche LightCycler LC480 .
selection_reasoning: Key method for assessing gene expression relevant to the study's main question.

fact: Castasterone, a brassinosteroid hormone, was detected in styles of L-morph Primula plants but was virtually undetectable in styles of S-morph plants.
source_span: While castasterone was readily detectable in styles of L-morph plants , but virtually undetectable in styles of S-morph plants , brassinolide was undetectable in styles of either morph .
selection_reasoning: Principal finding linking hormone levels to floral morphs, central to the study's biological mechanism.

fact: Brassinolide was undetectable in styles of both L- and S-morph Primula plants.
source_span: While castasterone was readily detectable in styles of L-morph plants , but virtually undetectable in styles of S-morph plants , brassinolide was undetectable in styles of either morph .
selection_reasoning: Clarifies which brassinosteroids are present or absent, important for understanding hormone involvement.

fact: Young flower buds of Primula vulgaris and Primula forbesii were treated with homobrassinolide to test the effect of brassinosteroids on floral organ size.
source_span: For the brassinosteroid treatment experiment , young flower buds of commercially grown P . vulgaris and of P . forbesii were injected every other day with solutions containing 1 nM , 100 nM or 10 μM homobrassinolide ( dissolved in DMSO ) , 0 . 1% Tween-20 or a mock solution containing 0 . 1% DMSO ( corresponding to the DMSO concentration in the solution with 10 μM homobrassinolide ) , 0 . 1% Tween .
selection_reasoning: Describes a key experimental approach to test the functional role of brassinosteroids.

fact: Virus-induced gene silencing (VIGS) was used to silence CYP734A50 in Primula forbesii to study its functional role.
source_span: To prepare vectors for virus-induced gene silencing ( VIGS ) , a fragment containing exon 4 and exon 5 of CYP734A50 in P . forbesii was cloned and inserted into vector TRV2 ( Liu et al . , 2002 ) to produced TRV2-CYP734A50 .
selection_reasoning: Indicates a key method used to investigate gene function, relevant to main findings.

fact: Bone morphogenic protein (BMP) signalling helps maintain pluripotency and promotes mesodermal differentiation over neural differentiation in pluripotent cells.
source_span: Bone morphogenic protein ( BMP ) signalling contributes towards maintenance of pluripotency and favours mesodermal over neural fates upon differentiation
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential background on BMP's dual role in pluripotency and lineage choice, central to the study's motivation and findings.

fact: BMP regulates differentiation by preventing the downregulation of the cell adhesion molecule E-Cadherin (Cdh1), which normally decreases during early neural and mesodermal differentiation.
source_span: We report that BMP regulates differentiation by blocking downregulation of Cdh1 , an event that accompanies the earliest stages of neural and mesodermal differentiation
selection_reasoning: This identifies a key mechanism by which BMP controls differentiation, a principal finding of the study.

fact: Loss of Cdh1 is a necessary step for pluripotent cells to differentiate into neural or mesodermal lineages.
source_span: We find that loss of Cdh1 is a limiting requirement for differentiation of pluripotent cells
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a critical biological requirement for differentiation, central to understanding BMP's role.

fact: Experimental suppression of Cdh1 activity can overcome the BMP-imposed block to differentiation in pluripotent cells.
source_span: experimental suppression of Cdh1 activity rescues the BMP-imposed block to differentiation
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates the functional importance of Cdh1 in mediating BMP's effects on differentiation.

fact: BMP acts before and independently of Cdh1 to prime pluripotent cells for mesoderm differentiation, reinforcing the block to neural differentiation.
source_span: BMP acts prior to and independently of Cdh1 to prime pluripotent cells for mesoderm differentiation , thus helping to reinforce the block to neural differentiation
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the timing and dual role of BMP in lineage priming and differentiation control.

fact: BMP signalling maintains high levels of Cdh1, which helps protect the pluripotent state while promoting mesodermal over neural differentiation.
source_span: BMP maintains high levels of Cdh1 , which help to protect the pluripotent state , whilst imposing a posterior identity that ultimately favours mesodermal over neural differentiation
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the integrated role of BMP in maintaining pluripotency and directing lineage choice.

fact: The BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in pluripotent epiblast cells during early development and contributes to blocking differentiation by maintaining Cdh1 expression.
source_span: We find an unanticipated ability of BMP/Id to block differentiation by maintaining the expression of the cell adhesion molecule E-Cadherin ( Cdh1 )
selection_reasoning: This links a specific BMP target gene to the mechanism controlling differentiation, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Id1 imposes a proximal posterior identity on epiblast cells, priming them for mesodermal fates while transiently restraining overt mesoderm differentiation.
source_span: BMP acts through Id1 to impose a proximal posterior identity on epiblast cells , priming them for mesodermal fates whilst transiently restraining them from overt mesoderm differentiation
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how BMP/Id1 signaling influences early patterning and lineage priming.

fact: The transition from pluripotency to lineage commitment depends on both extrinsic signals like BMP and morphogenetic events controlling cell receptivity to differentiation cues.
source_span: We conclude that differentiation depends not only on exposure to appropriate extrinsic cues but also on morphogenetic events that control receptivity to those differentiation cues , and we explain how a key pluripotency signal , BMP , feeds into this control mechanism
selection_reasoning: This provides a conceptual framework for understanding how BMP integrates signaling and morphogenetic control during differentiation.

fact: BMP signalling is required for mesoderm formation in vivo and is commonly used to induce mesoderm from embryonic stem cells in vitro.
source_span: BMP signalling is also required for the formation of mesoderm in vivo ... and BMP is commonly used to induce mesoderm from embryonic stem ( ES ) cells
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the biological and experimental relevance of BMP in mesoderm differentiation.

fact: The mechanisms by which BMP influences neural and mesodermal specification, including the role of Id proteins, were previously unclear and are addressed in this study.
source_span: It has been known for many years that BMP signalling protects pluripotency and suppresses neural specification ... but the underlying mechanisms remain unclear ... We set out to examine more closely the effects of BMP and Id1 on neural and mesoderm differentiation
selection_reasoning: This states the knowledge gap and study motivation, important for framing the research question.

fact: The BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in a subpopulation of pluripotent epiblast cells prior to overt mesoderm differentiation in mouse embryos.
source_span: We conclude that the direct BMP target gene Id1 is expressed in a subpopulation of Nanog+ epiblast cells prior to overt mesoderm differentiation, in addition to its previously described expression in migrating mesoderm (Jen et al., 1997).
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a key gene expression pattern relevant to early embryonic development and BMP signaling, central to the study's focus.

fact: Id1 expression in E6.5 mouse embryos is highest in the proximal epiblast regions fated for mesoderm and surface ectoderm but not neural fates.
source_span: Id1V is readily detectable at E6.5 throughout the proximal epiblast with expression declining more distally. The highest levels of Id1V therefore mark regions of the epiblast fated for mesoderm and surface ectoderm but not neural fates (Cajal et al., 2012; Li et al., 2013).
selection_reasoning: This spatial expression pattern provides important background on the developmental context of Id1 relevant to the study.

fact: The majority of Id1-positive cells in the proximal epiblast co-express the pluripotency marker Nanog, indicating Id1 is expressed in pluripotent cells.
source_span: The majority (>65%) of Id1V+ cells in the proximal epiblast co-express Nanog, with this proportion increasing to >80% within the posterior regions of the proximal epiblast.
selection_reasoning: This finding links Id1 expression to pluripotency, a key biological insight for understanding BMP's role.

fact: Most Id1-positive cells do not express the mesoderm marker T at E6.5, indicating they are not yet specified or committed to mesoderm fate.
source_span: In contrast, the majority (>80%) of Id1V+ cells do not express T, indicating that they are neither specified nor committed to a mesodermal fate at this stage of development.
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the developmental state of Id1-expressing cells, important for interpreting BMP/Id1 function.

fact: The mesoderm marker T is expressed in cells that also co-express Nanog at E6.5, indicating T marks both differentiating mesoderm and pluripotent epiblast cells with posterior identity.
source_span: We also confirmed that most (>80%) of the T+ cells at this stage co-express Nanog, confirming that T marks not only differentiating mesoderm but also pluripotent epiblast cells with a proximal posterior positional identity (Osorno et al., 2012).
selection_reasoning: This fact refines understanding of marker expression and cell identity relevant to the study's developmental focus.

fact: BMP4 signaling blocks neural differentiation and maintains pluripotency in embryonic stem cells cultured under serum-free conditions without other growth factors.
source_span: We examined the effect of BMP4 on cells cultured in serum-free conditions in the absence of any other exogenous growth factors. This system allows us to monitor the kinetics as well as the direction of differentiation. We used Sox1-GFP reporter ES cells to confirm that BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key experimental approach and a principal finding about BMP4's role in cell fate decisions.

fact: BMP4 permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T but prevents progression to overt mesoderm differentiation in embryonic stem cells.
source_span: BMP4 permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T, as expected. However, despite expressing T, BMP-treated cells do not progress to overt mesoderm differentiation.
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals a nuanced role of BMP4 in early differentiation, central to the study's conclusions.

fact: BMP signaling maintains expression of the epithelial marker Cdh1 during differentiation of pluripotent cells, delaying epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and overt mesoderm differentiation while permitting surface ectoderm differentiation.
source_span: BMP signaling maintains Cdh1 expression during differentiation of pluripotent cells. We propose that BMP imposes a posterior positional identity whilst delaying both EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation but permitting surface ectoderm differentiation.
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight links BMP signaling to regulation of cell state transitions important for embryonic development.

fact: BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1 and permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T in mouse embryonic stem cells.
source_span: We used Sox1-GFP reporter ES cells ( Ying et al . , 2003b ) to confirm that BMP4 blocks the upregulation of the early neural marker Sox1 ( Figure 2B ) and permits expression of the primitive streak/early mesoderm marker T ( Figure 2C , D ) , as expected ( Ying et al . , 2003a ) .
selection_reasoning: This establishes BMP4's role in directing cell fate away from neural differentiation and towards a mesoderm-primed state, a core finding relevant to the study's focus.

fact: Despite expressing the mesoderm marker T, BMP4-treated cells do not progress to overt mesoderm differentiation and retain epithelial marker Cdh1 for at least five days.
source_span: However , despite expressing T , BMP-treated cells do not progress to overt mesoderm differentiation . Differentiation of epiblast to mesoderm is characterised by the loss of Oct4 and Cdh1 , whereas BMP4-treated cells remain uniformly Cdh1+ at least for the first 5 days of BMP treatment ( Figure 2B–D ) .
selection_reasoning: This highlights that BMP4 induces a mesoderm-primed but not fully differentiated mesoderm state, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: BMP4 delays downregulation of Oct4 and prevents upregulation of epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) markers during early differentiation.
source_span: Furthermore , in the presence of BMP4 , downregulation of Oct4 is delayed , and markers that characterise EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation are not upregulated within the 5-day time frame of this experiment ( Figure 2D ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how BMP4 maintains cells in a less differentiated, epithelial-like state, central to understanding BMP4's effect.

fact: BMP4 imposes a posterior positional identity marked by T expression coexisting with epithelial marker Cdh1, rather than directly driving mesoderm commitment.
source_span: We therefore considered whether the ability of BMP4 to upregulate T may represent an effect on positional identity within the epiblast rather than a direct effect to drive mesoderm commitment . In support of this idea , we found that in the presence of BMP4 , T is coexpressed with Cdh1 ( Figure 2C ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the nature of BMP4's effect on cell identity, a key conceptual advance.

fact: A subpopulation of BMP4-treated cells differentiate into Cdh1+ Tcfap2a (AP2α)+ epithelial cells resembling early surface ectoderm.
source_span: Not all cells persist in a T+ Cdh1+ state: a subpopulation of cells ( typically between 10 and 25% ) are able to differentiate into a Cdh1+ Tcfap2a ( AP2α ) + epithelial cell type similar to early surface ectoderm ( Mitchell et al . , 1991 ) ( Figure 2C ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding links BMP4 treatment to surface ectoderm differentiation, expanding the understanding of BMP4's differentiation outcomes.

fact: Exogenous BMP4 promotes surface ectoderm differentiation when added to explants from the E7.0 mouse epiblast.
source_span: This is consistent with the recent finding that exogenous BMP4 promotes surface ectoderm differentiation when added to explants from the E7 . 0 mouse epiblast ( Li et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the biological relevance of BMP4's effect on surface ectoderm differentiation in vivo.

fact: BMP4-treated cells either remain in a Cdh1+ posterior-epiblast-like state or differentiate into Cdh1+ surface-ectoderm-like cells, showing delayed differentiation.
source_span: BMP-treated cells are delayed in their differentiation and either persist in a Cdh1+ posterior-epiblast like state or ultimately differentiate into Cdh1+ surface-ectoderm-like cells ( Figure 2E ) .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the dual fate outcomes under BMP4 treatment, a principal finding.

fact: The BMP target gene Id1 maintains Cdh1 expression and delays epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition during differentiation of pluripotent cells.
source_span: We next asked whether the BMP target gene Id1 mediates the effects of BMP to maintain Cdh1 expression during differentiation of pluripotent cells . ... Under serum-free monolayer conditions in the absence of exogenous growth factors , Id1 delays the loss of Cdh1 and suppresses the upregulation of EMT markers Cdh2 , Zeb1 and Zeb2 ( Thiery et al . , 2009 ) ( Figure 3A ) .
selection_reasoning: Identifying Id1 as a mediator of BMP4's effects is a key mechanistic insight relevant to the study's conclusions.

fact: Induction of Id1 expression blocks neural induction and maintains a mesoderm-primed positional identity in embryonic stem cells.
source_span: We first confirmed that dox-mediated induction of Id1 is able to block neural induction as expected ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1 ) ... We propose that the BMP target gene Id1 imposes a posterior positional identity whilst delaying both EMT and overt mesoderm differentiation .
selection_reasoning: This links Id1 function to BMP4's role in controlling cell fate, a central conclusion.

fact: Cells overexpressing Id1 preferentially differentiate into mesoderm rather than neuroectoderm or endoderm under neural differentiation conditions.
source_span: Id1 overexpressing cells differentiate preferentially into mesoderm rather than neuroectoderm or endoderm . qRT-PCR analysis of cell lines stably transfected with loxP flanked Id1 transgene ( Id1 ) or after Cre-mediated removal of the Id1 transgene ( Id1 reverted ) undergoing neural differentiation in N2B27 .
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates the functional consequence of Id1 expression on lineage choice, important for the study's implications.

fact: Id1 promotes the upregulation of T, a marker of posterior epiblast and primitive streak, while delaying the downregulation of epiblast markers Oct4, Fgf5, and Otx2 during differentiation.
source_span: Id1 promotes the upregulation of T , a marker of posterior epiblast and primitive streak ( Blum et al . , 1992; Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson , 2005 ) , but delays the downregulation of the epiblast markers Oct4 , Fgf5 and Otx2 ( Figure 3B ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key molecular effect of Id1 on cell differentiation relevant to the study's main question about Id1's role in epiblast identity and differentiation.

fact: Id1 favors a posterior proximal epiblast identity by promoting Nanog re-expression and reducing Sox2 expression, markers of posterior and anterior pluripotent epiblast respectively.
source_span: In keeping with this idea , Id1 favours the re-expression of Nanog , which marks posterior pluripotent epiblast , and Id1 also reduces expression of Sox2 , which marks anterior pluripotent epiblast ( Osorno et al . , 2012 ) ( Figure 3B ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the specific epiblast regional identity influenced by Id1, central to understanding its biological role.

fact: Id1 delays differentiation by maintaining T+ cells that coexpress Cdh1 and Oct4, indicating these cells resemble early posterior epiblast cells rather than differentiated mesoderm.
source_span: In further support of the idea that Id1 delays differentiation , we used quantitative immunofluorescence to demonstrate that in the presence of exogenous Id1 , T+ cells remain predominantly Cdh1+ and >90% of them coexpress Oct4 ( Figure 3D , E ) . These T+ cells are therefore unlikely to be differentiated mesoderm cells and are more likely to be equivalent to the T+ cells in the proximal epiblast of the early embryo that have not yet entered the primitive streak ( Rivera-Pérez and Magnuson , 2005 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides mechanistic insight into how Id1 maintains a primed pluripotent state, a principal finding.

fact: Constitutive overexpression of Id1 in embryonic stem cells completely blocks neurogenesis and delays downregulation of Oct4 under neural differentiation conditions.
source_span: Unlike the dox-inducible system , this constitutive expression system is sufficient to completely block neurogenesis throughout the culture ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1G ) . Constitutive Id1 expression is sufficient to delay the downregulation of Oct4 ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2 ) and to block neurogenesis ( Figure 3—figure supplement 1G ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a key experimental approach and principal finding about Id1's functional effect on neural differentiation.

fact: Id1-overexpressing cells eventually differentiate predominantly into mesoderm rather than neuroectoderm or endoderm, even under neural differentiation conditions.
source_span: However , it is not sufficient to completely block differentiation . Id1-overexpressing cells eventually differentiate predominantly into mesoderm rather than neurectoderm or endoderm , even under neural differentiation conditions ( Figure 3—figure supplement 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the differentiation bias imposed by Id1, important for understanding its biological significance.

fact: The BMP target gene Id1 maintains Cdh1 expression and a primed pluripotent state similar to post-implantation epiblast, imposing a proximal posterior (T+ Nanog+) epiblast identity primed for mesoderm differentiation.
source_span: Taken together , these data suggest that the BMP target gene Id1 does not drive overt mesoderm differentiation but rather maintains Cdh1 and helps to maintain a primed pluripotent state similar to that of the post-implantation epiblast , whilst imposing a proximal posterior ( T+ Nanog+ ) epiblast identity that is primed for mesoderm differentiation .
selection_reasoning: This fact integrates the study's main conclusions about Id1's role linking BMP signaling to epiblast identity and differentiation potential.

fact: Cdh1 expression is downregulated in synchrony with Oct4 during neural differentiation both in vitro and in vivo.
source_span: We confirmed a similar correlation between loss of Oct4 and downregulation of Cdh1 in vivo: Cdh1 and Oct4 protein expression decline in synchrony within the developing neuroepithelium ( Figure 4C , D ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides important background and mechanistic insight into the relationship between pluripotency and neural differentiation relevant to the study.

fact: Loss of Cdh1 expression is closely associated with the upregulation of early neural markers during differentiation at the single cell level.
source_span: We confirmed that Cdh1 is largely absent from cells that have upregulated early neural markers ( Figure 4A ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the link between Cdh1 downregulation and neural differentiation, a key biological process studied.

fact: The earliest stages of neural differentiation in embryonic stem cells are accompanied by the downregulation of the cell adhesion molecule Cdh1.

selection_reasoning: This fact establishes a key biological change during neural differentiation, central to the study's focus.

fact: A subpopulation of embryonic stem cells that fail to downregulate Cdh1 during neural differentiation also fail to become neural cells.
source_span: We observed that the subpopulation of cells that fail to respond appropriately to a neural environment by upregulating Sox1-GFP also fail to downregulate Cdh1, either remaining as Oct4+ Cdh1+ undifferentiated cells or differentiating into Cdh1+ Krt8+ epithelial cells.

fact: Transient blocking of Cdh1 activity at the start of neural differentiation accelerates the loss of pluripotency marker Oct4 and promotes neural marker Sox1 expression in embryonic stem cells.

selection_reasoning: This experimental manipulation shows that Cdh1 activity limits neural differentiation, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Transient loss of Cdh1 adhesive function is sufficient to drive embryonic stem cells efficiently towards neural differentiation.
source_span: This indicates that transient loss of Cdh1 activity at the very start of the differentiation process is sufficient to drive ES cells efficiently towards neural differentiation.
selection_reasoning: This conclusion highlights the functional importance of Cdh1 downregulation in neural differentiation.

fact: At P9, glutamate triggers Müller cell calcium transients primarily through activation of AMPA-type ionotropic glutamate receptors, with a modest contribution from metabotropic glutamate receptors.
source_span: Application of exogenous L-glutamate reliably evoked MC calcium transients ( Figure 3A–C; Video 3 ) . These responses were not blocked by atropine , ruling out the possibility that this agonist acted indirectly by stimulating release of ACh from amacrine cells . L-glutamate-evoked MC calcium transients were significantly reduced by a cocktail of ionotropic glutamate receptor antagonists ( iGluR: 20 μM AMPA/kainate receptor antagonist DNQX , 50 μM NMDA receptor antagonist D-AP5; Figure 3D ) , but were only slightly reduced by a mixture of metabotropic glutamate receptor antagonists ( mGluR: 8 μM LY341495 , 100 μM MCPG , 100 μM MTEP; Figure 3D ) . Blocking AMPA receptors produced substantial but incomplete inhibition of the L-glutamate-evoked response , whereas blocking NMDA receptors had no significant effect . These results suggest that glutamate elicits MC calcium transients primarily through activation of AMPA receptors , although a modest contribution of mGluRs is also observed .

selection_reasoning: Identifying a key organism driving community changes during decomposition is central to understanding microbial dynamics and succession.

fact: The nematode bloom during decomposition may be influenced by the closed nature of the mouse graves, which likely prevented entry of nematode predators.

fact: Consistent shifts in the presence and abundance of specific bacterial and microbial eukaryotic taxa occur during known stages of decomposition, suggesting microbial succession can be used to estimate postmortem interval (PMI).
source_span: Because consistent shifts in the presence and abundance of specific bacterial and eukaryotic taxa occurred during known stages of decomposition , these data suggested that succession of bacterial and microbial eukaryotic communities may be used to estimate PMI .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking microbial succession to forensic applications.

fact: A Random Forests machine learning model regressing known postmortem interval on taxon relative abundances was used to estimate PMI from microbial community data.
source_span: By regressing known postmortem interval directly on the taxon relative abundances using a Random Forests model . Random Forests is a machine learning technique that creates random decision trees based on subsets of the features ( e . g . , taxa ) in the data , then chooses the subsets of features that are best able to classify samples into predefined groups using only part of the data .
selection_reasoning: Describes the key analytical method used to estimate PMI from microbial data.

fact: Temporal changes in microbial communities on the skin of the head allowed estimation of PMI within approximately 3.3 days mean absolute error.
source_span: We discovered that the temporal change in microbial communities of the skin of the head allowed us to estimate PMI within as little as 3 . 30 +/− 2 . 52 days ( mean absolute error +/− standard deviation ) .

fact: Microbial data from skin and soil sites were more informative for estimating PMI than data from the abdominal cavity.
source_span: For both 16S and 18S datasets , skin and soil sites were more informative for estimating PMI than data from the abdominal cavity .
selection_reasoning: Identifies which sample sites provide the most useful microbial information for PMI estimation.

fact: Variability in the timing of major microbial community shifts in the abdominal cavity reduced the usefulness of abdominal data for estimating PMI.

fact: Combining bacterial (16S) and microbial eukaryotic (18S) datasets resulted in the best estimates of PMI, although the improvement over individual datasets was not statistically significant.

fact: Certain bacterial taxa, such as those in the Order Rhizobiales, were among the most important predictors for estimating PMI at each sample site.
source_span: For bacteria , taxa in the Order Rhizobiales were among the most important predictive taxa at each sample site .

fact: The nematode genus Oscheius was the most important microbial eukaryotic taxon for PMI prediction at skin and abdominal sites.

fact: Microbial community ecology of decomposing corpses has potential to be developed into a complementary forensic tool for estimating postmortem interval (PMI).

fact: Combining bacterial 16S and microbial eukaryotic 18S sequencing datasets resulted in the best estimates of postmortem interval (PMI).

fact: Certain bacterial taxa, such as those in the Order Rhizobiales, and fungal taxa, such as those in the family Boletales, are important predictors of PMI at different sample sites.

fact: A small number of highly predictive microbial taxa (5–10 taxa) can provide approximately the same accuracy in PMI prediction as models using all taxa.

selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a practical implication for forensic microbial analysis by simplifying predictive models.

fact: The study used a laboratory experiment with 40 mice decomposing on soil graves under controlled conditions to generate microbial time-series data for PMI estimation.

selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental model and setting used to generate the data supporting the study's conclusions.

fact: This study provides the first bacterial high-throughput sequence time-series dataset for the abdominal cavity and gravesoil, and the first microbial eukaryotic high-throughput sequence time-series dataset for the abdominal cavity, gravesoil, and skin sites of a decomposing animal.
source_span: We have provided the first bacterial high-throughput sequence time-series dataset for the abdominal cavity and gravesoil as well as the first microbial eukaryotic high-throughput sequence time-series dataset for the abdominal cavity, gravesoil, and skin sites of a decomposing animal.

fact: The approach of using microbial community data for PMI estimation has advantages including declining DNA sequencing costs and ease of swab-based sampling at crime scenes.

fact: Environmental factors such as temperature, moisture, soil type, and soil texture likely affect postmortem microbial communities and thus influence PMI estimation accuracy.

It is likely that these parameters will affect postmortem microbial communities.

fact: Future studies are needed to determine how environmental and host factors influence microbial community changes during decomposition to develop PMI estimation methods admissible in criminal justice.

Consequently, the relationship between these parameters, decomposition, and postmortem microbial communities must be understood to develop a method to estimate PMI that is admissible as physical evidence within the criminal justice system.

fact: The study used a rigorous leave-one-out cross-validation approach to evaluate the predictive strength of microbial community models for PMI estimation.

fact: Microbial communities were sampled from mouse skin, abdominal cavity, and surrounding soil during decomposition to study microbial succession.

fact: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are critical ionotropic glutamate receptors involved in synaptic strength and plasticity in the brain.
source_span: The position and dynamics of the two major ionotropic glutamate receptors ( iGluRs ) , α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid receptors ( AMPARs ) and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor ( NMDARs ) , are critical for synaptic strength .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological importance of AMPARs, which is essential for understanding the study's motivation.

fact: It is unclear what mechanisms limit AMPAR entry into and exit out of post-synaptic densities (PSDs) under normal conditions.
source_span: Despite much elegant work , it is still unclear what mechanisms limit AMPAR entry into and exit out of PSDs ( Malinow and Malenka , 2002 ) ( Park et al . , 2004 ) ( Wang et al . , 2008 ) .
selection_reasoning: This knowledge gap motivates the research question addressed by the study.

fact: Previous studies using large quantum dots (bQDs) suggested that 50–80% of AMPARs are extrasynaptic and highly mobile.
source_span: Studies of AMPARs tagged with bQDs led to the conclusion that 50–80% of AMPARs are extrasynaptic and highly mobile ( Groc et al . , 2007; Opazo et al . , 2010 ) .
selection_reasoning: This prior finding sets the context for the study's investigation into AMPAR localization and mobility.

fact: The large extrasynaptic pool of mobile AMPARs was proposed to result from slow entry of AMPARs into PSDs due to limited availability of 'slots' in PSDs.
source_span: This significant highly mobile pool of extrasynaptic AMPARs has been proposed to exist because of the slow rate that extrasynaptic AMPARs enter PSDs . This slow rate of motion and accumulation of extra-synaptic AMPARs is thought to occur because of the limited availability of ‘slots’ in PSDs ( See Figure 1a , route 3 ) ( Shi et al . , 2001; Opazo et al . , 2012 ) . Slots are defined as placeholders for AMPARs in PSDs ( Malinow et al . , 2000 ) .
selection_reasoning: This hypothesis is central to the study's aim to test AMPAR entry dynamics into PSDs.

fact: Using super-resolution microscopy, the study examined how fluorophore size and photostability affect AMPAR trafficking inside and outside PSDs in rat neurons.
source_span: Using super-resolution microscopy , we examined how fluorophore size and photostability affected AMPAR trafficking outside of , and within , post-synaptic densities ( PSDs ) from rats .
selection_reasoning: This describes the high-level method used to address the research question.

fact: Organic fluorescent dyes (~4 nm) and small quantum dots (~10 nm) labeled more than 90% of AMPARs as diffusing in confined nanodomains within PSDs that were stable for 15 minutes or longer.
source_span: We find that >90% of AMPARs labeled with fluorescent dyes or sQDs were diffusing in confined nanodomains in PSDs , which were stable for 15 min or longer .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding that contrasts with previous observations using larger probes.

fact: Less than 10% of AMPARs labeled with small quantum dots were extrasynaptic and highly mobile.
source_span: Less than 10% of sQD-AMPARs were extrasynaptic and highly mobile .
selection_reasoning: This finding challenges the previously reported large extrasynaptic mobile AMPAR pool.

fact: In contrast, 90–95% of AMPARs labeled with big quantum dots were extrasynaptic, consistent with previous observations.
source_span: In contrast , 5–10% of bQD-AMPARs were in PSDs and 90–95% were extrasynaptic as previously observed .
selection_reasoning: This confirms that probe size affects observed AMPAR localization and mobility.

fact: The study's findings suggest that AMPARs rapidly enter stable nanodomains within PSDs with lifetimes longer than 15 minutes and do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes.
source_span: Contrary to the hypothesis that AMPAR entry is limited by the occupancy of open PSD ‘slots’ , our findings suggest that AMPARs rapidly enter stable ‘nanodomains’ in PSDs with lifetime >15 min , and do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes .
selection_reasoning: This is the key conclusion that revises the existing model of AMPAR trafficking.

fact: Synaptic plasticity, the leading cellular correlate of learning and memory, depends on changes in synapses involving AMPAR trafficking.
source_span: A major goal of cellular and molecular neuroscience is to characterize how synapses change during synaptic plasticity , the leading cellular correlate of learning and memory ( Volk et al . , 2015; Huganir and Nicoll , 2013; Kneussel and Hausrat , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides the broader significance and motivation for studying AMPAR dynamics.

fact: Determining whether AMPA receptors (AMPARs) are located inside or outside synapses has been difficult due to limitations in microscopy resolution, three-dimensional structure, probe specificity, and photostability.
source_span: Determining whether AMPARs or other neurotransmitter receptors are synaptic (outside PSDs) or extrasynaptic (inside PSDs) has been difficult because of four factors: (1) Synapses are nanometer in scale below the diffraction limit of visible microscopy; (2) Most microscopy has been limited to two-dimensions, where in reality, the dimensions are three-dimensional; (3) Recombinantly tagged imaging probes cannot readily distinguish intracellular vs. cell-surface receptors; (4) Probe photostability limits the localization precision and the length of image acquisition, particularly for single-molecule studies.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the main technical challenge motivating the study and is essential for understanding the research question.

fact: This study used 3-dimensional super-resolution microscopy with different-sized fluorescent probes to label cell-surface AMPARs in cultured neurons.
source_span: Here we use 3-dimensional super-resolution microscopy on cell-surface AMPARs labeled with different-sized fluorescent probes—bQDs (>20 nm), small quantum dots (sQD ≈10 nm) or organic fluorophore (≈4 nm) in cultured neurons.
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is central to the study's approach and aligns with the abstract-level description of what was done.

fact: More than 90% of AMPARs labeled with organic fluorescent dyes or small quantum dots are found within postsynaptic densities (PSDs), with less than 10% being highly mobile and extrasynaptic.
source_span: We find that > 90% of AMPARs labeled with organic fluorescent dyes or sQDs are found in PSDs. Less than 10% of these labeled AMPARs are highly mobile and extrasynaptic.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about AMPAR localization and mobility that contrasts with previous contradictory results.

fact: When AMPARs are labeled with big quantum dots (bQDs), nearly all (90–95%) appear highly mobile and extrasynaptic, likely because bQDs are too large to enter synaptic clefts.
source_span: However, when AMPARs are labeled with bQDs, virtually all AMPARs (90–95%) are highly mobile and extrasynaptic, presumably because bQDs are sterically hindered from entry into synaptic clefts.
selection_reasoning: This finding explains why previous studies using bQDs may have mischaracterized AMPAR mobility and location.

fact: The study concludes that mobile AMPARs enter PSDs and do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes as previously thought based on bQD labeling studies.
source_span: We conclude that mobile AMPARs enter PSDs and do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes as previously observed in studies using the AMPARs labeled with bQDs.
selection_reasoning: This is a key conclusion that revises prior understanding of AMPAR distribution.

fact: AMPARs diffuse within stable nanodomains inside PSDs that may regulate their access to presynaptic glutamate release.
source_span: Instead AMPARs are found to diffuse within surprisingly stable ‘nanodomains’ confining AMPARs to sites within PSDs that may regulate access to presynaptic glutamate release.
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight is a principal finding with implications for synaptic function.

fact: The study used Homer1c tagged with fluorescent proteins as a super-resolution marker to better resolve PSD dimensions.
source_span: To better resolve PSD dimensions, we used 3-D super-resolution imaging of a PSD protein, Homer1c.
selection_reasoning: This methodological detail is important for understanding how PSD localization was determined.

fact: The uPAINT technique with organic dyes selectively labels cell-surface AMPARs and allows relatively long observation times due to dye photostability.
source_span: One advantage of the uPAINT technique using organic dyes compared to sptPALM is that the uPAINT technique only labels cell-surface receptors if cell-impermeable organic dyes are used. By choosing fairly photostable dyes, uPAINT also allows a relatively long time (limited by the photobleaching) for the motion to be measured.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the rationale for using uPAINT and organic dyes, relevant to the study's methods and data quality.

selection_reasoning: This establishes the synaptic localization of AMPARs, a key biological context for the study.

fact: Super-resolution imaging with organic fluorophores shows that AMPA receptors are predominantly localized at synaptic regions.
source_span: Thus , by all three techniques ( with sQDs , with live- and fixed-neurons labeled with organic fluorophores ) we find that the localization of AMPA receptors is predominantly at the synaptic regions .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about AMPAR localization relevant to the study's main question.

fact: Typically, there is one nanodomain of AMPA receptors per synapse, although multiple nanodomains can exist.

selection_reasoning: This describes a key structural feature of AMPAR organization at synapses.

fact: Heat maps plotting AMPAR diffusion constants versus trajectory range show that receptors with slow diffusion and limited movement are constrained by postsynaptic density proteins.
source_span: In general , the lower left-hand corner of the map shows the diffusion of AMPARs where the trajectory range is limited , constrained by PSD ( or slot ) proteins ( Shi et al . , 2001; Opazo et al . , 2012 ) , and the diffusion coefficient of these receptors was slow; those in the upper right-hand corner are not constrained and move faster .
selection_reasoning: This explains the relationship between AMPAR mobility and synaptic protein constraints, central to interpreting diffusion data.

fact: Using big quantum dots (bQDs) to label AMPARs shows large pools of receptors outside synapses with mostly fast diffusion one day after transfection.
source_span: We used bQDs and were able to reproduce results from previous work showing large pools of receptors outside of the synapses . At post-transfection day one there are primarily two peaks in the heat map in Figure 3a with the majority ( 73% of all AMPAR , peakα ) having a fairly fast diffusion constant ( 10-1 . 25=0 . 056 μm2/s ) with about a ~ 1 . 3 μm travel length ...
selection_reasoning: This finding contrasts with other labeling methods and is important for understanding AMPAR distribution and mobility.

fact: On post-transfection day 3, the fraction of AMPARs with slow diffusion increases and the fraction with free diffusion decreases when labeled with bQDs.
source_span: On post-transfection day 3 , the heat map in Figure 3b is significantly changed with a broader distribution of the diffusion coefficients and trajectory range ... the population of free diffusion ( i . e . the α peak ) has significantly decreased , while the population of slow diffusion ( i . e . the β peak ) has increased .
selection_reasoning: This temporal change in AMPAR mobility is a key observation about receptor dynamics.

fact: The change in AMPAR mobility over days after transfection when labeled with bQDs may be due to cross-linking by multivalent bQDs or increased extracellular matrix.
source_span: Because we observed a change in mobility we reasoned that this could be due to cross-linking of AMPAR by the multivalent bQD , or due to an increase in the amount of extracellular matrix . Both factors are known to influence the diffusion of surface-expressed AMPARs ( Chamma et al . , 2016; Frischknecht et al . , 2009 ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides a mechanistic explanation for observed changes in receptor mobility, relevant for interpreting results.

fact: Labeling AMPARs with small quantum dots (sQDs) shows no accumulation of large pools of extrasynaptic receptors and reveals largely constrained diffusion within postsynaptic density nanodomains.
source_span: When using sQDs , we found no accumulation of large pools of extra-synaptic receptors . Instead , we found that motion is largely constrained-diffusion in PSD nanodomains .
selection_reasoning: This contrasts with bQD labeling and supports a different model of AMPAR localization and mobility.

fact: Labeling AMPARs with small quantum dots (sQDs) results in mostly constrained diffusion within postsynaptic density (PSD) nanodomains, unlike labeling with big quantum dots (bQDs) which shows more extra-synaptic receptors and faster diffusion.
source_span: When using sQDs , we found no accumulation of large pools of extra-synaptic receptors . Instead , we found that motion is largely constrained-diffusion in PSD nanodomains . The heat maps for the AMPARs labeled with sQDs ( Figure 4 ) are strikingly different from the heat maps for AMPARs labeled with bQDs ( Figure 3 ) .
selection_reasoning: This contrasts two labeling methods and their impact on AMPAR diffusion, a core finding relevant to interpreting receptor localization and mobility.

fact: The size and valency of the probe used to label AMPARs influence the measured diffusion coefficients, with smaller and monovalent probes showing slower diffusion and more constrained receptor movement.
source_span: Results were different depending on which linker was used with the mean diffusion constant varying from 10-2 . 41±0 . 02μm2/s for the SA linker ... 10-2 . 53±0 . 02μm2/s for the GBP linker ... and 10-2 . 59 ± 0 . 02μm2/s for the mSA linker ... These results suggest that both the size as well as the valency of the probe can influence the measurements .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how labeling strategy affects measurement accuracy, important for interpreting experimental results.

fact: Labeling AMPARs with sQDs does not show a time-dependent change in diffusion or trajectory between day 14 and day 16 in vitro, indicating stable receptor behavior over this period.
source_span: We find that labeling with sQD to AMPAR is not a function of DIV , as day 14 is essentially identical to day 16 , for all three ligands used . This says that the diffusion time and trajectory is a not a function of time ...

fact: Approximately 75% of AMPARs labeled with sQDs are localized within 0.5 µm of the PSD marker Homer1c, and 91% are within 1.0 µm, indicating that most AMPARs reside within or near the PSD.
source_span: The histogram shows that 75% of receptors are localized within 0 . 5 µm of Homer1c and 91% within 1 . 0 µm , generally undergoing constrained-diffusion ... This strongly implies that the great majority of AMPARs are within the PSD .
selection_reasoning: This spatial localization is a key biological finding about receptor distribution relevant to synaptic function.

fact: Small organic fluorophores conjugated to streptavidin, such as Atto647N and CF633, label AMPARs with high brightness and photostability, allowing detailed measurement of receptor diffusion in live neurons.
source_span: We labeled AMPARs using SA-Atto647N or SA-CF633 ... Both of these dyes are bright , especially when several dyes are conjugated per streptavidin , and fairly photostable , >50 s observation time ...
selection_reasoning: This describes a key methodological advance enabling improved receptor imaging.

fact: AMPARs labeled with SA-CF633 show more specific labeling and a higher proportion (93%) of receptors constrained in nanodomains compared to those labeled with Atto647N.
source_span: With Atto647N , fitting the trajectories regardless of the diffusion constants , there is 27% of the AMPAR which has longer trajectory range and larger diffusion constants ... these are not much present with the CF633 dye , where we find 93% are constrained in nanodomains .

fact: For AMPARs labeled with SA-CF633, 81% are localized within 0.5 µm of Homer1c and 98% within 1 µm, confirming close association between AMPARs and the PSD.
source_span: Figure 5d indicates that 81% of AMPAR-SA-CF633 is localized within 0 . 5 µm of Homer1c , and this number increases to 98% within 1 μm .
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the spatial relationship between AMPARs and PSD, a principal biological finding.

fact: Native AMPARs labeled with GluA2 antibody-Alexa647 in fixed neurons show that 71% of receptors are localized within close proximity to Homer1c clusters.
source_span: We imaged native AMPARs labeled with antibody ( GluA2 ) -Alexa647 ... the results show that 71% of AMPARs are localized within ...
selection_reasoning: This confirms findings with endogenous receptors, supporting physiological relevance.

fact: AMPARs (AMPA receptors) are closely associated with Homer1c clusters, with the majority localized within 0.5 to 1 µm of Homer1c in both fixed and live neurons.
source_span: For fixed neurons , labeled with Cy3B , the results are similar Figure 5—figure supplement 3 ) : 85% of the receptors are localized within 0 . 5 µm of Homer1c . For any of the dyes chosen , whether fixed or live , they indicate a close association between the Homer1c and AMPARs . We imaged native AMPARs labeled with antibody ( GluA2 ) -Alexa647 and measured the distance between native AMPARs and Homer1c clusters using fixed neurons which we transfected with Homer1-mGeos . As shown in Figure 5e and Figure 5—figure supplement 4 , the results show that 71% of AMPARs are localized within 0 . 5 μm , and 96% within 1 μm .
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the spatial relationship between AMPARs and Homer1c, a key synaptic scaffold protein, which is central to understanding receptor localization in synapses.

fact: The extracellular matrix (ECM) surrounding brain cells can influence the lateral diffusion of surface receptors such as AMPARs in synapses.
source_span: The extra-cellular matrix ( ECM ) is a dense meshwork structure in surrounding brain cells ( Syková and Nicholson , 2008 ) . In neurons , surface receptors such as AMPARs and NMDARs , possibly interact directly or indirectly with the ECM , so that the ECM may affect the lateral diffusion of surface receptors in the synapses and surrounding locations ( Dityatev and Schachner , 2003 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why the ECM is relevant to the study of AMPAR mobility and synaptic function.

fact: Previous studies suggested that enzymatic removal of the ECM increases the diffusion rate of extrasynaptic AMPARs and enhances synaptic receptor exchange, implicating the ECM in regulating short-term synaptic plasticity.
source_span: In particular , one recent study claimed that when the ECM was enzymatically removed , the extra-synaptic AMPA receptors moved at a higher diffusion rate and the exchange of synaptic receptors was increased ( Frischknecht et al . , 2009 ) . They therefore concluded that the ECM might regulate short-term synaptic plasticity .
selection_reasoning: This fact motivates the current study's re-examination of ECM effects on AMPAR diffusion and synaptic plasticity.

fact: Using big quantum dots (bQDs) to label AMPARs, two populations were observed: a fast-moving extrasynaptic population and a slow-moving synaptic population constrained near Homer1c clusters.
source_span: Recall that with bQD , in the presence of ECM ( Figure 3a and dotted lines in Figure 6a ) , we have two populations of AMPAR-bQD: 73% are fast moving ( D ~ 10-1 . 20 ± 0 . 01 = 0 . 063 µm2/s ) over a large distance and 27% are slow moving ( D ~ 10-2 . 0 - 10-3 . 0 µm2/s ) , and constrained to be approximately 0 . 5 μm from the Homer1C .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes key observed AMPAR mobility patterns relevant to synaptic localization and ECM influence.

fact: After enzymatic removal of the ECM, the slow-moving synaptic AMPAR population labeled with bQDs disappeared, leaving only fast-diffusing extrasynaptic AMPARs.
source_span: After ECM removal , we find that the slow-moving ones ( the β peak in Figure 3a or the white dotted line in Figure 6b ) are gone . All of the remaining AMPAR-bQDs freely diffuse outside of synapses on the membrane of dendrites .
selection_reasoning: This finding challenges previous conclusions about ECM regulation of synaptic AMPAR diffusion and highlights the effect of ECM on extrasynaptic receptors.

fact: Small quantum dot (sQD)-labeled AMPAR diffusion is not significantly affected by ECM removal, indicating that these receptors are confined within postsynaptic densities (PSDs) where diffusion is limited by scaffold proteins.
source_span: In contrast , with small qdots , we observe that the average and distribution of the diffusion coefficient of AMPA receptors was almost the same before ( Dave=0 . 015 ± 0 . 0006 µm2/s ) ( Figure 6b , dotted line ) and after ( Dave=0 . 013±0 . 0004 µm2/s ) ECM removal ( Figure 6c ) . Thus , sQD-tagged AMPAR diffusion is not significantly affected by the presence of ECM , presumably because virtually all of these AMPARs are confined to PSDs where diffusion is limited by interactions with PSD scaffold proteins .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies that ECM effects are specific to extrasynaptic AMPARs and that synaptic AMPAR mobility is scaffold-constrained.

fact: The difference in AMPAR diffusion observed with bQD and sQD labeling is explained by the ability of sQDs to enter synaptic clefts and nanodomains within PSDs, unlike bQDs which label mostly extrasynaptic receptors.
source_span: We find that AMPARs labeled with sQDs differ from AMPARs labeled with bQDs in being able to consistently enter synaptic clefts and nanodomains within PSDs .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains methodological differences affecting observed receptor mobility and localization.

fact: sQDs have significantly longer photostability than organic fluorophores, enabling long-term imaging of single AMPAR nanodomains in synapses.
source_span: The feature that distinguishes sQDs from organic fluorophores is the significantly longer photostability of the sQDs compared to the ≈ 1 min lifetime with the organic fluorophores .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the use of sQDs for extended dynamic studies of AMPAR behavior.

fact: Using sQD-labeled AMPARs, nanodomains within PSDs were observed to remain stable in position for at least 15 minutes during repeated imaging.
source_span: The nanodomain of the AMPAR , which was ~ 200 nm , remained in approximately the same position in the synapse for the entire fifteen minutes .
selection_reasoning: This finding provides insight into the stability of AMPAR organization within synapses over time.

fact: AMPAR nanodomains, defined by the constrained area of a single AMPA receptor, are extremely stable in shape and size for at least fifteen minutes.
source_span: This indicates that the nanodomain , defined by the constrained area of a single AMPAR , was extremely stable for the fifteen-minute measurement period .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about the stability of AMPAR nanodomains, relevant to understanding synaptic receptor organization.

fact: AMPAR nanodomains can reposition within the postsynaptic density (PSD) after initially arriving at the PSD.
source_span: These images suggest that AMPARs immediately enter nanodomains as they arrive at PSDs after which the nanodomain can reposition within the PSD to a more stable location .
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals dynamic behavior of AMPAR nanodomains important for synaptic function.

fact: Under basal conditions, AMPA receptors are constantly recycling and moving in and out of synaptic clefts and PSDs through endocytosis and exocytosis.
source_span: With synaptic plasticity , the numbers of AMPARs in PSDs change . Even under basal conditions , the AMPARs are recycling and therefore constantly moving in and out of synaptic clefts and PSDs . AMPAR endocytosis and exocytosis is very likely ongoing at synapses ( Greger and Esteban , 2007 ) and occurs at sites outside of spines ( Anggono and Huganir , 2012 ) or within spines away from PSDs ( Henley et al . , 2011 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the dynamic nature of AMPAR trafficking relevant to synaptic regulation.

fact: Most AMPA receptors are immobilized within PSDs, with approximately 84–97% localized there, and only a small fraction (5–16%) freely diffusing in the dendritic membrane.
source_span: when using when AMPARs that are tagged by significantly smaller fluorophores—sQDs or organic fluorophores ( Figures 4 and 5 ) —they are overwhelmingly in the synapse:~84–97% of AMPA receptors were immobilized within PSDs and only 5–16% were freely diffusing in the dendrite membrane .
selection_reasoning: This key quantitative finding challenges previous views and clarifies AMPAR localization.

fact: Previous studies using large quantum dot tags (bQDs) likely overestimated the pool of mobile extrasynaptic AMPARs because the large size of bQDs prevents AMPARs from entering the synaptic cleft.
source_span: Consequently , we believe that bQDs are too large to enable AMPARs to enter the synaptic cleft . We therefore believe that the previous results with bQDs have been misleading .
selection_reasoning: This addresses a major methodological limitation affecting prior conclusions about AMPAR mobility.

fact: Electrophysiological and imaging studies support that the vast majority of AMPA receptors are localized at synapses rather than extrasynaptic regions in mature neurons.
source_span: First , electrophysiology has estimated the population of receptors in the synapses as well as in the dendrites . Cottrell et al . observed ... less than 1% of AMPA receptors were populated in the extra-synaptic regions after synaptogenesis ... studies using fluorescence microscopy showed that AMPARs ... were co-localized with PSD-95 ... more than 75% of AMPA receptors ... were colocalized with Shank at the synaptic regions ... electron microscopy ... showed that AMPA receptors were localized at synapses ...
selection_reasoning: This background and confirmatory evidence supports the main conclusion about AMPAR synaptic localization.

fact: The study used small quantum dots (sQDs) and organic fluorophores to tag AMPARs, enabling more accurate localization within synapses compared to larger tags.
source_span: when using when AMPARs that are tagged by significantly smaller fluorophores—sQDs or organic fluorophores ( Figures 4 and 5 ) —they are overwhelmingly in the synapse ...
selection_reasoning: This high-level methodological fact explains how the study improved measurement accuracy.

fact: The study found very little evidence for a sizeable pool of mobile extrasynaptic AMPARs in or around dendritic spines.
source_span: In this study , we find very little evidence for a sizeable pool of mobile extrasynaptic receptors in or around the spines .
selection_reasoning: This is a key finding that challenges previous assumptions about AMPAR distribution.

fact: The vast majority of AMPARs rapidly enter postsynaptic densities (PSDs) and are confined to sub-synaptic nanodomains where their diffusion is about 10 times slower than that of free extrasynaptic AMPARs.
source_span: We conclude that the vast majority of AMPARs rapidly enter PSDs and are confined to sub-synaptic diffusion in nanodomains . The diffusion constant is about 10x slower than that of free extrasynaptic AMPARs .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding about AMPAR localization and mobility critical to understanding synaptic function.

fact: AMPARs do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes as previously inferred from studies using AMPARs labeled with big quantum dots (bQDs).
source_span: The AMPARs therefore do not accumulate in extrasynaptic membranes as previously inferred in studies using AMPARs labeled with bQDs .
selection_reasoning: This corrects a prior misconception and is central to the study's main conclusion.

fact: The previously observed highly mobile pool of extrasynaptic AMPARs is an artifact caused by labeling AMPARs with large quantum dots (bQDs).
source_span: We do not observe the highly mobile AMPAR pool when bQDs are replaced by a variety of smaller ( organic and sQDs ) fluorophores and linkers indicating that the highly mobile pool is an artifact of using bQDs attached to the AMPARs .
selection_reasoning: This challenges earlier interpretations and clarifies the impact of labeling methods on observed AMPAR behavior.

fact: The number of synaptic AMPARs is not limited by whether PSD 'slots' are occupied, suggesting other factors regulate AMPAR numbers in PSDs.
source_span: Our conclusion that the number of synaptic AMPARs is not limited by whether PSD slots are occupied suggests that other factors regulate AMPAR numbers in PSDs .
selection_reasoning: This addresses a key mechanistic question about synaptic AMPAR regulation.

fact: Potential factors limiting AMPAR numbers in PSDs include AMPAR exocytosis rate, endocytosis rate, and extracellular matrix barriers that regulate AMPAR membrane diffusion.
source_span: Potential candidates for what limits AMPAR numbers in PSDs are AMPAR exocytosis rate ( Figure 1a , route 1 ) , AMPAR endocytosis rate ( Figure 1a , route 3 ) and/or barriers such as extracellular matrix ( Figure 6 ) that regulate AMPAR membrane diffusion on the membrane ( Figure 1a , route 2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides insight into mechanisms controlling AMPAR synaptic abundance, relevant for understanding synaptic plasticity.

fact: The extracellular matrix (ECM) acts as a diffusion barrier for extrasynaptic AMPARs, affecting their mobility and entry into PSDs.
source_span: Previous studies found that ECM was acting as a diffusion barrier for extrasynaptic AMPARs during their membrane diffusion from extrasynaptic sites to entry into PSDs ( Frischknecht and Gundelfinger , 2012 ) . Our data is consistent with this conclusion ...
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains an important environmental factor influencing AMPAR dynamics.

fact: Removal of the extracellular matrix affects the diffusion of bQD-tagged AMPARs, which are largely extrasynaptic and highly mobile, but does not affect sQD-tagged AMPARs that are mostly within PSDs.
source_span: The diffusion of sQD-tagged AMPARs was not affected by enzymatic removal of the ECM because they are almost all within the PSDs away from the effects of ECM removal . Diffusion of bQD-tagged AMPARs was significantly affected because they are largely highly mobile and extrasynaptic .
selection_reasoning: This experimental finding supports the role of ECM as a diffusion barrier and distinguishes AMPAR populations.

fact: After entry into PSDs, AMPARs remain mobile but are confined within stable sub-synaptic nanodomains that last for more than 15 minutes.
source_span: The picture that emerges from our data is that after entry into PSDs , AMPARs are mobile but constrained within confined sub-synaptic nanodomains that are surprisingly stable , lasting for more than 15 min .
selection_reasoning: This finding reveals the spatial and temporal dynamics of AMPARs critical for synaptic signaling.

fact: The positioning of AMPAR nanodomains within PSDs is likely critical for AMPARs to receive glutamate from presynaptic release sites.
source_span: The positioning of these nanodomains is likely critical for the AMPARs to receive glutamate from the presynaptic release sites ( Tang et al . , 2016; Jeyifous et al . , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This links AMPAR localization to synaptic function and neurotransmission.

fact: Neurons are negatively charged and require coating with both poly-lysine and laminin on fiduciary-patterned coverslips to adhere and be stably cultured.
source_span: We found that dissociated neurons could be stably cultured on fiduciary-patterned coverslips after coating them with both poly-lysine and laminin, sequentially...
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the necessary surface treatment to culture neurons on fiduciary-patterned coverslips, which is essential for the imaging method.

fact: Fiduciary-patterned coverslips coated with poly-lysine and laminin allow stable neuron culture, successful transfection, and super-resolution imaging with reduced stage drift.
source_span: Hence, these coated fiduciary patterned coverslips are very useful to exclude stage drift, allowing for the culture, transfection, and super-resolution imaging and tracking of live neurons.
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the key methodological advance enabling improved imaging of live neurons.

fact: Neurons were transfected with plasmids expressing the post-synaptic protein homer1 fused to photoactivable fluorescent proteins and glutamate receptors tagged for biotinylation to enable super-resolution imaging.
source_span: Here, to demonstrate the method for taking super-resolution fluorescence images, neurons were transfected with two plasmids, one allowing expression of the post-synaptic protein homer1 with a photoactivable fluorescence protein, mGeos or mEOS3.2, and the other allowing expression of glutamate receptors, AMPARs with AP tag to biotinylate.
selection_reasoning: This describes the biological system and labeling strategy used for super-resolution imaging, central to the study.

fact: Glutamate receptors were labeled with quantum dots conjugated to streptavidin or anti-GFP nanobodies to visualize them in super-resolution imaging.
source_span: We then labeled the glutamate receptors using qdots conjugated with either streptavidin or anti-GFP nanobodies.
selection_reasoning: This fact details the labeling method critical for detecting receptors in the imaging experiments.

fact: Infrared illumination allows clear observation of fiduciary markers without interfering with fluorescence imaging of neurons.
source_span: Furthermore, IR illumination... is effective to allow clear observation of uniformly patterned fiduciary markers without affecting the visibility of fluorescence color channels.
selection_reasoning: This explains how stage drift is monitored without compromising fluorescence imaging quality.

fact: Fiduciary markers tracked in the infrared channel enable accurate calculation and correction of stage drift during super-resolution imaging of live neurons.
source_span: The IR camera electronically synchronizes with the visible camera so that the traces of fiduciary markers as recorded by the IR camera accurately calculates the stage drift at the time the cells are imaged. We can then correct the super-resolution cell images for stage drift accordingly.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the key technical improvement in image stability and accuracy.

fact: Using fiduciary markers, stage drift can be controlled within approximately 1 nm in the x and y axes and 15 nm in the z axis during imaging.
source_span: As shown in Figure 6, using fiduciary markers, stage drift can be controlled within an error of around 1 nm for x and y and 15 nm for z.
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the precision improvement in imaging stability, important for super-resolution microscopy.

fact: Chromatic aberration causes color shifts in multi-color super-resolution images, leading to spatial mismatches of about 80 nm between color channels.
source_span: We measured the chromatic aberration between the green (GFP) 530 nm channel and red (RFP) 600 nm channel and 705 nm channels... the average difference in the location of the nanoholes... is about 80 nanometers.
selection_reasoning: This identifies a key imaging artifact that limits accuracy in multi-color super-resolution microscopy.

fact: Most commercial objective lenses correct chromatic aberration only within about 100 nm, which is insufficient for super-resolution microscopy with 20-30 nm spatial resolution.
source_span: Most commercially available objective lenses are designed to optically minimize chromatic aberration... this optical design for objective lenses will corrects within the margin of error of about 100 nm; however... a margin of the error of 100 nm is a significant error.
selection_reasoning: This explains why existing optical corrections are inadequate for the study's imaging needs.

fact: The authors developed a method to correct chromatic aberration within a margin of error of 2 nm using a nano-hole pattern on a silver-coated coverslip.
source_span: Using our method, chromatic aberration can be corrected within a margin of error of 2 nm. We accomplish this... In order to correct chromatic aberration, we made a nano-hole pattern on a silver-coated coverslip.
selection_reasoning: This presents the key technical innovation for improving multi-color super-resolution imaging accuracy.

fact: The error of co-localizations between any two colors in multi-color super-resolution images is expected to be at least approximately 80 nanometers.
source_span: This means that , when obtaining multi-color super-resolution images , the error of co-localizations of any two colors is expected possible to be at least approximately 80 nm .
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to understanding the precision limits of the imaging method used in the study.

fact: The mapping function obtained at the focal point z=0 is accurate enough to correct chromatic aberration in 3D super-resolution images using astigmatism within ±400 nm along the z axis.
source_span: we conclude that when getting 3D images using astigmatism , the mapping function at z=0 is accurate enough to correct chromatic aberration . This is because a 3 D super-resolution image using astigmatism is not discrete along the z axis .
selection_reasoning: This finding supports the validity of the imaging correction method used for 3D super-resolution microscopy.

fact: Primary hippocampal neurons were cultured from embryonic day 18 rats to study AMPA receptor labeling and imaging.

fact: Improving the dissociation kinetics of monomeric streptavidin by slowing its off rate is important to maintain fluorescence intensity during live cell imaging.
source_span: Although extremely high affinity is not needed for labeling live cells , rapid dissociation of bound biotin interferes with detection and measurement because it results in loss of fluorescence intensity over time . As such , improving the dissociation kinetics ( i . e . slowing the off rate koff ) of mSA is important to develop a useful imaging reagent .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the motivation for engineering streptavidin variants to improve imaging stability.

fact: Replacing serine 25 with histidine in monomeric streptavidin reduces the biotin dissociation rate by 7.5 fold by blocking solvent entry into the binding pocket.
source_span: We have previously demonstrated that replacing S25 with histidine reduces koff by 7 . 5 fold by blocking solvent entry into the binding pocket through steric hindrance ( Demonte et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight supports the engineering approach to improve streptavidin-based imaging reagents.

fact: Rapid dissociation of bound biotin from monomeric streptavidin (mSA) interferes with detection and measurement by causing loss of fluorescence intensity over time.
source_span: Although extremely high affinity is not needed for labeling live cells , rapid dissociation of bound biotin interferes with detection and measurement because it results in loss of fluorescence intensity over time .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the motivation for improving mSA binding kinetics, a core background claim relevant to the study.

fact: Improving the dissociation kinetics of mSA by slowing the off rate (koff) is important to develop a useful imaging reagent.
