selection_reasoning: This states the main research goal and significance of the study.

fact: Replacing serine 25 (S25) with histidine in mSA reduces the dissociation rate (koff) by 7.5 fold by blocking solvent entry into the binding pocket.
source_span: We have previously demonstrated that replacing S25 with histidine reduces koff by 7 . 5 fold by blocking solvent entry into the binding pocket through steric hindrance ( Demonte et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This prior finding provides key background and rationale for further engineering.

fact: Water molecules entering the mSA binding pocket compete with mSA-biotin hydrogen bonds and lead to biotin dissociation.
source_span: Keeping water molecules out of the binding pocket is important because they compete with mSA-biotin hydrogen bonds and lead to biotin dissociation .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains why solvent exclusion is critical for improving binding stability.

fact: The loop between β-strands 1 and 2 (L1,2) in mSA is solvent exposed, unlike in streptavidin where it forms a subunit interface, allowing solvent entry.
source_span: S25 is located in the loop between β−strands 1 and 2 ( L1 , 2 ) , which is found at the subunit interface of streptavidin but is solvent exposed in mSA .
selection_reasoning: This structural difference motivates engineering to recreate a solvent barrier in mSA.

fact: Modeling mSA binding pocket on high affinity dimer bradavidin II (Brad2) allowed identification of key residues to reconstruct the solvent barrier in mSA.
source_span: To improve the dissociation kinetics further , we modeled the binding pocket of mSA using high affinity dimer bradavidin II ( Brad2 ) , which binds biotin with Kd <10−10 M ( Helppolainen et al . , 2008 ) .
selection_reasoning: This describes the high-level method used to guide mSA engineering.

fact: Mutating S25 to arginine (S25R) in mSA slows the dissociation rate more than S25H or wild-type mSA by better blocking solvent entry.
source_span: To reconstruct the solvent barrier in mSA , we mutated S25 to R , and measured the dissociation rate of the mutant mSA using fluorescence polarization spectroscopy . The dissociation rate of mSA-S25R is slower than that of mSA or mSA-S25H .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing improved binding stability by a specific mutation.

fact: Introducing a hydrophobic lid mutation T48F in mSA-S25R further reduces the dissociation rate cooperatively, resulting in a 37-fold lower koff compared to original mSA.
source_span: We therefore introduced the corresponding mutation T48F in mSA-S25R to create a hydrophobic binding pocket and further reduce the dissociation rate . The measured koff of mSA-S25R/T48F ( mSA-RF ) is 37 fold lower compared to original mSA , that is . t½=402 min , and ~5 fold lower than the best mutant to date , thst is mSA-S25H .
selection_reasoning: This key result demonstrates the cooperative effect of two mutations in improving mSA-biotin binding.

fact: The single point mutant mSA-T48F alone results in only limited improvement in biotin dissociation, indicating cooperative function of the two mutations.
source_span: The single point mutant mSA-T48F resulted in only limited improvement in biotin dissociation ( t½=13 min ) , indicating that the two mutations function cooperatively .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that both mutations are needed for maximal effect.

fact: An alternative hydrophobic lid design with tryptophan (mSA-S25R/T48W/D124T) also shows similarly slow dissociation kinetics.
source_span: We also tested an alternative design of the hydrophobic lid with a tryptophan , mSA-S25R/T48W/D124T ( or mSA-RWT ) , which had similarly slow dissociation kinetics , t½=330 min .
selection_reasoning: This shows robustness of the approach to different hydrophobic lid mutations.

fact: Cooperative mutations in loops L1,2 and L3,4 can modulate dissociation kinetics and improve the mSA-biotin interaction by constructing solvent barriers.
source_span: Therefore , construction of solvent barriers through cooperative mutations in L1 , 2 and L3 , 4 can modulate the dissociation kinetics and improve the mSA-biotin interaction .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the mechanistic insight and engineering strategy.

fact: Engineered mSA-RF fused to EGFP specifically labels biotinylated cell surface proteins on HEK293 cells with stable fluorescence intensity over time.
source_span: The cells were fixed and labeled with mSA-RF—EGFP for imaging by confocal microscopy . The CFP positive cells were selectively labeled , suggesting high specificity of interaction between mSA-RF and biotin . Furthermore , the intensity of EGFP fluorescence remained high after 1 hr , indicating that the interaction is stable and mSA-RF remained stably bound during measurement .
selection_reasoning: This demonstrates the practical utility and improved stability of the engineered mSA in cell labeling.

fact: Normal streptavidin conjugated quantum dots (SA-qdots) frequently cross-link multiple biotinylated molecules, resulting in slower diffusion on lipid bilayers.
source_span: We found this to be the case , as represented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 . Figure 4—figure supplement 3 shows that there was little difference in the diffusion rate of molecules labeled with normal SA-qdots , whether conjugated with small or big qdots: there were a large number of slow diffusive qdots for both normal streptavidin conjugates , indicating that they had cross-linked to multiple molecules , even at the 0 . 2% biotin concentration .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a limitation of normal streptavidin for labeling due to cross-linking.

fact: Monomeric streptavidin conjugated quantum dots (mSA-qdots) do not show cross-linking and mostly diffuse freely on lipid bilayers at both low and high biotin concentrations.
source_span: By contrast , in the case of mSA qdot conjugates , we found that most qdot conjugates were freely diffusive at 0 . 2% as well as at 1 . 0% biotin concentration; that is , mSA-qdots do not show a slow diffusive population of labeled molecules at either 0 . 2% or 1 . 0% concentrations .
selection_reasoning: This demonstrates the advantage of mSA conjugates in avoiding cross-linking artifacts.

fact: Cross-linking by streptavidin-qdots can be detected by increased run length of kinesin motor protein cargo, as cargo bound to multiple motors travels farther.
source_span: It is well known that when the cargo ( in this case the streptavidin-qdot conjugate ) binds to multiple motor proteins , the cargo will be transported over a longer distance than when the cargo binds to a single motor protein .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a functional assay to detect cross-linking, relevant to validating the improved monomeric streptavidin.

fact: Normal streptavidin frequently cross-links to multiple molecules, while monomeric streptavidin does not.
source_span: These observations showed that normal streptavidin frequently cross-links to multiple molecules while monomeric streptavidin did not.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes a key difference in molecular behavior relevant to the study's investigation of cross-linking.

fact: Cargo bound to multiple motor proteins is transported over a longer distance than cargo bound to a single motor protein.
source_span: It is well known that when the cargo (in this case the streptavidin-qdot conjugate) binds to multiple motor proteins, the cargo will be transported over a longer distance than when the cargo binds to a single motor protein.
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the rationale for using run length as a measure of cross-linking.

fact: A single motor protein transports cargo approximately 1 micrometer, while multiple motor proteins can transport cargo farther than 1 micrometer.
source_span: A single motor protein transports cargo approximately 1 um, while multiple motor proteins can walk farther than 1 um.
selection_reasoning: This quantitative background supports interpretation of run length data in the study.

fact: Monomeric streptavidin-quantum dots (mSA-qdots) bind to a single kinesin motor protein, as indicated by run lengths matching those of single kinesin motors even at high kinesin to qdot ratios.
source_span: In the case of mSA-qdots, we found the run length was the same as that of a single kinesin at a ratio of 2:1 (two kinesin molecules to one qdot). As expected, the run length was not changed even when the ratio of kinesin to qdots was increased to 6:1.
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates that mSA-qdots do not cause cross-linking, a key experimental result.

fact: Normal streptavidin-quantum dots (SA-qdots) cause cross-linking of multiple kinesin motors, as shown by increased run lengths beyond typical single kinesin run lengths at increasing kinesin to qdot ratios.
source_span: By contrast, in the case of SA-qdots, the run length of kinesin was more than the typical run length of kinesin. Even at a ratio of 2:1, some kinesin walked longer than the typical kinesin run length. At 6:1, we found that the run length significantly increased, indicating cross-linking.
selection_reasoning: This principal finding confirms that normal streptavidin induces cross-linking, central to the study's conclusions.

fact: The run length experiments with kinesin and streptavidin-qdots mirror results obtained from diffusion rate measurements of labeled molecules in lipid bilayers.
source_span: These results mirror the results we obtained in our first experiment about diffusion rates of labeled molecules in the lipid bilayer.
selection_reasoning: This links two independent experimental approaches supporting the same conclusion about cross-linking.

fact: Post-synaptic protein Homer1c was used as a marker for post-synaptic density in super-resolution PALM imaging.
source_span: Post-synaptic protein Homer1c was used as the PSD marker and its C-terminus was fused to photoactivatable protein mGeos.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key biological marker and method used to study synaptic structures.

fact: PALM imaging was performed by activating mGeos proteins with a 405 nm laser and exciting fluorescence with a 488 nm laser to collect thousands of frames for super-resolution imaging.
source_span: A 100 ms 405 nm laser pulse was used to activate mGeos proteins from dark to green fluorescent state. The sample was then excited with a 488 nm read out laser and emission was collected with a 535/50 band-pass filter. The cycle was repeated for 200–300 times, collecting 4000–6000 frames.
selection_reasoning: This high-level method description is relevant to understanding how super-resolution imaging was achieved.

fact: Cy3B-labeled streptavidin was used to label neurons for STORM imaging to visualize native AMPA receptors after fixation.
source_span: We labeled neurons with Cy3B-SA (2 μM) following the procedure of sQD labeling. ... In order to image native AMPARs, we labeled AMPARs using Anti-GluA2-Alexa647 after fixation.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the labeling strategy for imaging native receptors, important for the study's biological relevance.

fact: Diffusion coefficients of quantum dot-labeled molecules were calculated by fitting the first four points of the mean-square-displacement curve from single particle tracking data.
source_span: The diffusion coefficients from the trajectories were calculated in Matlab by fitting the first 4 points of mean-square-displacement curve.
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the key analytical approach used to quantify molecular mobility.

fact: Trajectories within 0.55 micrometers average distance from synapse centers were considered synaptic in the analysis of receptor movement.
source_span: Any trajectories with an average distance smaller than 0.55 μm were considered synaptic.
selection_reasoning: This defines a critical criterion for classifying receptor localization relevant to synaptic function.

fact: Acute hypoxia increases voltage-gated sodium current (INa) in central neurons, which is the earliest neuronal response to low oxygen.
source_span: At the cellular level , the first effect of hypoxia is to increase INa ( Boening et al . , 1989; Stys et al . , 1992 ) ; this precedes a series of events that include depolarization of the plasma membrane , excitotoxic elevation of intracellular calcium , mitochondrial dysfunction , ATP depletion , increased production of reactive oxygen species and , ultimately , cell death
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological context and importance of the study's main question about hypoxia-induced changes in sodium current.

fact: Hypoxia activates the Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier (SUMO) pathway in rat cerebellar granule neurons, leading to SUMOylation of NaV1.2 sodium channels.
source_span: Here , we show that hypoxia activates the Small Ubiquitin-like Modifier ( SUMO ) pathway in rat cerebellar granule neurons ( CGN ) and that SUMOylation of NaV1 . 2 channels increases INa .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the key molecular mechanism discovered that links hypoxia to increased sodium current.

fact: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels increases the voltage-gated sodium current (INa) by shifting the voltage-dependence of channel activation to more negative potentials.
source_span: Within 40 s , hypoxia-induced linkage of SUMO1 to the channels is complete , shifting the voltage-dependence of channel activation so that depolarizing steps evoke larger sodium currents .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how SUMOylation functionally alters sodium channel behavior to increase INa.

fact: Mutation of the lysine residue at position 38 (Lys38) on NaV1.2 channels or application of a deSUMOylating enzyme prevents hypoxia-induced increases in INa.
source_span: both are prevented by mutation of NaV1 . 2-Lys38 or application of a deSUMOylating enzyme .
selection_reasoning: This supports the causal role of SUMOylation at Lys38 in mediating the hypoxic response.

fact: The increase in INa induced by hypoxia occurs rapidly, within 40 seconds, and is long-lasting even after restoration to normal oxygen levels.
source_span: Within 40 s , hypoxia-induced linkage of SUMO1 to the channels is complete ... The hypoxia-induced increase in INa was long-lasting , remaining unchanged 10 min after neurons were restored to ambient O2
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the rapid and sustained nature of the hypoxic effect on sodium current.

fact: Blocking NaV1.2 channels with µ–Conotoxin-TIIIA abolishes the hypoxia-induced increase in INa in rat cerebellar granule neurons.
source_span: The response of INa to hypoxia was ablated by µ–Conotoxin-TIIIA ( CnTX ) , a potent blocker of NaV1 . 2 channels .
selection_reasoning: This confirms that NaV1.2 channels mediate the hypoxia-induced increase in sodium current.

fact: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels at the plasma membrane occurs without changing the number of channels present, indicating modulation of channel activity rather than channel trafficking.
source_span: acute hypoxia leads to monoSUMOylation of single NaV1 . 2 channels already at the plasma membrane without a change in the number of channels on the surface .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the mechanism by which hypoxia increases INa is via functional modification rather than increased channel expression.

fact: The SUMO pathway regulates neuronal excitability by modifying ion channels, including NaV1.2 sodium channels and previously reported potassium channels.
source_span: the SUMO pathway was recognized to regulate the trafficking and activity of nuclear transcription factors when we discovered it to operate as well at the plasma membrane to regulate neuronal excitability via direct SUMOylation of K+ channel α-subunits ... Here , seeking to determine if the SUMO pathway also regulated sodium channels , we documented SUMOylation of NaV1 . 2 channels in CGN and then recognized it to be the basis for acute , hypoxic augmentation of INa .
selection_reasoning: This provides important background and mechanistic context for the study's focus on SUMOylation.

fact: Acute hypoxia contributes to brain damage in common conditions such as stroke, heart attack, and head trauma by increasing sodium current and triggering downstream pathological events.
source_span: Acute hypoxia contributes to brain damage arising from such common conditions as stroke , heart attack , and head trauma . ... the first effect of hypoxia is to increase INa ... this precedes a series of events ... ultimately , cell death
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the clinical and translational relevance of understanding hypoxia-induced sodium current changes.

fact: Inhibition of voltage-gated sodium current by tetrodotoxin reduces hypoxia-induced neuronal depolarization and cell death, indicating the critical role of INa in hypoxic brain injury.
source_span: inhibition of INa by tetrodotoxin ( TTX ) attenuates hypoxia-induced depolarization and reduces neuronal death in the hippocampus , hypothalamus , and neocortex ... The neuroprotective effects of TTX have been judged to occur both independent of , and by reduction of the excitotoxic effects that follow INa-induced membrane depolarization .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the significance of targeting sodium currents for neuroprotection.

fact: Acute hypoxia increases sodium current (INa) in rat cerebellar granule neurons (CGN) by approximately 70%.
source_span: stable level that was ~70% higher , −294 ± 25 pA/pF ( Figure 1a and Table 1 ) , reminiscent of increases in INa in response to acute hypoxia reported by others studying rat neurons from the hypothalamus ( Horn and Waldrop , 2000 ) and hippocampus ( Raley-Susman et al . , 2001 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing hypoxia augments INa, a core physiological effect relevant to the study.

fact: Hypoxia causes a leftward shift of about −11 mV in the voltage dependence of activation (V½) and steady-state inactivation (SSI) of INa in rat CGN, allowing greater sodium currents at the same depolarization.
source_span: Augmentation of INa by hypoxia was associated with a leftward shift of −11 ± 2 mV in both V½ and SSI , allowing the same amount of depolarization to evoke larger INa currents ( Figure 1b ) .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic detail explains how hypoxia increases INa, a key functional change.

fact: The hypoxia-induced increase in INa is long-lasting and remains unchanged 10 minutes after neurons are returned to normal oxygen levels.
source_span: The hypoxia-induced increase in INa was long-lasting , remaining unchanged 10 min after neurons were restored to ambient O2 ( Supplementary file 1a ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the persistence of hypoxia effects, important for understanding physiological impact.

fact: Hypoxia does not alter the kinetics of recovery of INa from the fast-inactivated state in rat CGN.
source_span: Hypoxia did not alter the kinetics of recovery of INa from the fast-inactivated state ( Figure 1—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies that hypoxia selectively affects current amplitude and voltage dependence but not recovery kinetics.

fact: SUMO1 protein increases INa in rat CGN and occludes further augmentation by hypoxia.
source_span: SUMO1 in the pipette ( red ) increased INa and no further augmentation was observed by subsequent hypoxia ( red dashes ) .
selection_reasoning: This shows SUMO1 mimics hypoxia effects on INa, indicating a shared pathway or mechanism.

fact: SENP1 protein decreases INa in rat CGN and suppresses the response to hypoxia.
source_span: SENP1 in the pipette ( blue ) decreased INa and suppressed the response to hypoxia ( blue dashes ) .
selection_reasoning: This indicates that SENP1 counteracts hypoxia-induced INa increases, suggesting regulatory control.

fact: The sodium current in rat CGN is primarily carried by NaV1.2 channels, as shown by ~90% inhibition with µ-conotoxin TIIIA (CnTx).
source_span: mean normalized peak current histograms showing 90 ± 0 . 8% inhibition by CnTx , 10 ± 0 . 3% inhibition by AnTTX and 98 ± 0 . 02% inhibition by both toxins with 21% O2 ( black bars ) .
selection_reasoning: Identifying the channel subtype responsible for INa is essential for understanding the molecular basis of hypoxia effects.

fact: The INa remaining after inhibition of NaV1.2 channels does not respond to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1, indicating that NaV1.2 mediates the hypoxia-sensitive sodium current.
source_span: Mean normalized peak current histograms show that the INa remaining after inhibition of NaV1 . 2 by CnTx did not respond to acute hypoxia at 5% O2 ( green ) , SUMO1 ( red ) or SENP1 ( blue ) .
selection_reasoning: This links the hypoxia and SUMO1/SENP1 modulation specifically to NaV1.2 channels.

fact: SUMOylation regulates sodium current (INa) in cerebellar granule neurons (CGN) by shifting the voltage dependence of channel activation and inactivation.
source_span: We observed SUMO-induced changes in INa like those produced by acute hypoxia: peak INa increased by ~76% and V½ and SSI were left-shifted by −13 ± 1 mV and −10 ± 3 mV , respectively ... Also like hypoxia , SUMO1 did not change the kinetics of recovery from fast inactivation ... intracellular application of 250 pm SENP1 deSUMOylase via the pipette suppressed peak INa by ~75% to −42 ± 12 pA/pF and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 15 ± 1 mV and 14 ± 2 mV , respectively ... currents increased by SUMO1 were not further augmented by hypoxia , nor did hypoxia overcome suppression of INa by SENP1
selection_reasoning: This fact captures the core finding that SUMOylation modulates INa in CGN similarly to hypoxia, demonstrating a key regulatory mechanism central to the study.

fact: Acute hypoxia increases peak sodium current (INa) in cerebellar granule neurons and shifts the voltage dependence of activation and inactivation to more negative potentials.
source_span: We observed SUMO-induced changes in INa like those produced by acute hypoxia: peak INa increased by ~76% and V½ and SSI were left-shifted by −13 ± 1 mV and −10 ± 3 mV , respectively ... When these neurons were studied with SUMO1 in the pipette or subjected to 5% O2 , the maximal current was observed at −20 ± 2 mV and −20 ± 3 mV , respectively , shifts of ~15 mV analogous to those seen in V½
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main physiological effect of hypoxia on INa, which is a key background and principal finding.

fact: The deSUMOylating enzyme SENP1 decreases peak sodium current (INa) and shifts the voltage dependence of activation and inactivation to more positive potentials in cerebellar granule neurons.

selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the opposing effect of SENP1 on INa, supporting the role of SUMOylation in regulating sodium channels.

fact: SUMO1 and hypoxia do not have additive effects on sodium current (INa), indicating that hypoxia acts via the SUMOylation pathway in cerebellar granule neurons.
source_span: currents increased by SUMO1 were not further augmented by hypoxia , nor did hypoxia overcome suppression of INa by SENP1
selection_reasoning: This fact provides mechanistic insight linking hypoxia effects to the SUMOylation pathway, a key conclusion.

fact: The point mutation K38Q in NaV1.2 channels does not affect recovery kinetics from fast inactivation or modulation by hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1.
source_span: Neither the point mutation K38Q , nor treating cells with hypoxia , SUMO1 or SENP1 modulated recovery kinetics
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies that the K38Q mutation does not alter key channel properties or their regulation, relevant to understanding the molecular mechanism.

fact: The maximal sodium current in cerebellar granule neurons shifts to more negative voltages under hypoxia or SUMO1 treatment, consistent with shifts in voltage dependence of activation.
source_span: The maximal current in CGN cultured at 21% O2 and studied in ambient O2 was at −5 ± 1 mV ... when these neurons were studied with SUMO1 in the pipette or subjected to 5% O2 , the maximal current was observed at −20 ± 2 mV and −20 ± 3 mV , respectively , shifts of ~15 mV analogous to those seen in V½
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the functional consequence of SUMOylation and hypoxia on sodium channel gating, a principal finding.

fact: SUMOylation and deSUMOylation enzymes are present on the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane in neurons and tissue culture cells, enabling regulation of ion channels.
source_span: we found that the enzymes that mature , activate , and conjugate SUMO to the channels reside on the cytosolic face of the plasma membrane in tissue culture cells and neurons
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the cellular localization of the SUMO pathway components, important for understanding the mechanism.

fact: The sodium current (INa) in rat cerebellar granule neurons (CGN) is primarily carried by NaV1.2 channels, with smaller contributions from NaV1.6, NaV1.3, and NaV1.1 channels.
source_span: INa is passed mainly by NaV1 . 2 in rat CGN with smaller contributions by other channel isoforms , NaV1 . 2 >> NaV1 . 6 >> NaV1 . 3 and NaV1 . 1 ( Schaller and Caldwell , 2003; Shah et al . , 2001 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact is essential to understand which sodium channel isoforms mediate the current studied and the focus on NaV1.2 in the research.

fact: Hypoxia and SUMOylation modulate the activity of NaV1.2 channels in rat cerebellar granule neurons, altering sodium current without changing the number of channels or their conductance.
source_span: Supporting the notion that rapid changes in INa were due to shifts in the conductance-voltage ( G-V ) relationship , rather than changes in the number of channels on the surface passing current or unitary channel conductance ... Taken together , the toxin data are consistent with the conclusion that hypoxia , SUMO1 and SENP1 act to alter the activity of native NaV1 . 2 channels in CGN .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking hypoxia and SUMOylation to functional modulation of NaV1.2 channels, central to the study's main question.

fact: The SUMO pathway exerts tonic control over sodium current (INa) in rat cerebellar granule neurons under normal oxygen conditions.
source_span: Indicating that the SUMO pathway exerted tonic control over INa under normoxic conditions , CGN studied with control pipette solution rested midway between the V½ extremes .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the physiological relevance of SUMOylation in regulating sodium channel function under baseline conditions.

fact: NaV1.2 channels and SUMO1 proteins physically associate at the surface of rat cerebellar granule neurons, and this association increases under hypoxic conditions.
source_span: Many voxels exhibiting NaV1 . 2 immunoreactivity ( donor ) showed an increase in fluorescence following bleaching of the acceptor ( SUMO ) , demonstrating FRET between the fluorophores ( Figure 2a–c ) .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic finding supports the molecular basis for SUMOylation's effect on NaV1.2 channels and its enhancement by hypoxia.

fact: Acute hypoxia increases the molecular interaction between NaV1.2 channels and SUMO1 at the neuronal surface, as shown by a four-fold increase in FRET signal.
source_span: Histogram showing a four-fold increase in the voxels with NaV1 . 2 demonstrating FRET from ambient conditions ( 7 . 8 ± 2 . 3% ) with hypoxia ( 29 . 6 ± 7 . 6% , n = 8 on five coverslips ) ; * indicates p<0 . 001 .
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates the dynamic regulation of NaV1.2 SUMOylation by oxygen levels, relevant to the study's focus on hypoxia.

fact: Toxins selective for NaV1.2 (CnTX) and NaV1.6 (AnTTX) confirm that NaV1.2 is the main contributor to sodium current in rat cerebellar granule neurons under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
source_span: In keeping with this expression pattern , 250 nm CnTX , a toxin that blocks NaV1 . 2 ~100-fold more effectively than NaV1 . 6 ( Wilson et al . , 2011 ) , inhibited ~90% of INa at −20 mV in CGN ... When CGN were subjected to acute hypoxia , or SUMO1 was applied in the pipette , CnTX still blocked over 90% of INa ... Supporting the notion that most of the residual current is passed by NaV1 . 6 , 50 nm 4 , 9 anhydro-tetrodotoxin ( AnTTX ) , a toxin that blocks NaV1 . 6 ~150-fold more effectively than NaV1 . 2 ( Rosker et al . , 2007 ) , inhibited ~10% of INa under control conditions and >90% of the current remaining after CnTX application .
selection_reasoning: This methodological fact supports the conclusion that NaV1.2 channels dominate sodium current and are the main target of hypoxia and SUMOylation effects.

fact: NaV1.2 channels in cerebellar granule neurons (CGN) interact with SUMO1 at the plasma membrane under ambient oxygen conditions.
source_span: Triple co-localization delineated the circumference of the neuronal soma ( n = 5 ) , consistent with plasma membrane localization of SUMOylated NaV1 . 2 , as predicted by the electrophysiological studies .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the key molecular interaction and localization relevant to the study's mechanism.

fact: No FRET was observed between NaV1.2 and GAD67, supporting the specificity of the interaction between NaV1.2 and SUMO1.
source_span: Supporting specificity of signals generated between NaV1 . 2 and SUMO1 , no FRET was observed between NaV1 . 2 and GAD67 , an abundant cytosolic protein ( Figure 2—figure supplement 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: This confirms the specificity of the NaV1.2-SUMO1 interaction, a core mechanistic claim.

fact: The baseline oxygen level in mammalian brain tissue is approximately 7% under healthy conditions and can drop below 2% during ischemia.
source_span: The baseline O2 level in mammalian brain tissue has been estimated to be as low as ~7% under normal , healthy conditions and to drop to under 2% with ischemia ( Ponce et al . , 2012; Lyons et al . , 2016 ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact motivates studying neuronal responses at physiologically relevant oxygen levels.

fact: Cerebellar granule neurons cultured at 7% oxygen tolerate long-term culture and respond to acute hypoxia with increased sodium current (INa).
source_span: First , rat CGN were confirmed to tolerate long-term culture in 7% O2 , as we previously observed for rat hippocampal neurons ( Shelat et al . , 2013 ) . Next , CGN cultured for 7–10 days at 7% O2 were evaluated at 7% O2 and then on exposure to 1 . 5% O2; the decrease in O2 led to an acute increase in mean peak INa of ~65% ...
selection_reasoning: This describes the experimental model and the key physiological response to hypoxia.

fact: Acute hypoxia (1.5% O2) causes a leftward shift in voltage dependence of activation and steady-state inactivation of sodium currents in CGN cultured at 7% O2.
source_span: Starting from a baseline for V½ of −42 ± 1 . 5 mV and −57 ± 3 mV , V½ and SSI were left-shifted by −8 ± 2 mV and −11 ± 3 mV , respectively .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal electrophysiological finding linking hypoxia to sodium channel gating changes.

fact: SUMO1 increases sodium current (INa) in CGN cultured at 7% oxygen and causes leftward shifts in voltage dependence of activation and inactivation similar to hypoxia.
source_span: Similarly , SUMO1 increased INa in CGN cultured at 7% O2 by ~68% , in association with left-shifts in V½ and SSI of − 8 ± 1 . 5 mV and −12 ± 3 mV , respectively ...
selection_reasoning: This shows SUMO1 mimics hypoxia effects on sodium channel function, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: SENP1 suppresses sodium current (INa) in CGN cultured at 7% oxygen and causes rightward shifts in voltage dependence of activation and inactivation.
source_span: SENP1 suppressed INa by ~70% and right-shifted V½ and SSI by 9 ± 1 mV and 8 ± 2 mV , respectively .
selection_reasoning: This identifies SENP1 as a negative regulator of sodium channel activity, important for understanding modulation.

fact: The increase in sodium current induced by SUMO1 is not further enhanced by hypoxia, and hypoxia cannot overcome the suppression of sodium current by SENP1.
source_span: As observed when CGN were cultured in ambient O2 , the increase in INa induced by SUMO1 when cells were incubated at 7% O2 was not further augmented when O2 was decreased to 1 . 5% nor could subsequent exposure to 1 . 5% O2 overcome suppression of INa by SENP1 .
selection_reasoning: This indicates that SUMOylation and hypoxia act via a shared pathway affecting sodium current.

fact: Pharmacological blockade studies identify NaV1.2 as the sodium channel responsible for the hypoxia-responsive sodium current in CGN cultured at 7% oxygen.
source_span: Blockade studies with CnTX and AnTTX supported the identification of NaV1 . 2 as the channel passing hypoxia-responsive INa in CGN cultured at 7% O2 ...
selection_reasoning: This links the functional sodium current changes specifically to NaV1.2 channels.

fact: NaV1.6 channels mediate a residual sodium current in CGN that is insensitive to hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1.
source_span: … and the proposal that NaV1 . 6 is responsible for the residual current that was insensitive to hypoxia , SUMO1 or SENP1 .
selection_reasoning: This distinguishes the roles of different sodium channel subtypes in hypoxia response.

fact: SUMOylation of the NaV1.2 sodium channel α-subunit at Lys38 mediates the channel's response to acute hypoxic challenge.
source_span: One Lys in the 2005 amino acid, pore-forming NaV1.2 channel α-subunit was shown to be subject to SUMOylation, and to mediate the response to acute hypoxic challenge, using heterologous expression of wild type and mutant proteins in CHO cells.
selection_reasoning: This identifies the key molecular modification and its functional relevance to hypoxia, a principal finding central to the study.

fact: Mutating Lys38 to Gln in the NaV1.2 α-subunit prevents SUMOylation and abolishes FRET with SUMO1 and Ubc9, indicating Lys38 is necessary for SUMOylation.
source_span: Mutating Lys38 to Gln, removing the side chain subject to SUMO modification, produced CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln subunits that reached the CHO cell surface like wild type CFP-NaV1.2. However, in contrast with CFP-NaV1.2, the mutant failed to exhibit FRET with either YFP-SUMO1 or YFP-Ubc9.
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic fact confirms the specific site of SUMOylation, supporting the molecular basis of the channel's regulation.

fact: FRET experiments demonstrated that NaV1.2 and SUMO1 associate at the plasma membrane of CHO cells, confirming SUMOylation occurs at the cell surface.
source_span: Both YFP-SUMO1 and CFP-NaV1.2 were visualized at the plasma membrane when expressed together in CHO cells... Consistent with SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2, the time course of CFP decay with continuous illumination... was prolonged from under 10 s to ~30 s when the channel was expressed with YFP-SUMO1.
selection_reasoning: This provides key experimental evidence for the physical interaction and localization of SUMOylation relevant to channel function.

fact: The relative contributions of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 to sodium current (INa) are not altered when cells are cultured at 7% oxygen.
source_span: These ratios indicate that the relative contribution of NaV1.2 and NaV1.6 to INa is not altered when cells are cultured at 7% O2.
selection_reasoning: This contextualizes the oxygen conditions used and confirms that hypoxia does not change channel subtype contributions, important for interpreting hypoxia effects.

fact: SUMO1 shifts the voltage dependence of activation and steady-state inactivation of NaV1.2 channels, making them insensitive to hypoxia.
source_span: SUMO1 left shifted the V½ of Act (red triangle) and SSI (open red triangle). The relationships were then insensitive to hypoxia.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key functional effect of SUMOylation on channel gating and hypoxia sensitivity, central to the study's conclusions.

fact: SENP1 reverses the effects of SUMOylation by right shifting the voltage dependence of activation and steady-state inactivation of NaV1.2 channels, also making currents insensitive to hypoxia.
source_span: SENP1 right shifted the V½ of Act (blue triangle) and SSI (open blue triangle) and currents were then insensitive to hypoxia.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the reversible regulation of NaV1.2 by SUMOylation and its functional consequences, important for understanding the mechanism.

fact: Lys38 in the α-subunit of NaV1.2 is a critical site for SUMOylation of the channel complex.
source_span: Mutating Lys38 to Gln, removing the side chain subject to SUMO modification, produced CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln subunits that reached the CHO cell surface like wild type CFP-NaV1.2. However, in contrast with CFP-NaV1.2, the mutant failed to exhibit FRET with either YFP-SUMO1 or YFP-Ubc9. The absence of FRET supported the conclusion that Lys38 was required for SUMOylation of the NaV1.2 channel complex and suggested that no other Lys in the α subunit or the β1 subunit was subject to SUMOylation.
selection_reasoning: Identifying the specific lysine residue required for SUMOylation is central to understanding the molecular mechanism underlying channel regulation.

fact: Acute hypoxia increases NaV1.2 channel current density and shifts voltage-dependence of activation and inactivation in CHO cells similarly to native neuronal sodium currents.
source_span: NaV1.2 channels responded to acute hypoxia with an increase in mean peak current-density of ~70% in less than 40 s in association with leftward shifts in V½ and SSI of −11 ± 1 mV and −13 ± 2 mV, respectively.
selection_reasoning: Demonstrating that hypoxia modulates NaV1.2 channel function is a key physiological finding linking oxygen levels to channel activity.

fact: SUMO1 application mimics the effects of acute hypoxia on NaV1.2 channel current and voltage-dependence, while SENP1 reverses these effects.
source_span: SUMO1 in the pipette increased current-density and left-shifted V½ and SSI to the same extent as acute hypoxia and SENP1 decreased current-density and right-shifted the V½ and SSI from baseline by ~75%.
selection_reasoning: Showing that SUMOylation modulates channel function similarly to hypoxia supports a mechanistic link between SUMOylation and hypoxic regulation.

fact: NaV1.2 channels with the Lys38Gln mutation do not respond to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, or SENP1, indicating that Lys38 SUMOylation is essential for these regulatory effects.
source_span: Expression of NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels produced currents that were insensitive to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, and SENP1. The current-density, V½ and SSI values for NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels under all three conditions were like those measured for wild-type NaV1.2 channels subjected to deSUMOylation by SENP1.
selection_reasoning: This finding confirms the functional importance of Lys38 SUMOylation in mediating hypoxia and SUMO pathway effects on channel activity.

fact: The β1 subunit does not influence the hypoxic or SUMOylation-dependent regulation of NaV1.2 channel activity.
source_span: The β1 subunit did not appear to play a role in the hypoxic response of NaV1.2 via Lys38 or to the regulation of channel activity by the SUMO pathway. Expression of the α subunits without β1 did not modify the responses of NaV1.2 channels to acute hypoxia, SUMO1, and SENP1 nor did it alter insensitivity of NaV1.2-Lys38Gln channels to the same three manipulations.
selection_reasoning: Clarifying the subunit specificity of the regulatory mechanism is important for understanding channel complex modulation.

fact: The Lys38 residue is located in a conserved Pro-Lys-Gln-Glu motif near the N-terminus of NaV1.2 channels across species from zebrafish to humans.
source_span: Lys38 is in a sequence motif, Pro-Lys38-Gln-Glu, which is conserved near the N-terminus of NaV1.2 from zebrafish to humans.

fact: Mass spectrometry confirmed that SUMO1 is covalently attached to Lys38 of the NaV1.2 channel.
source_span: The spectrum included a peak at the predicted size for a fragment carrying Lys38 linked via its side-chain to the Gly-Gly SUMO1 remnant, and MS-MS sequencing identified it uniquely to be the three-ended product.
selection_reasoning: Direct biochemical evidence of SUMOylation at Lys38 validates the molecular mechanism proposed.

fact: SUMO1 is covalently attached to the NaV1.2 sodium channel at lysine residue 38.

fact: Hypoxia increases the fraction of NaV1.2 channels modified by SUMO1 at the cell surface approximately fourfold.
source_span: Acute hypoxia increased the fraction of CFP-NaV1.2 particles with mCherry-SUMO1 ~4-fold (from 20% to 80%), as expected due to hypoxia-induced SUMOylation.
selection_reasoning: Demonstrates the physiological stimulus (hypoxia) that regulates SUMOylation of NaV1.2, a key functional finding.

fact: Each NaV1.2 channel at the cell surface is modified by only one SUMO1 monomer, indicating a 1:1 stoichiometry of SUMO1 to NaV1.2 subunit.
source_span: When CFP-NaV1.2 and SUMO1 tagged with mCherry were co-expressed, particles showed only a single bleaching step for each fluorophore under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions, indicating the presence of one fluorescent subunit of each type.
selection_reasoning: Establishes the stoichiometry of SUMOylation, which is important for understanding the molecular mechanism.

fact: Mutation of lysine 38 to glutamine in NaV1.2 prevents SUMO1 modification and colocalization at the cell surface under both normoxic and hypoxic conditions.
source_span: Expression of CFP-NaV1.2-Lys38Gln and mCherry-SUMO1 rarely yielded colocalization of the fluorophores in both ambient O2 and hypoxic conditions.
selection_reasoning: Confirms the critical role of Lys38 in SUMOylation and validates the specificity of the modification.

fact: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels at the cell surface is reversible by the SUMO protease SENP1, which suppresses both baseline and hypoxia-induced SUMOylation.
source_span: SENP1 in the recording pipette suppressed both baseline and hypoxia-induced SUMOylation of CFP-NaV1.2 by mCherry-SUMO1 so that colocalized particles were decreased.
selection_reasoning: Shows the dynamic regulation of SUMOylation, relevant for physiological and potentially therapeutic contexts.

fact: NaV1.2 channels are monomeric and do not form polySUMO1 chains or SUMOylate the β1 subunit.
source_span: Because channels are formed with one NaV1.2 subunit, observing only a single mCherry-SUMO1 in particles confirmed that only Lys38 on the α-subunit was SUMOylated; polySUMO1 chains were not formed; and the β1 subunit was not SUMOylated.
selection_reasoning: Clarifies the molecular specificity of SUMOylation on NaV1.2, important for understanding the modification's functional impact.

fact: Exposure to hypoxia rapidly increases the number of SUMO1 monomers co-localized with NaV1.2 channels at the cell surface within 40 seconds.
source_span: Exposure to hypoxia increased the number of SUMO1 monomers observed at the cell surface within 40 s and almost all were co-localized with NaV1.2.
selection_reasoning: Highlights the rapid physiological response of NaV1.2 SUMOylation to hypoxia, a key functional insight.

fact: Whole-cell peak sodium current density through NaV1.2 channels increases by approximately 70% within 40 seconds of hypoxia and remains stable during continued hypoxia and recovery.
source_span: Whole-cell, peak current-density, measured at −20 mV, increased by ~70% within 40 s of hypoxia and remained stable during 2 min of hypoxia and 20 min of recovery at ambient levels of O2.
selection_reasoning: Links SUMOylation changes to functional electrophysiological effects, a principal finding.

fact: Acute hypoxia rapidly increases the recruitment of SUMO1 to the cell surface at sites where NaV1.2 channels are present without changing the number of NaV1.2 channels on the surface.

fact: Hypoxia increases the fraction of NaV1.2 channels modified by SUMO1 from 16% to 65% on the cell surface.

selection_reasoning: This quantifies the hypoxia-induced increase in SUMOylation of NaV1.2, a core finding relevant to the study's main conclusion.

fact: Hypoxia increases the peak current density of NaV1.2 channels by approximately 70% within 40 seconds, and this increase remains stable during 2 minutes of hypoxia and 20 minutes of recovery at normal oxygen levels.

fact: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels during hypoxia occurs rapidly, within 40 seconds of reduced oxygen exposure.

selection_reasoning: The rapid time course of SUMOylation and functional change is important for understanding the physiological relevance and mechanism.

fact: SUMOylation of NaV1.2 channels at the plasma membrane causes an immediate increase in sodium current (INa) in response to acute hypoxia in cultured neurons and CHO cells.

selection_reasoning: This is the principal finding linking SUMOylation of NaV1.2 to hypoxia-induced changes in sodium current, central to the study's main claim.

fact: Hypoxia increases the fraction of SUMOylated NaV1.2 channels at the cell surface approximately fourfold in both cerebellar granule neurons (CGN) and CHO cells.

fact: Hypoxia or intracellular SUMO application shifts the voltage dependence of NaV1.2 channel activation and steady-state inactivation leftward, increasing sodium current by about 70% in both CGN and CHO cells.

fact: The increase in SUMOylation and sodium current during hypoxia occurs rapidly, within less than 40 seconds, and is reversible upon return to normal oxygen levels.

fact: Relative R0 describes thermal suitability for Ross River virus transmission and provides key temperature values: upper and lower thermal limits and the temperature that maximizes transmission potential.
source_span: Relative R0 describes thermal suitability for transmission . Combined with factors like breeding habitat availability , vector control , humidity , human and reservoir host density , host immune status , and mosquito exposure , relative R0 can be used to predict disease incidence . In this approach , only the relative thermal response of each trait influences R0 , which is desirable since traits can differ substantially due to other factors and in laboratory versus field settings ( particularly mosquito survival: Clements and Paterson , 1981 ) . Relative R0 does not provide a threshold for sustained disease transmission ( i . e . where absolute R0 = 1 ) , since this threshold is not controlled solely by temperature . Instead , relative R0 preserves the temperature-dependence of R0 to provide three key temperature values: upper and lower thermal limits where transmission is possible ( R0 >0; a conservative threshold where transmission is not excluded by high or low temperatures ) and the temperature that maximizes R0 .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the modeling metric used to quantify temperature effects on transmission.

source_span: The lower thermal limit for RRV was constrained by fecundity and survival at all stages , while the upper thermal limit was constrained by fecundity and adult lifespan . By contrast , thermal limits for malaria transmission were set by parasite development rate at cool temperatures and egg-to-adulthood survival at high temperatures ( Mordecai et al . , 2013 ) .
selection_reasoning: This comparison highlights unique aspects of RRV transmission relevant to disease modeling and prediction.

fact: The model was parameterized using temperature-dependent data from two key mosquito vector species, Culex annulirostris and Aedes vigilax.
source_span: Here , we parameterized a temperature-dependent model for transmission of RRV ( Figure 2 ) with data from two important vector species ( Cx . annulirostris and Ae . vigilax; Figure 1 ) .
selection_reasoning: Describing the data sources and vectors used is important for understanding the model's basis.

fact: Current data limitations include sparse temperature data for key traits and incomplete trait data across vector species, requiring composite models.
source_span: The trait thermal response data were limited in two keys ways . First , two traits ( fecundity and adult lifespan ) had data from only three temperatures . ... Second , no vector species had data for all traits ( Figure 1 ) , so we combined mosquito traits from Cx . annulirostris and pathogen infection traits in Ae . vigilax to build composite relative R0 models .
selection_reasoning: Acknowledging data limitations is important for interpreting the model's reliability and guiding future research.

fact: Different RRV mosquito vector species have distinct thermal niches, which may explain the virus's persistence across diverse climates in Australia.
source_span: Geographic and seasonal variation in vector populations suggests that Ae . camptorhynchus and Ae . vigilax have different thermal niches ( cooler and warmer , respectively ) and Cx . annulirostris has a broader thermal niche ( Figure 1 ) ( Russell , 1998 ) . ... Hypothesized species differences in thermal niche could explain why RRV persists over a wide climatic and latitudinal gradient .
selection_reasoning: This fact links vector ecology to disease distribution, a key implication for understanding RRV epidemiology.

fact: Understanding temperature effects on mosquito-borne disease transmission is critical as climate warms and new pathogens emerge worldwide.
source_span: As the climate warms , it is critical to understand effects of temperature on transmission of mosquito-borne disease , particularly as new mosquito-borne pathogens emerge and spread worldwide .
selection_reasoning: This background fact motivates the study's relevance and public health importance.

fact: There is an 8–10 week lag between temperature changes and reported human cases of Ross River virus (RRV) due to the time required for mosquito population growth, virus incubation, and human symptom development and reporting.
source_span: the a priori predicted lag ( 8–10 weeks , or 2 months ) for temperature to affect reported human cases ( Hu et al . , 2006; Jacups et al . , 2008b; Stewart Ibarra et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017 ) . This lag between temperature and reported human cases arises from the time it takes for mosquito populations to increase , bite humans and reservoir hosts , acquire RRV , become infectious , and bite subsequent hosts; for pathogens to incubate with vectors; for humans to potentially develop symptoms , seek treatment , and report cases .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the temporal relationship between temperature and disease incidence, which is central to understanding the study's focus on temperature effects on RRV transmission.

fact: Ross River virus transmission by the mosquito Culex annulirostris in inland areas shifts southward as temperatures increase from spring into summer.
source_span: RRV transmission by Cx . annulirostris in inland areas often moves south as temperatures increase from spring into summer ( Russell , 1998 ) , matching the model prediction ( Figure 6 ) .
selection_reasoning: This spatial-temporal pattern links temperature changes to disease spread, supporting the study's mechanistic model and its relevance.

fact: It is difficult to establish causality between temperature and Ross River virus disease incidence from statistical inference alone due to strong seasonality and potential confounding factors.
source_span: Although temperature is often invoked as a potential driver for these types of patterns , it is difficult to establish causality from statistical inference alone , particularly if temperature and disease both exhibit strong seasonality and could both be responding to another latent driver .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the motivation for using a mechanistic model to better understand temperature's role in RRV transmission.

fact: A mechanistic unimodal thermal model explains both broad-scale and previously contradictory local-scale patterns of temperature effects on Ross River virus transmission.
source_span: Thus , the mechanistic model is a critical piece of evidence linking temperature to patterns of disease . In addition to explaining broad-scale patterns , the unimodal thermal model explains previously contradictory local-scale results .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the main methodological advance and its explanatory power, central to the article's claims.

fact: Ross River virus incidence is often positively associated with warmer temperatures, but this relationship varies across space and time due to an intermediate thermal optimum for transmission.
source_span: RRV incidence is often—but not always—positively associated with warmer temperatures ( Tong and Hu , 2001; Tong et al . , 2002a; Tong et al . , 2004; Hu et al . , 2004; Hu et al . , 2010; Jacups et al . , 2008b , Williams et al . , 2009; Werner et al . , 2012; Koolhof et al . , 2017 ) . However , variation in the effects of temperature on transmission across space and time is expected from an intermediate thermal optimum , especially when observed temperatures are near or varying around the optimum .
selection_reasoning: This fact captures a key biological insight about temperature's nonlinear effect on disease transmission.

fact: The strongest statistical signal of temperature on Ross River virus disease is expected in temperate regions where mean temperatures are near 20–25°C, the rapidly rising portion of the transmission curve.
source_span: The strongest statistical signal of temperature on disease is expected in temperate regions where mean temperature varies along the rapidly rising portion of the R0 curve ( ~20–25°C ) .

fact: A nonlinear mechanistic model is critical for estimating temperature impacts on Ross River virus transmission because increasing temperature can have positive, negligible, or negative effects depending on the thermal response curve position.
source_span: A nonlinear mechanistic model is critical for estimating temperature impacts on transmission because the effect of increasing temperature by a few degrees can have a positive , negligible , or negative impact on R0 along different parts of the thermal response curve .
selection_reasoning: This justifies the modeling approach and explains why simple linear models may fail.

fact: High temperatures above 32°C constrain Ross River virus transmission and mosquito vector populations, with mosquito populations peaking at around 25°C.
source_span: there is some evidence for high temperatures constraining RRV transmission and vector populations: outbreaks were less likely with more days above 35°C in part of Queensland ( Gatton et al . , 2005 ) and populations of Cx . annulirostris peaked at 25°C and declined above 32°C in Victoria ( Dhileepan , 1996 ) .

source_span: Breeding habitat availability also drives mosquito abundance and mosquito-borne disease . Local rainfall or river flow have been linked to the abundance of RRV vector species ( Barton et al . , 2004; Tall et al . , 2014; Jacups et al . , 2015 ) and RRV disease cases ( Tong and Hu , 2001; Tong et al . , 2002a; Hu et al . , 2004; Kelly-Hope et al . , 2004b; Tong et al . , 2004; Gatton et al . , 2005; Jacups et al . , 2008b; Bi et al . , 2009; Williams et al . , 2009; Werner et al . , 2012 ) , as have high tides in coastal areas with saltmarsh mosquitoes , Ae . vigilax and Ae . camptorhynchus ( Tong and Hu , 2002b; Tong et al . , 2004; Jacups et al . , 2008b; Kokkinn et al . , 2009 ) .

source_span: Since breeding habitat can only impact vector populations when temperatures do not exclude them , it is critical to consider thermal constraints on mosquito abundance , even when breeding habitat is considered a stronger driver .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the importance of integrating temperature effects with habitat factors in transmission models.

fact: Many mechanistic temperature-dependent models of vector-borne disease transmission do not include thermal effects on vector density, which can critically impact model results near thermal limits.
source_span: Nonetheless , many mechanistic , temperature-dependent models of vector-borne disease transmission do not include thermal effects on vector density ( Martens et al . , 1997; Craig et al . , 1999; Paull et al . , 2017; Caminade et al . , 2017; Hamlet et al . , 2018 ) . They should also integrate species-specific drivers of breeding habitat availability , like rainfall and tidal patterns , infrastructure ( e . g . drainage ) , and human activities ( e . g . deliberate and accidental water storage ) .

source_span: However , climate change will likely decrease transmission potential in tropical areas like Darwin , where moderate warming ( ~3°C ) would push temperatures above the upper thermal limit for transmission for most of the year ( Figure 5 ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding shows that climate change effects on transmission are regionally variable and depend on thermal limits.

fact: The full R0 model assumes temperature drives mosquito density and includes vector life history trait thermal responses.
source_span: The ‘full R0 model’ ( Equation 1 ) assumes temperature drives mosquito density and includes vector life history trait thermal responses ( Parham and Michael , 2009; Mordecai et al . , 2013; Mordecai et al . , 2017 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main modeling framework used to link temperature and transmission.

fact: The constant M model assumes mosquito density does not depend on temperature.
source_span: The ‘constant M model’ ( Equation 2 ) assumes mosquito density ( M ) does not depend on temperature ( Dietz , 1993 ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides a contrasting modeling assumption important for interpreting results.

fact: Key mosquito traits affecting transmission include biting rate, vector competence, adult mosquito mortality rate, parasite development rate, fecundity, egg-to-adult survival, and mosquito development rate, many of which depend on temperature.
source_span: In both equations , ( T ) indicates that a parameter depends on temperature , a is mosquito biting rate , bc is vector competence ( proportion of mosquitoes becoming infectious post-exposure ) , µ is adult mosquito mortality rate ( adult lifespan , lf = 1/µ ) , PDR is parasite development rate ( PDR = 1/EIP , the extrinsic incubation period ) , N is human density , and r is the recovery rate at which humans become immune ( all rates are measured in days−1 ) . The latter two terms do not depend on temperature . In the full R0 model , mosquito density ( M ) depends on fecundity ( EFD , eggs per female per day ) , proportion surviving from egg-to-adulthood ( pEA ) , and mosquito development rate ( MDR ) , divided by the square of adult mortality rate ( µ ) ( Parham and Michael , 2009 ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies the biological traits incorporated in the transmission model, essential for understanding the mechanistic basis of R0 variation.

fact: Thermal responses of mosquito traits were fit using Bayesian inference with Brière or quadratic functions to capture asymmetrical or symmetrical temperature effects.
source_span: Traits with asymmetrical thermal responses were fit as Brière functions: qT ( T–Tmin ) ( Tmax–T ) 1/2 ( Briere et al . , 1999 ) . Traits with symmetrical thermal responses were fit as quadratic functions: -q ( T–Tmin ) ( T–Tmax ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological approach to modeling temperature dependence of vector traits.

fact: Priors for thermal response models were derived from data on other mosquito species to improve fit accuracy and uncertainty representation.
source_span: For priors we used gamma distributions with hyperparameters derived from thermal responses fit to data from other mosquito species ( Figure 2—source data 2 ) ( Davis , 1932; Jalil , 1972; McLean et al . , 1974; Watts et al . , 1987; Rueda et al . , 1990; Focks et al . , 1993; Joshi , 1996; Teng and Apperson , 2000; Tun-Lin et al . , 2000; Alto and Juliano , 2001; Briegel and Timmermann , 2001; Kamimura et al . , 2002; Calado and Navarro-Silva , 2002; Focks and Barrera , 2006; Wiwatanaratanabutr and Kittayapong , 2006; Lardeux et al . , 2008; Delatte et al . , 2009; Beserra et al . , 2009; Yang et al . , 2009; Westbrook et al . , 2010; Muturi et al . , 2011; Carrington et al . , 2013; Tjaden et al . , 2013; Eisen et al . , 2014; Xiao et al . , 2014; Ezeakacha , 2015; Morin et al . , 2015 ) . These priors allowed us to more accurately represent the fit and uncertainty .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the robustness of the thermal trait modeling, relevant to the study's methodological rigor.

fact: Biting rate and parasite development rate traits decline at high temperatures, approaching zero near 40°C.
source_span: Data from other mosquito species (Mordecai et al., 2013; Mordecai et al., 2017) and principles of thermal biology (Dell et al., 2011) imply these traits must decline at high temperatures. Thus, for those traits we included an artificial data point where the trait value approached zero at a very high temperature (40°C), allowing us to fit the Brière function.
selection_reasoning: This fact is central to modeling temperature effects on transmission traits and thus on R0, a core aspect of the study.

fact: Bayesian inference was used to estimate posterior distributions of trait thermal responses and R0, with medians reported to reduce sensitivity to outliers.
source_span: Bayesian inference produces estimated posterior distributions rather than a single estimated value. Because these distributions can be non-normal and asymmetric, we report and apply medians rather than means, since medians are less sensitive to outlying values in extended tails.
selection_reasoning: Describes the key statistical approach used to model uncertainty and trait responses, important for understanding the study's methodology.

fact: Sensitivity and uncertainty analyses were conducted to determine how individual trait thermal responses influence the overall temperature-dependent transmission potential (R0).
source_span: We conducted sensitivity and uncertainty analyses of the full R0 model (Equation 1) to understand how trait thermal responses shape the thermal response of R0.
selection_reasoning: This highlights the main analytical approach to identify which traits most affect transmission across temperatures.

fact: The study used monthly mean temperatures from seven Australian cities spanning a latitudinal and temperature gradient to calculate temperature-dependent R0 values.
source_span: We took monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim for seven cities spanning a latitudinal and temperature gradient (from tropical North to temperate South: Darwin, Cairns, Brisbane, Perth, Sydney, Melbourne, and Hobart) and calculated the posterior median R0 (T) for each month at each location.
selection_reasoning: Describes the geographic and climatic scope of the temperature-based transmission modeling, relevant for understanding the study context.

fact: A population-weighted average R0 (T) was calculated for Australia's fifteen most populous urban areas and compared with nationally aggregated Ross River virus (RRV) case data.
source_span: We used 2016 estimates for the fifteen most populous urban areas, which together contain 76.6% of Australia’s population. We calculated R0 (T) for each location and estimated a population-weighted average. We compared this country-scale estimate of R0 (T) with data on mean monthly human cases of RRV nationwide from 1992 to 2013.
selection_reasoning: Connects modeled transmission potential to observed human disease data, a key validation and significance point.

fact: There is an estimated two-month time lag between temperature-driven transmission potential (R0) and reported human Ross River virus cases.
source_span: With monthly case data, we hypothesize a two-month time lag between R0 (T) and RRV disease cases.
selection_reasoning: This lag is important for interpreting the relationship between temperature and observed disease incidence.

fact: Maps of temperature suitability for Ross River virus transmission across Australia were generated by projecting R0 (T) onto spatial climate data at high resolution.
source_span: To illustrate temperature suitability for RRV transmission across Australia, we mapped the number of months for which relative R0 (T) >0 and >0.5 for the posterior median, 2.5 and 97.5% credibility bounds for the full R0 model. We calculated R0 (T) at 0.2°C increments and projected it onto the landscape for monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim data at a 5 min resolution (approximately 10 km2 at the equator).
selection_reasoning: Demonstrates the spatial application and public health relevance of the temperature-dependent transmission model.

fact: The study calculated the basic reproduction number (R0) for mosquito-borne disease transmission across temperature gradients using high-resolution climate data.
source_span: We calculated R0 ( T ) at 0 . 2°C increments and projected it onto the landscape for monthly mean temperatures from WorldClim data at a 5 min resolution ( approximately 10 km2 at the equator ) .
selection_reasoning: Calculating R0 across temperature gradients is central to understanding how temperature affects disease transmission, a core scientific claim likely reflected in the abstract.

fact: The geographic area for climate data extraction was defined using the Global Administrative Boundaries Databases (GADM, 2012).
source_span: Climate data layers were extracted for the geographic area , defined using the Global Administrative Boundaries Databases (GADM , 2012 ) .
selection_reasoning: Defining the geographic scope is important background for interpreting the spatial modeling of disease transmission.

fact: The study used mosquito fecundity and adult survival data from McDonald et al. (1980) to fit thermal response models for mosquito life-history traits.
source_span: The fecundity and adult survival data in McDonald et al . ( 1980 ) were published as time series of one experimental population at each temperature . The resulting data needed to be transformed to fit the corresponding trait thermal responses .
selection_reasoning: Using empirical life-history data to model thermal responses is a key methodological step supporting the study's main findings.

fact: Mosquito survival data were converted from percent surviving over time into lifespan data to fit thermal response models.
source_span: For survival , McDonald et al . reported the percent surviving approximately every other day ( hereafter: ‘semi-daily’ ) . We used these data—along with the number of female adults alive on the first day of oviposition at each temperature—to generate a semi-daily time series estimating the number surviving . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we converted this time series into the number of female individuals who died on each day ( i . e . lifespan data ) .
selection_reasoning: Transforming survival data into lifespan data is a key data processing step enabling accurate thermal response modeling.

fact: Mosquito fecundity data were adjusted by binning over gonotrophic cycle durations and weighting by survival to better represent daily fecundity for thermal response fitting.
source_span: Because the population was synchronized , and because mosquitoes lay discrete clutches of eggs separated by several days ( the gonotrophic cycle duration ) , there were many data points when the populations did not produce offspring . These zero-inflated fecundity data are not ideal for fitting thermal responses . Therefore , after digitizing the semi-daily fecundity time series , we binned periods of several days ( the bin size varied by temperature , since the gonotrophic cycle duration varies with temperature ) and took a survival-weighted average within each bin ( so days with more individual mothers contributing to offspring production counted more ) . To generate the dataset that we used to directly fit the thermal responses , we weighted the values within each bin by the mean number of surviving mothers in that bin .
selection_reasoning: Adjusting fecundity data to account for mosquito reproductive biology and survival is critical for accurate modeling of temperature effects on reproduction.

fact: The study used the genus name Aedes for mosquitoes despite a temporary taxonomic change to Ochlerotatus, reflecting current consensus.
source_span: In 2000 there was a proposed shift in mosquito taxonomy: several subgenera within the genus Aedes were elevated to genus status ( Wilkerson et al . , 2015 ) . This change affected Aedes vigilax and Aedes camptorhynchus , which were called Ochlerotataus vigilax and Ochlerotatus camptorhynchus for a time by some researchers . More recently , there has been a consensus to return to the previous naming system , so we use Aedes here , although many of the papers we cite use Ochlerotatus instead .
selection_reasoning: Clarifying mosquito taxonomy is important background for understanding the species studied and aligning with current nomenclature.

fact: Motor cortical beta oscillations have been observed for decades, but their specific behavioral correlates remain unclear.
source_span: Motor cortical beta oscillations have been reported for decades , yet their behavioral correlates remain unresolved .

selection_reasoning: This fact provides necessary background on when beta oscillations occur in motor behavior, relevant to understanding their role.

fact: The study used a novel neurofeedback task in which three macaque monkeys volitionally modulated their motor cortical beta oscillatory power before performing an arm reach.
source_span: To investigate how changes in population neural activity , beta oscillations , and behavior are linked , we recorded multi-scale neural activity from motor cortex while three macaques performed a novel neurofeedback task . Subjects volitionally brought their beta oscillatory power to an instructed state and subsequently executed an arm reach .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental approach linking beta oscillations and behavior.

source_span: Reaches preceded by a reduction in beta power exhibited significantly faster movement onset times than reaches preceded by an increase in beta power .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal behavioral finding directly linking beta oscillations to movement speed.

source_span: Thus , in this study we interpret beta oscillations as a statistic of synchronization of the underlying neural signals , not as a signal that can independently and causally influence neural spiking via ephaptic effects .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the conceptual framework for interpreting beta oscillations in the study.

fact: Prior studies showed that single neurons synchronize to beta oscillations but do not change their mean firing rate, though spiking variability decreases during oscillations.
source_span: Prior studies investigating neural activity changes during beta oscillations used acute , single-electrode recording preparations and showed that single cells are synchronized to ongoing oscillations but that the strength of this synchronization is unrelated to the involvement of the neuron during the motor task ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996a ) . These studies also show individual cells do not change their mean spike firing rate but do exhibit a reduction in spiking variability during oscillations compared to the variability exhibited before the oscillation ( Murthy and Fetz , 1996b ) .
selection_reasoning: This background fact helps contextualize the neural activity changes associated with beta oscillations.

source_span: Explaining when beta oscillations emerge and how they reflect underlying neural population computations is challenging given their presence during a multitude of behaviors .

fact: Beta oscillations in the 25–40 Hz range are associated with movement-related desynchronization in the macaque motor cortex during reaching tasks.
source_span: A movement onset-aligned trial-averaged spectrogram from the intracortical recordings in contralateral motor and premotor cortex (e.g. Monkey C in Figure 1d) showed that the clearest movement-related desynchronization was in the 25–40 Hz band for all monkeys, consistent with early reports of beta oscillations in the macaque motor cortex (Baker et al., 1997; Murthy and Fetz, 1992).
selection_reasoning: This fact provides key background on the neural signature (beta oscillations) relevant to motor behavior, which is central to the study's focus.

fact: Three macaque monkeys were trained to perform a center-out arm-reaching task and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task to study how beta oscillations reflect changes in spiking activity and movement parameters.
source_span: To explore how beta oscillations reflect changes in spiking activity and movement parameters, we trained three macaque monkeys to perform a typical center-out arm-reaching task (CO task) and a novel sequential beta neurofeedback arm-reaching task (NR task).
selection_reasoning: This describes the main experimental approach used to investigate the relationship between beta oscillations and motor behavior.

fact: During the neurofeedback-reaching task, monkeys modulated their motor cortical beta band power to control a cursor and successfully completed the neurofeedback epoch above chance levels.
source_span: Subjects modulated endogenous motor cortical local field potential signals to move the vertical position of the beta cursor... During NR task performance from these days, subjects exhibited above chance performance.

source_span: Notably, this shift in neural population was also seen in naturally occurring beta oscillations during reaching tasks, suggesting that beta oscillations reflect a common signature of spiking patterns even in different task contexts.

fact: Beta oscillatory events were identified by filtering local field potential signals at 25–40 Hz and labeling timepoints exceeding the 60th percentile amplitude threshold as 'on-beta' if they lasted at least 125 ms.
source_span: To determine when the beta oscillatory events occurred , the following procedure was applied . The local field potential ( LFP ) signal from one of the electrodes used in the neurofeedback task was selected , and filtered at 25–40 Hz with a fifth order Butterworth filter . The amplitude of the filtered signal was estimated with the Hilbert transform . Each day , a distribution of amplitude values was computed by aggregating all rewarded trials from that day . A threshold was set at the 60th percentile of the resultant distribution . Then , all timepoints surpassing the threshold were labeled with a 1 . All other points were labeled with a 0 . Then , the length of each block of uninterrupted '1s' was computed , and if the block was longer than 125 ms ( so the oscillatory episode lasted at least 3–4 cycles as described in Murthy and Fetz ( 1996a ) ; Sherman et al . , 2016 ) , the block remained as is . If the block was less than 125 ms , all points in the block were changed back to '0s' .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key method for detecting beta oscillations, central to the study's analysis of neural activity.

This threshold was chosen because using it yielded the best discrete classifier performance separating slow spiking patterns from fast spiking patterns in Monkeys G and C’s CO task in comparison with other thresholds ( data not shown ) .

fact: Movement onset time during the arm-reaching epoch was computed by projecting cursor velocity onto a vector toward the target and identifying when speed rose above 20% of peak speed.
source_span: To compute movement onset time for the arm-reaching epoch in the NR task , we used a method inspired by Churchland and Shenoy ( 2007 ) . First , the x and y cursor velocity over the course of the reach ( t x 2 ) was projected onto a unit vector pointing from the center to peripheral target . The norm of the projected cursor velocities yielded a single time series of projected speed ( t x 1 ) . The index and value of maximum projected hand speed was computed and called ( i , M ) . Starting at i , we scanned backwards in time ( i-1 , i-2 , … ) until the value of the projected hand speed fell below 20% of the peak hand speed ( 0 . 2*M , see Figure 1f ) . This timepoint was called the movement onset time and was used because it allowed for comparisons across different reach targets , animals , and experimental setups without having to define absolute hand velocity cutoffs .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key method for defining movement onset, important for aligning neural and behavioral data.
