fact: Supernumerary chromosomes in N. haematococca MPVI may have originated through interspecific hybridization or parasexual cycles allowing DNA exchange between fungal species.
source_span: It also has been proposed that B chromosomes could arise from A chromosomes following interspecific hybridization in sexual crosses [66]... Extending the mechanism of hybridization to include the well-known parasexual cycle that occurs in some fungi provides another explanation of the origin of supernumerary chromosomes in N. haematococca MPVI.
selection_reasoning: This fact presents a plausible mechanism for the origin of these chromosomes, important for interpreting their evolutionary significance.

fact: The exchange of supernumerary chromosomes has been demonstrated experimentally but only between members of the same fungal species.
source_span: The exchange of supernumerary chromosomes has been demonstrated in the laboratory, but thus far only between members of the same species [71], [72].
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the possibility of chromosome transfer as a mechanism for genetic variation, relevant to the study's implications.

fact: Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) may contribute to the presence of unique genes on non-supernumerary chromosomes in N. haematococca MPVI.
source_span: Unique genes on non-supernumerary chromosomes with atypical G+C content and codon preference are also potential pseudoparalogs obtained by HGT [41], [44], [46], [47].
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses an additional mechanism of gene acquisition relevant to genome evolution and adaptation.

fact: Although horizontal gene transfer is not considered common in fungi, increasing evidence suggests it occurs and may contribute to gene acquisition in N. haematococca MPVI.
source_span: Although HGT has not been considered to be a common mechanism of gene acquisition in fungi [73], there is an increasing number of examples of apparent HGT [74]–[76].
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context on the significance of HGT in fungal genome evolution, relevant to interpreting findings.

fact: The supernumerary chromosomes of N. haematococca MPVI share properties with genomic islands found in Aspergillus fumigatus, including species-specific genes and repetitive DNA.
source_span: Many of the properties of the supernumerary chromosomes are similar to genomic islands of A. fumigatus [42]. These species-specific regions of DNA can be as large as 400 kb, and contain A. fumigatus-specific genes and large amounts of repetitive DNA.
selection_reasoning: This fact links the study organism's genome features to known genomic structures in other fungi, supporting broader biological relevance.

fact: Genes on the supernumerary chromosomes and genomic islands encode metabolic processes involved in adaptation to different ecological niches.
source_span: The genes on these genomic islands, like those on the supernumerary chromosomes, encode metabolic processes that appear to be involved in the adaptation to different ecological niches.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the functional importance of these genomic regions for ecological adaptation, a key implication.

fact: The active RIP (Repeat-Induced Point mutation) system in N. haematococca MPVI limits gene duplication but gene acquisition via horizontal gene transfer or similar mechanisms can bypass this constraint.
source_span: The ability of N. haematococca MPVI to acquire genes by HGT or a similar mechanism would bypass the evolutionary restraint that an active RIP system places on a fungus by hindering the utility of gene duplications as a means to create new genes functions [50].
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key genomic mechanism affecting gene evolution and acquisition, central to understanding genome dynamics.

fact: In N. haematococca MPVI, unique genes are often located in sub-telomeric regions of certain chromosomes, which is a pattern also observed in other fungi for genes involved in habitat association and pathogenicity.
source_span: In N. haematococca MPVI, gene placements differ among the chromosomes. Chromosomes 1, 4, 5, and 9 have most of their unique genes in the sub-telomeric regions... In other fungi, genes involved in specific habitat associations, including pathogenicity, also are often located in the sub-telomeric regions [78].
selection_reasoning: This fact provides insight into genome organization related to function and adaptation, relevant to the study's findings.

fact: Chromosome 7 of N. haematococca MPVI is a large chromosome with many unique genes and the largest number of possible pseudoparalogs among all chromosomes.
source_span: Chromosome 7 is unusual in that it is a large chromosome (3.0 Mb) that has some properties of the smaller chromosomes. For example, the majority of the genes on chromosome 7 are unique to N. haematococca MPVI... Chromosome 7 also has the largest number of possible pseudoparalogs (159) of all the chromosomes.
selection_reasoning: This fact identifies a notable genomic feature that may be important for understanding gene content and evolution.

fact: The sequenced isolate of N. haematococca MPVI (77-13-4) is a third generation progeny from a laboratory cross between two field isolates.
source_span: Only one isolate of N. haematococca MPVI (77-13-4) was sequenced in the current study and it is a third generation progeny from a laboratory cross between two field isolates.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential context about the genetic background of the sequenced strain, relevant for interpreting results.

fact: Field isolates of N. haematococca MPVI show a high degree of chromosomal polymorphism and differences in gene locations.
source_span: An examination of field isolates of this fungus has revealed a high degree of chromosomal polymorphism and differences in the locations of studied genes [80].
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights natural genomic variation, important for understanding the species' genome diversity and evolution.

fact: Nectria haematococca MPVI isolate 77-13-4 was used for whole-genome sequencing to study its genome.
source_span: Whole-genome shotgun libraries ( 3-kb , 8-kb , and 40-kb DNA inserts ) of 77-13-4 were constructed and sequenced as previously described [84].
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main biological material and the high-level method used, which is central to the study.

fact: Two cDNA libraries were constructed from N. haematococca 77-13-4 mycelia grown in rich medium, one treated with the plant defense compound pisatin, to facilitate gene annotation.
source_span: Two cDNA libraries were constructed and sequenced to facilitate the automated gene calling programs. The RNA for the cDNA libraries was obtained from mycelia treated in two different ways: both were grown in a rich medium, potato dextrose broth, (PDB) ... and one of these was treated with pisatin.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key experimental approach used to improve gene prediction and to study gene expression relevant to plant interaction.

fact: The N. haematococca MPVI genome assembly consists of approximately 51 million base pairs with an estimated error rate of less than 1 in 100,000 base pairs.
source_span: The genome consists of 51,149,575 base pairs of finished sequence with an estimated error rate of less than 1 error in 100,000 bp.
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a key result about the genome size and quality, important for understanding the genomic resource generated.

fact: The genome assembly was validated and scaffolded using an optical map generated by NheI digestion, placing over 92% of the sequence onto 17 chromosome maps.
source_span: The resulting assembly was joined and validated by alignments to a N. haematococca optical map (generated by digestion with NheI), with 92.26% of the sequence (72 scaffolds or 47,191,137 bp) being placed onto 17 chromosome optical maps.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key method and validation step ensuring the genome assembly's accuracy and chromosome-level organization.

fact: A total of 15,707 gene models were predicted and automatically annotated in the N. haematococca MPVI genome using multiple gene prediction tools and EST evidence.
source_span: Gene models (15,707) were predicted and automatically annotated using the Joint Genome Institute (JGI) Annotation Pipeline. Several gene predictors were used on repeat masked assembly: ab initio FGENESH and homology-based FGENESH+ and Genewise. The predicted gene models were verified, corrected, and extended using 33,142 N. haematococca MPVI ESTs.
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the key outcome of genome annotation, which is central to the study's goal of characterizing the genome.

fact: Functional annotation of predicted genes was performed by homology to known proteins and classification according to Gene Ontology, KOGs, and KEGG pathways.
source_span: All predicted gene models were functionally annotated by homology to proteins from the NCBI non-redundant set and classified according to Gene Ontology, eukaryotic orthologous groups (KOGs), and KEGG metabolic pathways.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the important step of assigning biological meaning to gene predictions, relevant for interpreting the genome.

fact: N. haematococca MPVI proteins were compared to proteins from multiple fungal genomes to identify homologs and evolutionary relationships.
source_span: Each predicted protein from the N. haematococca MPVI genome was used as a query in a TBLASTN search of a database consisting of the genomes of A. oryzae, A. nidulans, C. globosum, C. immitis, F. graminearum, M. oryzae, N. crassa, and S. cerevisiae.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a comparative genomics approach to place the genome in an evolutionary context, a key scientific question.

fact: The genomes of multiple fungi species including Aspergillus oryzae, Aspergillus nidulans, Chaetomium globosum, Coccidioides immitis, Fusarium graminearum, Magnaporthe oryzae, Neurospora crassa, and Saccharomyces cerevisiae were analyzed to identify protein homologs.
source_span: the genomes of A . oryzae , A . nidulans , C . globosum , C . immitis , F . graminearum , M . oryzae , N . crassa , and S . cerevisiae . For each protein query , the genome with the best hit below a threshold of 1e-5 was identified .
selection_reasoning: This background fact establishes the comparative genomic context and species analyzed, which is essential for understanding the study scope.

fact: Repetitive regions in the genome were identified by dividing the genome into 1 kb windows and labeling windows as repetitive if they matched other regions longer than 500 bp.
source_span: To identify repetitive regions of the genome in the absence of a curated repeat library , the genome was divided into 1 kb non-overlapping windows and BLASTN was used to align each against the complete genome . If the only match greater than 500 bp was a self-match , then the window was labeled as unique , otherwise it was labeled as repetitive .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key method used to characterize genome structure relevant to the study's findings.

fact: A transformant of Neurospora haematococca containing multiple copies of the hph gene was crossed with another strain to study the linkage of the hph gene to the homoserine utilization phenotype.
source_span: A transformant ( Tr78 . 2 ) of N . haematococca that contained several copies of the hph gene from the transformation vector pCWHyg1 , was crossed ( cross 370 ) with 77-15-7 as previously described . The hph gene is linked to the homoserine utilization phenotype ( HUT ) in Tr78 . 2 and 370 progeny were screened for hygromycin sensitivity and HUT .
selection_reasoning: This fact relates to a genetic experiment central to understanding gene linkage and phenotype, a key finding.

fact: All progeny from the cross were sensitive to hygromycin, and half exhibited the homoserine utilization phenotype.
source_span: All forty progeny from cross 370 were sensitive to hygromycin , and half were HUT+ .
selection_reasoning: This result is a principal finding about the genetic linkage and phenotype segregation.

fact: Chromosome-sized DNA preparations and pulsed-field gel electrophoresis were used to analyze chromosomes of Neurospora haematococca isolates.
source_span: The preparation of chromosome-sized DNAs and the PFGE were performed essentially as described previously . Protoplasts were embedded in low melting temperature agarose and chromosome-sized DNAs were separated in 0 . 5× TBE buffer on a 1% pulsed field certified agarose gel with a contour-clamped homogeneous electric field apparatus .
selection_reasoning: This high-level method is important for understanding how chromosomal analysis was conducted.

fact: PCR was used to test for the presence of sequences at the ends of chromosomes 14, 15, and 17 in different Neurospora haematococca isolates.
source_span: PCR was used to test for the presence of sequences found on the ends of the assembled sequences representing chromosomes 14 , 15 , and 17 in isolates 77-13-7 , 77-13-4 , B-33 , and HT-1 .
selection_reasoning: This method is central to the study's investigation of chromosome structure and variation.

fact: Segmental duplicated regions in the genome were defined as regions sharing at least three genes in the same order and orientation with neighboring gene pairs less than 50 kb apart.
source_span: Segmental duplicated regions were defined as genomic regions that share at least three genes in the same order and orientation , while the distance between neighboring gene pairs is less than 50 kb .
selection_reasoning: This definition is key to understanding the genomic structural analysis and findings.

fact: Inherited mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations are a common cause of human disease and occur multiple times in the global population.
source_span: Inherited mitochondrial DNA ( mtDNA ) mutations have emerged as a common cause of human disease , with mutations occurring multiple times in the world population .
selection_reasoning: This provides essential background on the disease relevance and prevalence of mtDNA mutations, motivating the study.

fact: The clinical presentation of three pathogenic mtDNA mutations causing Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy (LHON) is strongly associated with specific mtDNA haplogroups.
source_span: Many of these variants have recurred several times in different populations and on diverse haplogroup backgrounds , but the clinical presentation of mutations causing Leber Hereditary Optic Neuropathy ( LHON: m . 14484T>C , m . 3460G>A , m . 11778G>A ) are strongly associated with a specific mtDNA haplogroup[3 , 4] .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a key known example linking mtDNA haplogroup background to disease expression, framing the main research question.

fact: It was unclear whether the association between mtDNA haplogroup background and pathogenic mutations is limited to a few examples or is a more general phenomenon.
source_span: The clinical presentation of three pathogenic mtDNA mutations is strongly associated with a background mtDNA haplogroup , but it is not clear whether this is limited to a handful of examples or is a more general phenomenon .
selection_reasoning: This states the main research question motivating the study.

fact: The study analyzed 30,506 globally sampled human mtDNA sequences to investigate the relationship between pathogenic mutations and mtDNA haplogroups.
source_span: To address this , we determined the characteristics of 30 , 506 mtDNA sequences sampled globally .
selection_reasoning: This describes the large dataset used to address the research question.

fact: The mean pathogenicity score for known disease-causing mtDNA mutations differed significantly between major mtDNA macro-haplogroups.
source_span: The mean pathogenicity score for known disease-causing mutations was significantly different between mtDNA macro-haplogroups .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking mutation pathogenicity to haplogroup background.

fact: Some pathogenic mtDNA mutations were found across all haplogroup backgrounds, while others were restricted to specific phylogenetic clades.
source_span: Several mutations were observed across all haplogroup backgrounds , whereas others were only observed on specific clades .
selection_reasoning: This finding shows variation in mutation distribution relevant to understanding mutation recurrence and haplogroup specificity.

fact: Certain pathogenic mtDNA mutations recurred multiple times but only within the same phylogenetic cluster, suggesting a role for haplogroup background in mutation recurrence.
source_span: In some instances this reflected a founder effect , but in others , the mutation recurred but only within the same phylogenetic cluster .
selection_reasoning: This supports the idea that haplogroup background influences mutation recurrence patterns.

fact: Disease-causing mtDNA mutations were more frequent on younger sequences, and genomes with two or more such mutations were more common than expected by chance.
source_span: Sequence diversity estimates showed that disease-causing mutations were more frequent on young sequences , and genomes with two or more disease-causing mutations were more common than expected by chance .
selection_reasoning: This finding relates to mutation age and accumulation, important for understanding mutation dynamics and selection.

fact: The mtDNA background influences recurrent mutation events that have been removed by natural selection in older populations.
source_span: These findings implicate the mtDNA background more generally in recurrent mutation events that have been purified through natural selection in older populations .
selection_reasoning: This provides a mechanistic explanation for observed mutation patterns and their evolutionary significance.

fact: The study's findings explain the low frequency of mtDNA disease reported in specific ethnic groups.
source_span: This provides an explanation for the low frequency of mtDNA disease reported in specific ethnic groups .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the clinical and population health relevance of the research.

fact: Human mtDNA is maternally inherited and undergoes negligible recombination, leading to geographically restricted haplogroups defined by single nucleotide variants.
source_span: Human mitochondrial DNA ( mtDNA ) is exclusively maternally inherited and undergoes negligible recombination at the population level . As humans emerged from Africa and populated the globe , different sub-populations acquired single nucleotide variants ( SNVs ) that define geographically-restricted mtDNA ‘haplogroups’[1] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact is necessary to understand the genetic structure underlying the study.

fact: The 30,506 mtDNA sequences analyzed were representative of global populations and not significantly enriched for rare or pathogenic variants from patient samples.
source_span: When taken together , these analysis ( Fig 1A–1E ) , indicate that the 30 , 506 GenBank sequences are a representative sample of the background populations and not significantly enriched for rare population variants or pathogenic mutations identified through patients presenting with mitochondrial diseases .
selection_reasoning: This supports the validity of the dataset for population-level conclusions.

fact: Ninety of the 202 proposed pathogenic mtDNA variants listed on the ClinVar database were found in the 30,506 mtDNA sequences studied.
source_span: Ninety of the 202 proposed pathogenic mtDNA variants listed on the ClinVar database[11] were found in the 30 , 506 mtDNA sequences studied here ( S3 Table ) .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the scope of pathogenic variants detected in the large dataset, relevant for understanding the study's basis.

fact: After incorporating published and online evidence of pathogenicity, the number of likely pathogenic mtDNA mutations was reduced from 90 to 57.
source_span: Incorporating published and on-line evidence of pathogenicity ( see Methods ) , the number of likely pathogenic mutations reduced from 90 to 57 ( S4 Table ) .
selection_reasoning: This refines the set of mutations considered truly pathogenic, a key step in the analysis.

fact: Variants with higher pathogenicity scores were less frequent in the population, and disease-causing mutations had significantly higher pathogenicity scores than all possible variants.
source_span: As expected , variants with a higher pathogenicity score were less frequent in the population , and disease-causing mutations with a higher pathogenicity score were less frequent in the population ( Fig 2C ) . Likewise , as expected , the probability distribution of pathogenicity scores for disease-causing mutations was significantly greater than the overall distribution of pathogenicity scores in the entire population ( mean = 0 . 59 for disease-causing mutations , mean = 0 . 37 for all possible variants; two-sample t-test , p-value < 2 . 2e-16 , Fig 2C ) .
selection_reasoning: This confirms the expected relationship between pathogenicity and variant frequency, supporting the validity of the pathogenicity scoring.

fact: Disease-causing mutations on macro-haplogroups N and M backgrounds had significantly higher pathogenicity scores than those on the macro-haplogroup L background.
source_span: However , we were surprised to see that disease-causing mutations on the macro-haplogroup N and M backgrounds had significantly higher pathogenicity score than those occurring on the macro-haplogroup L background ( mean = 0 . 47 for L group , mean = 0 . 62 for M group , mean = 0 . 59 for N group; L versus M: p-value = 1 . 959e-11 , L versus N: p-value = 7 . 992e-08 , M versus N: p-value = 8 . 967e-07 , two-sample t test , Fig 2D ) .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a key finding about how mtDNA background influences mutation pathogenicity.

fact: The proportion of mtDNA sequences carrying at least one disease-causing mutation was highest in macro-haplogroup M (7.8%), followed by N (5.2%), and lowest in L (2.2%).
source_span: 83 ( 2 . 2% ) mtDNA sequences carried at least one disease-causing mutation in L group , 481 ( 7 . 8% ) in M group and 1 , 057 ( 5 . 2% ) in N group . Group M sequences had a higher proportion of sequences carrying disease-causing mutations 481 ( 7 . 8% ) , followed by group N sequences 1 , 057 ( 5 . 2% ) , with the lowest in group L 83 ( 2 . 2% ) ( L versus M: p-value = 1 . 39e-36 , L versus N: p-value = 9 . 49e-19 , M versus N: p-value = 1 . 43e-13 , Fisher test , Fig 2E ) .
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the differential burden of disease-causing mutations across haplogroups, a central result.

fact: For macro-haplogroup N, the number of mtDNA sequences harboring two or more disease-causing mutations was six-fold lower than expected by chance, suggesting selective constraints.
source_span: For macro-haplogroups L and M , the observed frequency of mtDNAs with two of more disease-causing mutations was no different to the chance co-occurrence . However , for macro-haplogroup N sequences , the number of mtDNA sequences harboring two of more disease-causing mutations was 6-fold lower than expected by chance ( p-value = 5 . 96e-09 , Fisher test; Fig 2F ) .
selection_reasoning: This indicates haplogroup-specific differences in mutation co-occurrence, relevant to understanding mutation dynamics.

fact: Twenty-five of the 57 likely pathogenic mtDNA mutations were present on more than one macro-haplogroup, indicating recurrent mutation events.
source_span: Twenty-five ( 43 . 9% ) of the 57 diseases-causing mutations were present on more than one macro-haplogroup , and 34 ( 59 . 6% ) were present on more than one major haplogroup ( Fig 3A , S5 Fig ) , indicating recurrent mutation events .
selection_reasoning: This shows that many pathogenic mutations arise independently in different mtDNA backgrounds.

fact: Some pathogenic mtDNA mutations were only found on one haplogroup, consistent with single founder events or possibly being rare sub-haplogroup markers rather than directly pathogenic.
source_span: On the other hand , m . 5631G>A ( L ) , m . 10663T>C ( L ) , m . 8313G>A ( M ) , m . 12770A>G ( M ) , and m . 3890G>A ( N ) were only seen on one clade , consistent with a single founder event . This raises the possibility that these several ‘disease-causing’ mutations are actually rare sub-haplogroup markers and not directly pathogenic ( eg m . 4295A>G , m . 6489C>A ) .
selection_reasoning: This nuance is important for interpreting the pathogenicity of some mutations in the context of haplogroup background.

fact: There was statistical evidence of haplogroup clustering for 10 of the 34 recurrent disease-causing mtDNA mutations after correcting for sample size.
source_span: Overall , we found statistical evidence of haplogroup clustering for 10 ( 29 . 4% ) of the 34 recurrent disease-causing mtDNA mutations after correcting for the sample size within each comparison ( p-value < 0 . 01 , Fisher test; Fig 3B ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the idea that certain pathogenic mutations preferentially occur or persist in specific haplogroups.

fact: Across all macro-haplogroups, C>T/A>G and T>C/A>G substitutions were the most prominent mutation types for both all variants and disease-causing mutations.
source_span: Overall , across all macro-haplogroups we saw a greater prominence of C>T/A>G and T>C/A>G substitutions for all variants ( p< 2 . 2e-16 , Fisher test; Fig 4A–4C ) , and for disease causing mutations ( p< 2 . 2e-16 , Fisher test; Fig 4D–4F ) .
selection_reasoning: This identifies key mutational signatures relevant to understanding mtDNA mutation processes.

fact: The observed mutational signatures were not driven by the choice of reference sequence, as similar patterns were seen when aligning to the Reconstructed Sapiens Reference Sequence (RSRS).
source_span: In order to confirm the prominence of C>T and T>C mutations observed were not due to the selection of the rCRS [13] as the “reference” by which the mutations are classified , we realigned 30 , 506 mtDNA sequences to Reconstructed Sapiens Reference Sequence ( RSRS ) [14] . We observed similar patterns , with T>C and C>T substitutions frequently observed ( S6 Fig ) , suggesting the profiles of mutational signatures were not driven by the alignment process and are independent of the reference sequence used in the analysis .
selection_reasoning: This validates the robustness of the mutational signature findings.

fact: Disease-causing mutations showed a higher proportion of CpG dinucleotides compared to all variants, suggesting a role for CpG mutability in pathogenic mtDNA mutations.
source_span: We also observed that the higher mutability of CpG dinucleotides in disease-causing mutations when compared to all variants ( CpG% , p-value = 0 . 00017 , Fisher exact test; S7 Fig and S5 Table ) .
selection_reasoning: This implicates CpG sites as hotspots for pathogenic mutations, relevant for mutation origin hypotheses.

fact: Macro-haplogroup M had the highest proportion of CpG dinucleotides in both all variants and disease-causing mutations compared to haplogroups L and N.
source_span: Intriguingly , macro-haplogroup M had highest CpG% for all variants ( 19 . 93%; L versus M , p-value < 2 . 2e-16 and M versus N p-value < 2 . 2e-16 Fisher exact test ) and defined diseases-causing mutations ( 21 . 21%; L versus M , p-value = 0 . 00049; and M versus N , p-value = 1 . 06e-06 ) .
selection_reasoning: This suggests haplogroup-specific sequence context influences mutation patterns and pathogenicity.

fact: Macro-haplogroup L had a much lower proportion of CpG dinucleotides in disease-causing mutations compared to haplogroups M and N.
source_span: By contrast , macro-haplogroup L had much lower CpG% than other two groups for disease-causing mutations ( 5 . 88%; L versus M p-value = 0 . 00049 and L versus N p-value = 0 . 15 ) ( S7 Fig and S6 Table ) .
selection_reasoning: This further supports the influence of haplogroup-specific sequence context on mutation characteristics.

fact: Haplogroup-specific sequence context influences the acquisition of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) mutations.

fact: Coxsackievirus B3 (CVB3) almost completely inhibits antigen presentation via the MHC class I pathway, thereby evading CD8+ T cell immunity.
source_span: Herein , we employ transgenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells as sensors to evaluate in vitro and in vivo antigen presentation by coxsackievirus B3 ( CVB3 ) , and we show that this virus almost completely inhibits antigen presentation via the MHC class I pathway , thereby evading CD8+ T cell immunity .

A considerable proportion of CVB infections trigger severe acute and chronic diseases and cause morbidity and mortality , particularly in infants , young children , and immunocompromised individuals ; CVB are the most common cause of infectious myocarditis , a serious disease that can lead to dilated cardiomyopathy and cardiac failure , and also frequently induce pancreatitis and aseptic meningitis .

selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the effectiveness of the CRISPR gRNAs in generating targeted mutations, a core experimental finding.

fact: Whole genome sequencing (WGS) was performed on selected mice with varying numbers of alleles targeted by Tyr2R and Tyr2F gRNAs to analyze mutations.
source_span: In order to cover a representative range of alleles at the on-target site, we selected the following mice for WGS analysis: for the Tyr2R sample 1 mouse with one allele, 3 mice with two alleles and 1 mouse with three alleles; for the Tyr2F sample 1 mouse with one allele, 3 mice with two alleles and 1 mouse with three alleles (in total five embryos Tyr2F and five embryos for Tyr2R).
selection_reasoning: This describes the key method of selecting samples for detailed mutation analysis, relevant to the study design.

fact: The median sequencing coverage for whole genome sequencing of the mouse samples was approximately 39.5x, enabling reliable mutation detection.
source_span: The total mapped coverage varied from 34x to 47x, with a median of 39.5x (Fig 1B).
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the reliability of mutation detection from WGS data, important for interpreting results.

fact: The observed median allele fraction for on-target mutations was 28%, consistent with heterozygous mutations arising at the two-cell embryo stage.
source_span: Our median observed on-target variant allele fraction was 0.28 (median of column I, S6 Table). This allele fraction is represented by 11 variant reads out of 39.5 reads, and most likely arises from a heterozygous mutation in the two-cell embryo.
selection_reasoning: This finding links mutation allele frequency to developmental timing, a key biological insight.

fact: The sequencing depth and allele fraction provide over 99.5% power to detect de novo mutations occurring at or before the two-cell embryo stage.
source_span: This suggests that when we sequence our 12.5dpc embryos, we should detect DNMs, which occur in a two-cell embryo (or earlier) at least 99.5% of the time.
selection_reasoning: This fact establishes the sensitivity of the mutation detection approach, critical for interpreting negative or positive findings.

fact: De novo mutations were called jointly in parents and offspring using bcftools and TrioDeNovo software, producing thousands of candidate mutations per offspring before filtering.
source_span: Aligned sequence was jointly variant called for all parents and offspring using bcftools mpileup, bcftools call, bcftools norm and bcftools filter[7]... De novo mutation calling on all variants was performed by running TrioDeNovo software[8]... TrioDeNovo produced between 6,437 and 7,732 candidate mutations per offspring; with a median of 6,852 mutations (S4 Table).
selection_reasoning: This describes the key computational approach to identify candidate de novo mutations, central to the study.

fact: A stringent filtering pipeline was applied to candidate de novo mutations to remove false positives caused by low allele fraction variants in parents, known strain variants, repeats, and shared variants.
source_span: Based on the read depths and variant allele fractions seen in the expected on-target mutations called by TrioDeNovo, we filtered all candidate de novo variants with the following criteria... (1) minimum variant allele fraction of 10%... (2) removed variants with any alternate-allele reads present in either parent... (3) removed any variant coincident with an allele reported in the C57BL/6NJ strain or C57BL/6NTyr strain... (4) allowed a maximum contribution of only 2% alternate reads from all other samples... (5) removed any variant inside or 1bp adjacent to any merged repeat region... (6) removed any de novo variant shared by two or more samples... (7) every variant locus was visually inspected... (8) visually inspected all indel variants to remove any variant still in or adjacent to microsatellites/homopolymers.
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the critical quality control steps ensuring the reliability of mutation calls, important for the study's validity.

fact: The study investigated potential off-target mutations caused by CRISPR-Cas9 editing using two guide RNAs, Tyr2F and Tyr2R, in mouse embryos.
source_span: The CAS-OFFinder tool[9] was used to find all potential off-targets sites based on sequence homology to either the Tyr2F or Tyr2R gRNAs ...
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the main experimental focus and the biological system used, which is central to the study's question about CRISPR off-target effects.

fact: Potential off-target sites for Tyr2F and Tyr2R gRNAs were identified allowing up to 3 mismatches with 1 bp indel and up to 4 mismatches with no indels, resulting in 395 and 1,502 sites respectively.
source_span: The CAS-OFFinder tool[9] was used to find all potential off-targets sites based on sequence homology to either the Tyr2F or Tyr2R gRNAs, allowing up to 3 mismatches with 1 bp of inserted or deleted sequence and up to 4 mismatches with no inserted or deleted sequence. This resulted in 395 and 1,502 potential off-target sites being detected for Tyr2F and Tyr2R, respectively.
selection_reasoning: This high-level method detail is important to understand how off-target sites were predicted, which is key to the study's approach.

fact: The number of observed overlaps between candidate de novo mutations (DNMs) and predicted off-target sites was lower but of the same order of magnitude as expected by chance.
source_span: Using bedtools-2 . 23 window–w10, we found between 4 and 14 overlaps per sample ... which is lower, but the same order of magnitude as the estimate.
selection_reasoning: This finding addresses the main question about whether CRISPR editing causes off-target mutations, indicating no excess overlap beyond chance.

fact: Statistical tests found no significant difference in the number of overlaps between candidate DNMs and predicted off-target sites when comparing CRISPR-treated and untreated animals.
source_span: We assessed the null hypothesis ... and found no significant difference in intersection counts between the population of treated animals and the population of untreated animals.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding supporting the conclusion that CRISPR treatment did not increase off-target mutations.

fact: Visual inspection and filtering were used to remove false positive indel variants arising from un-annotated microsatellites or repeats.
source_span: We found indel variants to be especially susceptible to false positive calls arising from un-annotated microsatellites or repeats, so we visually inspected all indel variants to remove any variant still in or adjacent to microsatellites/homopolymers...
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a key quality control step important for the reliability of mutation calls.

fact: Using distantly related parents as controls in trio analyses inflates the number of detected de novo mutations by approximately 66.5 false positives per animal.
source_span: This demonstrates the effect of using unrelated or distantly related parents as controls, when searching for CRISPR off-targets, is an inflation of 66.5 false positive variants and reinforces the need for studies to use trios in these experiments.
selection_reasoning: This finding has important implications for experimental design and interpretation in CRISPR off-target studies.

fact: The majority of candidate single nucleotide variants (87%) and indels (73%) were validated by deep sequencing in embryos and parents.
source_span: We found that 87% of SNVs and 73% of indels were validated (S8 Table).
selection_reasoning: This supports the reliability of the mutation detection approach, which is critical for the study's conclusions.

fact: Using unrelated or distantly related parents as controls in CRISPR off-target studies inflates false positive variant counts by about 66.5 variants.
source_span: This demonstrates the effect of using unrelated or distantly related parents as controls, when searching for CRISPR off-targets, is an inflation of 66.5 false positive variants and reinforces the need for studies to use trios in these experiments.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key methodological consideration important for accurate detection of CRISPR off-target mutations, relevant to study design and interpretation.

fact: Somatic variant callers developed for cancer genome analysis can be applied to detect mutations in CRISPR-edited embryos by treating embryos as 'tumour' and parents as 'normal' samples.
source_span: We investigated the robustness of our results by re-analysing our aligned reads using somatic variant callers developed for the analysis of cancer genomes. We labelled each embryo as a “tumour” and each parent sample as a “normal”.
selection_reasoning: This describes a key methodological approach used to validate mutation detection in the study.

fact: After applying stringent filters, the somatic variant calling pipelines identified between 14 and 36 single nucleotide variants (SNVs) and between 0 and 6 indels per CRISPR-edited embryo sample.
source_span: After filtering SNVs and indels in this way, we obtained 14 to 36 SNVs per sample (median 21) and 0 to 6 indels per sample (median 2).
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the principal findings regarding mutation counts after rigorous filtering.

fact: The somatic variant calling pipelines identified 80% of the variants found by the de novo mutation calling pipeline, with variants unique to somatic pipelines having lower variant allele frequencies.
source_span: The somatic calling pipelines identified 80% (313 out of 389) of the variants identified by the de novo mutation calling pipeline. The mutations identified by the somatic pipelines, which were not identified by the de novo pipeline, had a lower variant allele frequency (median of 12%) compared to those identified by both methods (median of 34%).
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the robustness and complementarity of variant detection methods used.

fact: No significant difference in the number of single nucleotide variants or indels was found between CRISPR-treated and control groups after statistical testing.
source_span: We performed four such tests and they failed to produce any significant result at the Bonferroni-adjusted critical p-value of 0.0125. Finally, a Wilcoxon Rank Sum test comparing the combined untreated group to the combined treated group, also failed to produce a significant result.
selection_reasoning: This is a key conclusion about the effect of CRISPR treatment on mutation burden.

fact: An additional mosaic 337 base pair deletion was identified at the Tyr2F on-target location in one CRISPR-treated embryo by the somatic variant caller cgpPindel.
source_span: We also noticed that cgpPindel identified an additional mosaic 337 bp deletion at the Tyr2F on-target location for MD5638a.
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights a specific on-target mutation detected, relevant to understanding CRISPR editing outcomes.

fact: Stomatal pores on plant leaf epidermis regulate CO2 uptake for photosynthesis and water loss by transpiration.
source_span: The stomatal pores are located on the plant leaf epidermis and regulate CO2 uptake for photosynthesis and the loss of water by transpiration .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological importance of stomata, setting the context for the study.

fact: Stomatal aperture affects photosynthesis, water use efficiency, and agricultural crop yields.
source_span: Their stomatal aperture therefore affects photosynthesis , water use efficiency , and agricultural crop yields .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the physiological and agricultural significance of stomatal regulation, motivating the research.

fact: Blue light regulates plant stomatal aperture and is perceived by cryptochromes and phototropins.
source_span: Blue light , one of the environmental signals that regulates the plant stomatal aperture , is perceived by the blue/UV-A light-absorbing cryptochromes and phototropins .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the environmental cue and photoreceptors relevant to stomatal control, framing the study's focus.

fact: The signal transduction pathways linking light perception to stomatal opening are largely unknown.
source_span: The signal transduction cascades that link the perception of light to the stomatal opening response are still largely unknown .
selection_reasoning: This knowledge gap justifies the study's investigation into new molecular players.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 are two newly identified proteins involved in controlling stomatal aperture under blue light.
source_span: Here , we report two new players , Hypersensitive to Red and Blue 1 ( HRB1 ) and Protein Phosphatase 7 ( PP7 ) , and their genetic and biochemical interactions in the control of stomatal aperture .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding introducing the main molecular components studied.

fact: Mutations in HRB1 or PP7 cause misregulation of stomatal aperture and reduce water loss under blue light.
source_span: Mutations in either HRB1 or PP7 lead to the misregulation of the stomatal aperture and reduce water loss under blue light .
selection_reasoning: This finding links the proteins to functional stomatal regulation and water conservation.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 are expressed in guard cells and respond to light-to-dark and dark-to-light transitions.
source_span: Both HRB1 and PP7 are expressed in the guard cells in response to a light-to-dark or dark-to-light transition .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the physiological relevance of these proteins in stomatal response to light changes.

fact: HRB1 interacts with PP7 through its N-terminal ZZ-type zinc finger motif and requires functional PP7 for stomatal opening.
source_span: HRB1 interacts with PP7 through its N-terminal ZZ-type zinc finger motif and requires a functional PP7 for its stomatal opening response .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key molecular interaction essential for stomatal regulation.

fact: HRB1 is phosphorylated in vivo and can be dephosphorylated by PP7.
source_span: HRB1 is phosphorylated in vivo , and PP7 can dephosphorylate HRB1 .
selection_reasoning: This identifies a biochemical mechanism linking the two proteins.

fact: Blue light increases the size of the HRB1 protein complex, a shift impaired in the pp7 mutant where HRB1 remains phosphorylated.
source_span: HRB1 is mostly dephosphorylated in a protein complex of 193 kDa in the dark , and blue light increases complex size to 285 kDa . In the pp7 mutant , this size shift is impaired , and HRB1 is predominately phosphorylated .
selection_reasoning: This finding connects light signaling, protein complex assembly, and PP7 function.

fact: Modification of HRB1 by PP7 under blue light is essential for proper HRB1 protein complex assembly and function.
source_span: We propose that a modification of HRB1 by PP7 under blue light is essential to acquire a proper conformation or to bring in new components for the assembly of a functional HRB1 protein complex .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how PP7 regulates stomatal opening via HRB1.

fact: Guard cells control stomatal opening in response to multiple environmental and biotic stimuli including blue light, drought, elevated CO2, humidity, and pathogens.
source_span: Guard cells control stomatal opening in response to many environmental or biotic stimuli such as blue light , drought , elevated CO2 levels , high humidity , and pathogens [8]–[9] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact situates the study within broader environmental regulation of stomata.

fact: Stomata open during the day in response to blue light and close at night in diurnal cycles.
source_span: Stomata tend to be open during the day in response to blue light and to be closed at night over diurnal cycles [10]–[11] .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides physiological context for blue light’s role in stomatal behavior.

fact: Phototropins phot1 and phot2 contribute equally to blue light-induced stomatal opening at fluence rates above 0.5 µmol/m2/s.
source_span: In guard cells , phot1 and phot2 contribute equally to blue light-induced stomatal opening at fluence rates higher than 0 . 5 µmol/m2/s [7] .
selection_reasoning: This fact relates known photoreceptors to the blue light response, framing the new findings.

fact: The hrb1 mutant has a short hypocotyl under red or blue light and a late flowering phenotype.
source_span: The hypersensitive to red and blue 1 ( hrb1 ) mutant has a short hypocotyl phenotype under red or blue light and a late flowering phenotype [20]–[21] .
selection_reasoning: This fact characterizes the mutant phenotype relevant to HRB1 function.

fact: PP7 is a protein phosphatase with intrinsic phosphatase activity, but its substrates were largely unknown before this study.
source_span: PP7 has an intrinsic phosphatase activity although the substrates of PP7 remain largely unknown [25] .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the novelty of identifying HRB1 as a PP7 substrate.

fact: This study identifies genetic and biochemical interactions between HRB1 and PP7 that regulate stomatal aperture under blue light.
source_span: In this study , we report the involvement of both HRB1 and PP7 in the regulation of stomatal aperture under blue light and their genetic and biochemical interactions .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main research question and principal findings.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 proteins physically interact in plant cells, and this interaction occurs in the nucleus of guard cells.
source_span: Both the full-length and the truncated PP7 interacted with HRB1 ... HRB1∶CFP and PP7∶YFP in Nicotiana leaves showed that both proteins co-localized to the nucleus of epidermal cells ... HRB1 and PP7 also co-localized in the nucleus of guard cells in stable transgenic Arabidopsis plants carrying HRB1∶CFP and PP7∶YFP.
selection_reasoning: The physical interaction and co-localization of HRB1 and PP7 in guard cells is a key mechanistic finding relevant to their functional relationship.

fact: A conserved aspartate residue (D116) in PP7 is critical for its interaction with HRB1, suggesting that PP7's catalytic and substrate recognition sites are closely linked.
source_span: The A116 mutation in PP7 reduced the interaction of PP7 with either the full-length or N-terminal HRB1 ... D116 of PP1 is a critical residue in the catalytic core and interacts with a phosphorylated residue of the substrate ... This result also suggests that the catalytic and substrate recognition sites are closely linked in PP7.
selection_reasoning: Identifying a key residue in PP7 that affects interaction with HRB1 reveals important mechanistic insight into how PP7 recognizes its substrate.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 are both expressed in guard cells and other plant tissues, and their expression is regulated by light.
source_span: A search of the eFP gene expression database ... revealed that both HRB1 and PP7 are expressed in young seedlings, rosette leaves and guard cells ... PP7 is predominantly expressed in guard cells in mature leaves ... expression of HRB1 was induced by light ... expression of PP7 was suppressed by light and resumed following a light-to-dark transition.
selection_reasoning: Expression patterns and light regulation of HRB1 and PP7 provide important background for understanding their physiological roles.

fact: Blue light stabilizes HRB1 and PP7 proteins post-translationally, increasing their accumulation in plant cells.
source_span: The accumulation of the HRB1 protein was increased by a one-hour treatment with blue light and the accumulation of PP7 was also increased by blue light treatment for 3 hours ... The change in their protein levels indicates that both HRB1 and PP7 are post-translationally stabilized by blue light.
selection_reasoning: Post-translational regulation by blue light is a key finding linking these proteins to light signaling.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 interact in vivo in plant cells both in darkness and under blue light, indicating their interaction does not require light.
source_span: HRB1∶GFP∶His but not GFP∶His precipitated Myc∶PP7 from plant extracts either in darkness or under blue light ... suggesting that their interaction does not require light.
selection_reasoning: Demonstrating that the interaction occurs regardless of light conditions is important for understanding the regulation of their function.

fact: Mutations in HRB1 and PP7 reduce stomatal opening in response to blue light, indicating both proteins are important for blue light-regulated stomatal aperture.
source_span: The hrb1 mutant has a defective light response under both blue and red light ... hrb1 had a much smaller stomatal aperture compared with wild type under weak to intermediate blue light ... the pp7 mutant also had a reduced stomatal aperture across a relatively broad range of blue light intensities compared with the Columbia (Col) wild type.
selection_reasoning: Functional evidence that both proteins affect stomatal opening under blue light links them to physiological light responses.

fact: The stomatal opening phenotype of the hrb1 PP7 double mutant is similar to hrb1 alone, suggesting HRB1 functions downstream of PP7 in blue light signaling.
source_span: The stomatal opening response of the hrb1 PP7 RNAi double mutant was similar to that of hrb1 rather than additive, suggesting that HRB1 functions downstream of PP7.
selection_reasoning: Genetic epistasis analysis clarifies the functional relationship between PP7 and HRB1 in the signaling pathway.

fact: HRB1 functions downstream of PP7 in regulating stomatal opening in Arabidopsis.
source_span: The stomatal opening response of the hrb1 PP7 RNAi double mutant was similar to that of hrb1 rather than additive, suggesting that HRB1 functions downstream of PP7 (Figure 5B).
selection_reasoning: This genetic relationship clarifies the signaling order between two key proteins controlling stomatal aperture, a core mechanistic insight.

fact: Over-expression of HRB1 increases stomatal aperture, but this effect requires functional PP7.
source_span: Compared with Col, over-expression of HRB1 increased stomatal aperture, and this phenotype was suppressed by the pp7 mutation, suggesting that the action of the over-accumulated HRB1 requires functional PP7 (Figure 5C).
selection_reasoning: This finding links the functional interaction of HRB1 and PP7 to a physiological outcome relevant to plant water regulation.

fact: Blue light induces the expression of the stomatal regulator gene AtMYB60 in wild-type Arabidopsis.
source_span: As shown by others [17]–[18], the expression of AtMYB60 was induced by blue light in Ws (Figure 6).
selection_reasoning: This background fact establishes the light-dependent regulation of a key gene involved in stomatal function.

fact: The blue light-induced expression of AtMYB60 is partially reduced by either the hrb1 mutation or PP7 RNAi and completely blocked in the hrb1 PP7 RNAi double lines.
source_span: The blue light-induced expression of AtMYB60 was partially reduced by either the hrb1 mutation or PP7 RNAi and was blocked in the hrb1 PP7 RNAi lines.
selection_reasoning: This shows that HRB1 and PP7 jointly regulate a gene critical for stomatal response to blue light, linking molecular regulation to environmental response.

fact: Detached leaves of the hrb1 mutant lose less water under low to intermediate blue light intensities compared with the wild type.
source_span: Detached leaves of the hrb1 mutant lost less water under low to intermediate intensities of blue light compared with the Ws wild type (Figure 7A).
selection_reasoning: This physiological consequence of the hrb1 mutation demonstrates its role in controlling water loss via stomatal regulation.

fact: Loss-of-function pp7 mutants lose less water than wild type plants over a broad range of blue light intensities.
source_span: In contrast, the loss-of-function pp7 mutant lost much less water compared with Col over a broad range of blue light intensities (Figure 7C).
selection_reasoning: This supports the role of PP7 in promoting stomatal opening and water loss under blue light.

fact: HRB1 protein exists in phosphorylated and dephosphorylated forms, and PP7 can dephosphorylate HRB1 in vitro.
source_span: Western blot analysis reveals two bands of HRB1∶myc (Figure 3A). Treatment with lambda protein phosphatase eliminated the upper band, which was presumably the phosphorylated isoform of HRB1 (Figure 8A). ... The addition of PP7 depleted phosphorylated HRB1∶GFP protein (Figure 8B), and this activity was inhibited by Na3VO4.
selection_reasoning: This biochemical evidence identifies PP7 as a phosphatase acting on HRB1, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: A mutation in the conserved catalytic residue of PP7 abolishes its ability to dephosphorylate HRB1.
source_span: PP7 carrying a D to A mutation at position 116, a conserved residue in all protein serine/threonine phosphatases [25], failed to deplete phosphorylated HRB1 (Figure 8B).
selection_reasoning: This confirms the specificity and enzymatic requirement of PP7 for HRB1 dephosphorylation.

fact: In vivo, more phosphorylated HRB1 accumulates in the pp7 mutant compared to wild type under both dark and blue light conditions.
source_span: In Ws, HRB1∶Myc mostly existed in its dephosphorylated form in the dark or under blue light. In contrast, more phosphorylated HRB1∶Myc accumulated in pp7 in the dark or under blue light.
selection_reasoning: This in vivo evidence supports the role of PP7 in regulating HRB1 phosphorylation status.

fact: The pp7 mutation does not affect the nuclear localization or overall protein levels of HRB1.
source_span: The pp7 mutation did not affect the nuclear localization of the HRB1∶GFP protein (Figure S4). The level of either the HRB1∶Myc message or HRB1∶Myc protein accumulation in 35S::HRB1:Myc transgenic plants was not significantly altered in the pp7 mutant background (Figure 9B–9D).
selection_reasoning: This indicates that PP7 regulates HRB1 function via phosphorylation rather than expression or localization.

fact: Blue light induces a shift in the molecular size of the HRB1 protein complex to a larger form.
source_span: After blue or blue plus red light treatment for 2 hours, the peak of the HRB1∶Myc protein complex shifted to fraction 11, with a molecular mass of 285 kDa (Figure 9B).
selection_reasoning: This suggests that HRB1 undergoes light-dependent changes in protein complex formation, relevant to its function.

fact: Either pair of blue light receptors, cry1 cry2 or phot1 phot2, is required for the blue light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex.
source_span: The pattern of the blue light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex remained the same in either cry1 cry2 or phot1 phot2 double mutant, suggesting that either pair of blue light receptors is required for this light-induced response (Figure S5A and S5B).
selection_reasoning: This links HRB1 complex dynamics to known blue light photoreceptors, connecting molecular changes to light sensing.

fact: Blue light induces a size shift of the HRB1 protein complex to a larger molecular mass in Arabidopsis.
source_span: After blue or blue plus red light treatment for 2 hours , the peak of the HRB1∶Myc protein complex shifted to fraction 11 , with a molecular mass of 285 kDa ( Figure 9B ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding shows a key light-dependent biochemical change in HRB1 relevant to its function.

fact: The blue light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex is not altered in phot1 phot2 or cry1 cry2 double mutants, indicating HRB1 functions downstream or independently of these photoreceptors.
source_span: The pattern of the blue light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex remained the same in either cry1 cry2 or phot1 phot2 double mutant , suggesting that either pair of blue light receptors is required for this light-induced response ( Figure S5A and S5B ) .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the relationship between HRB1 and known blue light photoreceptors, important for understanding the signaling pathway.

fact: The blue light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex is compromised in the pp7 mutant, indicating PP7 is required for this light response.
source_span: The light-induced size shift of the HRB1 protein complex was , however , compromised in the pp7 mutant ( Figure 9C ) . First , the peak of the HRB1 protein complex remained in fraction 12 both in the dark and under blue light in the pp7 mutant ( Figure 9C ) .
selection_reasoning: This identifies PP7 as a key regulator of HRB1 complex dynamics under blue light.

fact: HRB1 is predominantly phosphorylated in the pp7 mutant both in the dark and under blue light, suggesting PP7 regulates HRB1 phosphorylation status.
source_span: Second , HRB1∶Myc was predominately phosphorylated in the pp7 mutant plants both in the dark and under blue light ( Figure 9C ) .
selection_reasoning: This links PP7 phosphatase activity to HRB1 posttranslational modification, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Blue light is a major environmental cue regulating stomatal aperture, with phototropins (phots) and cryptochromes (crys) as responsible photoreceptors.
source_span: Blue light is one of the major environmental cues to regulate stomatal aperture with phots and crys being the responsible photoreceptors for this response .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological context and importance of studying HRB1 and PP7 in light responses.

fact: Both hrb1 and pp7 mutants show defects in the light-induced stomatal opening response in Arabidopsis.
source_span: Both hrb1 and pp7 were isolated as hypocotyl mutants under red and blue light or blue light alone [20] , [24] . We report their defects in the light-induced stomatal opening response in this study ( Figure 4 ) .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the physiological relevance of HRB1 and PP7 in stomatal regulation.

fact: Compared with hrb1, the pp7 mutant has a weaker stomatal aperture phenotype but a stronger water retention phenotype, possibly due to ecotype differences.
source_span: Compared with hrb1 , pp7 has a relatively weak stomatal aperture phenotype but a stronger phenotype in water retention , probably due to the difference between ecotypes , Col versus Ws ( Figure 4C and Figure 7C ) .
selection_reasoning: This highlights functional differences between the two genes relevant to plant water regulation.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 positively regulate stomatal opening but have opposing roles in hypocotyl elongation under blue light.
source_span: Both HRB1 and PP7 positively regulate the stomatal opening response but play opposing roles in hypocotyl elongation . Unlike PP7 , HRB1 negatively regulates hypocotyl elongation under blue light .
selection_reasoning: This dual role is a key biological insight linking light signaling to growth and stomatal function.

fact: HRB1 and PP7 physically interact via the N-terminal ZZ-type zinc finger motif of HRB1 and the catalytic domain of PP7.
source_span: The N-terminal ZZ-type zinc finger motif of HRB1 and the catalytic domain of PP7 mediate their interaction ( Figure 1B ) .
selection_reasoning: This molecular interaction supports their functional relationship in light signaling.

fact: HRB1 does not regulate the phosphatase activity of PP7 in vitro, suggesting HRB1 acts downstream or independently of PP7 activity.
source_span: The addition of recombinant HRB1 protein did not alter the phosphatase activity of PP7 toward its synthetic peptide substrate , suggesting that HRB1 may not act upstream of PP7 .
selection_reasoning: This clarifies the directionality of their functional relationship.

fact: PP7 dephosphorylates HRB1 in vivo, as treatment with PP7 or lambda phosphatase eliminates the phosphorylated form of HRB1.
source_span: Either lambda phosphatase or PP7 treatment eliminated the upper band of HRB1∶GFP , i . e . the phosphorylated form of HRB1 ( Figure 8A and 8B ) .
selection_reasoning: This provides biochemical evidence that PP7 regulates HRB1 phosphorylation.

fact: HRB1 belongs to the Drought-Induced 19 (Di19) protein family, members of which are involved in ABA-mediated stomatal aperture responses.
source_span: HRB1 belongs to the Drought-Induced 19 ( Di19 ) protein family [26] . Several Di19 family proteins were phosphorylated by the calcium-dependent protein kinases CPK4 and CPK11 to regulate ABA-mediated stomatal aperture responses [26] , [35]–[36] .
selection_reasoning: This situates HRB1 within a known protein family relevant to stomatal regulation and stress responses.

fact: HRB1 exists mostly in a dephosphorylated form within a protein complex of approximately 193 kDa in the dark, and blue light increases the size of this complex without altering HRB1 phosphorylation status.
source_span: HRB1 exists in a protein complex mostly in its dephosphorylated form , and the size of this complex is approximately 193 kDa in the dark . Blue light caused a size increase of the protein complex but did not alter the phosphorylation status of HRB1 ( Figure 9B ) .
selection_reasoning: This links HRB1 phosphorylation and complex formation dynamics to light signaling.

fact: HRB1 exists mostly in a dephosphorylated form within a protein complex of approximately 193 kDa in the dark.
source_span: HRB1 exists in a protein complex mostly in its dephosphorylated form , and the size of this complex is approximately 193 kDa in the dark .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides key background on the biochemical state and complex formation of HRB1, relevant to understanding its regulation.

fact: Blue light causes an increase in the size of the HRB1 protein complex but does not change the phosphorylation status of HRB1.
source_span: Blue light caused a size increase of the protein complex but did not alter the phosphorylation status of HRB1 ( Figure 9B ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking blue light to a structural change in the HRB1 complex without affecting phosphorylation, central to the study's focus.

fact: The phosphorylation status of HRB1 is not altered under various light wavelengths or in photoreceptor mutants including phyA, phyB, cry1 cry2, and phot1 phot2.
source_span: The phosphorylation status of HRB1 was not altered in the wild type under various light wavelengths ( Figure S7 ) . In addition , there was no alteration of HRB1 phosphorylation status in the phyA mutant under far-red light , in the phyB mutant under red light , and in the cry1 cry2 or phot1 phot2 double mutants under blue light .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies that HRB1 phosphorylation is stable across light conditions and photoreceptor mutations, highlighting the specificity of the blue light-induced size change.

fact: Both phototropins (phots) and cryptochromes (crys) photoreceptors mediate the blue light-induced size increase of the HRB1 protein complex.
source_span: This light-induced size shift was not altered in either the phot1 phot2 or cry1 cry2 double mutant , and both pairs of photoreceptors appear to mediate this response ( Figure S5A and S5B ) .

fact: Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections often form cutaneous abscesses that limit antibiotic penetration and efficacy.
source_span: S . aureus SSTIs routinely manifest as cutaneous abscesses which limit the penetration and efficacy of antibiotics [4] .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a clinical challenge motivating alternative therapies like vaccines.

fact: Community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (CA-MRSA) skin infections are increasing in healthy individuals and are difficult to treat due to antibiotic resistance.
source_span: Community-acquired methicillin resistant S . aureus ( CA-MRSA ) skin infections are increasing in frequency in healthy individuals [5] and the treatment of these infections has become increasingly difficult due to the emergence of antibiotic resistance .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the urgency for new preventive strategies against resistant S. aureus SSTIs.

fact: An effective anti-Staphylococcus aureus vaccine remains elusive despite significant efforts.
source_span: The development of an anti-S . aureus vaccine offers a potential solution to prevent infection regardless of antibiotic resistance; however , although significant efforts have been made , an effective anti-S . aureus vaccine remains elusive .
selection_reasoning: This fact motivates the need for identifying new vaccine targets like ClfB.

fact: A vaccine targeting specific clinical manifestations of Staphylococcus aureus infection, such as skin and soft tissue infections, may be more feasible than a universal vaccine.
source_span: Given the wide spectrum of pathologies caused by this bacterium it is unlikely that a universal anti-S . aureus vaccine will ever be realised [6] , and instead , a vaccine targeting specific clinical manifestations may need to be pursued . As skin is the most frequent site of S . aureus infection [7] , a vaccine specifically targeted against SSTIs would be of great benefit .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides rationale for focusing vaccine development on SSTIs.

fact: Greater understanding of the role of individual Staphylococcus aureus virulence factors during skin infection is needed to identify important targets for future therapy.
source_span: If prophylactic vaccines or other forms of immunotherapy to treat S . aureus SSTIs are to be developed as an alternative to antibiotics , a greater understanding of the specific role of individual virulence factors during infection at this site is needed to identify important targets for future therapy .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the study's motivation to investigate ClfB's role in SSTIs.

fact: Staphylococcus aureus expresses up to 25 different cell wall-anchored proteins involved in adhesion, invasion, biofilm formation, and immune evasion.
source_span: S . aureus expresses up to 25 different cell wall-anchored ( CWA ) proteins , which are covalently linked to the peptidoglycan layer by the enzyme sortase A and are primarily involved in adhesion and invasion of host cells and tissues , biofilm formation and immune evasion [8] .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides context on the diversity of surface proteins relevant to virulence.

fact: Sortase A-deficient Staphylococcus aureus mutants lacking most cell wall-anchored proteins show reduced virulence and bacterial burden in skin abscess models.
source_span: Sortase A-deficient mutants , which lack the majority of cell surface bound CWA proteins , have reduced virulence in a murine kidney abscess model [9 , 10] , while in a skin abscess model , a sortase A-deficient mutant resulted in lower bacterial burden in the skin and a significantly reduced pathology compared to wild-type infected mice [11] .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the importance of cell wall-anchored proteins in SSTI pathogenesis.

fact: Clumping factor A (ClfA) contributes to Staphylococcus aureus skin infection pathogenesis, but vaccines targeting ClfA provide only modest protection.
source_span: Clumping factor A has previously been shown to play a role in the pathogenesis of S . aureus SSTI , as mice inoculated with a ClfA-deficient mutant of S . aureus strain Newman demonstrated a lower bacterial burden in the skin compared to the wild type strain at Day 2 post-inoculation [11] . However , vaccination strategies targeting ClfA only provided modest protection in this model [12] suggesting that other surface proteins may also play an important role in the development of S . aureus SSTI .
selection_reasoning: This fact motivates investigation of other surface proteins like ClfB as vaccine targets.

fact: ClfB binds to plasma fibrinogen, cytokeratin 10, and loricrin, with loricrin being the most abundant protein of the cornified envelope of squamous cells.
source_span: ClfB binds to plasma fibrinogen [19] , cytokeratin 10 [20] , which is the dominant component of the interior of squamous cells , and to loricrin , which is the most abundant protein of the cornified envelope of squamous cells [21] .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes key molecular interactions of ClfB relevant to its function.

fact: Loricrin is a critical ligand for ClfB in vivo, as shown by significantly reduced Staphylococcus aureus nasal colonization in loricrin-knockout mice compared to wild-type mice.
source_span: Rates of S . aureus nasal colonization were significantly reduced in loricrin-knockout mice compared to wild-type mice , demonstrating that loricrin is a critical ligand for ClfB in vivo , at least in mice [13] .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the biological relevance of the ClfB-loricrin interaction.

fact: Mice infected with a ClfB-deficient Staphylococcus aureus strain formed significantly smaller abscess lesions and had reduced bacterial burden compared to mice infected with wild-type bacteria.
source_span: Mice infected with LAC::lux ΔclfB formed significantly smaller abscess lesions on day 3–6 compared to mice infected with LAC::lux ( Fig 1A and 1B ) . The bioluminescence signal was also reduced in LAC::lux ΔclfB infected animals compared to LAC::lux infected mice ( Fig 1C and 1D ) . The reduction in bioluminescence signal was validated by quantifying the bacterial burden in the skin on day 3 ( Fig 1E ) and day 6 ( Fig 1F ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides direct experimental evidence for ClfB's role in SSTI severity.

fact: ClfB affects both the rate of abscess formation and the overall size of the abscess formed during Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections.
source_span: Taken together , these results demonstrate that ClfB affects both the rate of abscess formation and the overall size of the abscess formed , which ultimately leads to greater bacterial burden in the skin .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding linking ClfB to abscess development and bacterial burden, central to the study's main question.

fact: ClfB has an important function during Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections, likely exerting its effect early in the infection process.
source_span: Crucially , these results have demonstrated for the first time that ClfB has an important function during S . aureus SSTIs , likely exerting its effect early in the infection process .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the novel discovery and timing of ClfB's role, key for background and significance.

fact: During nasal colonization, Staphylococcus aureus binding to the squamous epithelium is facilitated by the interaction between ClfB and the squamous cell envelope protein loricrin.
source_span: During nasal colonization , S . aureus binding to the squamous epithelium of the anterior nares is facilitated via the interaction between ClfB and the squamous cell envelope protein loricrin [13] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the known ClfB-loricrin interaction, providing biological context for the study.

fact: Loricrin is present in the epidermal layer and in the abscess wall structure during Staphylococcus aureus subcutaneous abscess formation.
source_span: At 48 h post-infection ( Fig 3 ) loricrin is clearly visible in the epidermal layer of the skin ( Fig 3B ) , which is to be expected as it is a major component of the cornified envelope . Interestingly , it is also detected in the abscess wall structure following challenge with both LAC::lux ( Fig 3C ) and LAC::lux ΔclfB ( S2 Fig ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the relevance of loricrin in the infection site, linking to the ClfB-loricrin interaction during SSTIs.

fact: Loricrin-deficient mice form significantly smaller abscesses and have reduced bacterial burden during Staphylococcus aureus skin and soft tissue infections compared to wild-type mice.
source_span: Lor-/- mice formed significantly smaller abscesses ( Fig 4A and 4B ) compared to WT mice and had reduced bioluminescence ( Fig 4C and 4D ) , indicating the presence of loricrin is important for abscess formation and bacterial burden during S . aureus SSTIs .
selection_reasoning: This finding demonstrates the functional importance of loricrin in abscess formation and bacterial growth, central to the study's mechanism.

fact: Abscess formation is impaired in loricrin-deficient mice at 12 hours post infection, with less well-structured and smaller abscesses formed.
source_span: Importantly , it can be seen that abscess formation is impaired in Lor-/- mice at 12 hours post infection ( Fig 4F ) with overall less well-structured ( Fig 4G ) and smaller ( Fig 4H ) abscesses being formed .
selection_reasoning: This supports the early role of loricrin in abscess development, reinforcing the timing and mechanism of infection.

fact: In wild-type mice, infection with Staphylococcus aureus lacking ClfB results in smaller abscess lesions and reduced bacterial burden compared to infection with wild-type bacteria.
source_span: WT mice that received LAC::lux ΔclfB formed smaller abscess lesions ( Fig 4A and 4B ) and had significantly reduced bioluminescence ( Fig 4C and 4D ) compared to WT mice that received LAC::lux which was confirmed by quantifying bacterial burden in the skin ( Fig 4E ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact shows the virulence role of ClfB in abscess formation and bacterial growth in normal mice.

fact: In loricrin-deficient mice, there is no significant difference in abscess lesion size or bacterial burden between infection with Staphylococcus aureus with or without ClfB.
source_span: In contrast , there was no significant difference in abscess lesion area ( Fig 4A and 4B ) , bioluminescence ( Fig 4C and 4D ) or skin CFUs ( Fig 4E ) between Lor-/- mice that received LAC::lux or LAC::lux ΔclfB .
selection_reasoning: This indicates that ClfB's effect depends on the presence of loricrin, clarifying the mechanism of interaction.

fact: Expression of loricrin within the tissue during abscess formation facilitates the binding of Staphylococcus aureus specifically via ClfB, contributing to the formation of a robust abscess.
source_span: Taken together these data suggest that expression of loricrin within the tissue during abscess formation facilitates the binding of S . aureus specifically via ClfB , thus contributing to the formation of a robust abscess .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the key mechanism linking loricrin and ClfB to abscess formation.

fact: Pre-incubation of Staphylococcus aureus with recombinant loricrin loop L2v reduces abscess lesion area and bacterial burden during skin infection compared to control treatment.
source_span: Abscess lesion area was measured over the 6 day infection period and mice that received LAC::lux+L2v had reduced abscess lesion area compared to the LAC::lux+GST group ( Fig 5A and 5B ) . In addition , bioluminescence signal was reduced throughout the infection period in LAC::lux+L2v infected mice compared to mice that received LAC::lux+GST ( Fig 5C and 5D ) and this reduction in bioluminescence was confirmed with a significant decrease in the bacterial burden in the skin on day 3 and 6 post-infection ( S4 Fig ) .
selection_reasoning: This demonstrates a potential therapeutic approach by blocking ClfB-loricrin interaction to reduce infection severity.

fact: Vaccination with ClfB combined with the TLR9 agonist CpG induces antigen-specific cellular and humoral immune responses in mice.
source_span: Immunization with ClfB in combination with CpG drove a significant increase in ClfB-specific IFNγ ( Fig 6A ) , IL-17 ( Fig 6B ) and IL-22 ( Fig 6C ) producing CD4+ T cells by inguinal lymph node ( ILN ) cells ( skin-draining lymph nodes ) compared to CpG-immunized mice . ClfB-specific CD8+ T cells producing IFNγ , IL-17 and IL-22 were also increased in the ILN of ClfB-vaccinated groups compared to the adjuvant alone group ( S5 Fig ) . Vaccination with ClfB also induced significantly elevated ClfB-specific serum IgG titres in mice compared to the control group ( Fig 7A ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a key translational finding showing that ClfB can be targeted by vaccination to elicit immune responses.

fact: Antibodies induced by ClfB vaccination inhibit the binding of ClfB-expressing bacteria to loricrin.
source_span: We confirmed that these antibodies were functional by investigating their ability to inhibit L . lactis expressing ClfB ( pKS80:clfB [13] ) to bind to immobilised loricrin ( Fig 7B ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the functional relevance of the vaccine-induced antibodies, linking immune response to mechanism.
