fact: About half of the mitochondrial DNA mutations causing diseases in humans occur in tRNA genes.
source_span: About half of the mitochondrial DNA ( mtDNA ) mutations causing diseases in humans occur in tRNA genes .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the significance of mitochondrial tRNA mutations in human disease, motivating the study.

fact: Pathogenic mitochondrial tRNA mutations that can reach homoplasmy often show very different penetrance among patients.
source_span: Particularly intriguing are those pathogenic tRNA mutations than can reach homoplasmy and yet show very different penetrance among patients .
selection_reasoning: This highlights a key biological and clinical puzzle motivating the research.

fact: Before this study, the only source of homoplasmic pathogenic mitochondrial tRNA mutations was human patients.
source_span: To date , the only source of this type of mutations is human patients .
selection_reasoning: This emphasizes the novelty and importance of generating a mouse model mutation.

fact: This study generated and characterized the first mitochondrial tRNA pathological mutation in mouse cells, an m.3739G>A transition in the mitochondrial mt-Ti gene.
source_span: We report here the generation and characterization of the first mitochondrial tRNA pathological mutation in mouse cells , an m . 3739G>A transition in the mitochondrial mt-Ti gene .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal methodological and novel finding central to the study.

fact: The mouse m.3739G>A mutation recapitulates the molecular hallmarks of a disease-causing human mt-Ti mutation, m.4290T>C.
source_span: This mutation recapitulates the molecular hallmarks of a disease-causing mutation described in humans , an m . 4290T>C transition affecting also the human mt-Ti gene .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the relevance of the mouse model to human disease.

fact: Both the mouse and human mt-Ti mutations cause a high frequency of abnormal folding of the tRNAIle that cannot be charged with isoleucine.
source_span: We could determine that the pathogenic molecular mechanism , induced by both the mouse and the human mutations , is a high frequency of abnormal folding of the tRNAIle that cannot be charged with isoleucine .
selection_reasoning: This identifies the key pathogenic molecular mechanism underlying the mutations.

fact: Cells harboring the mouse or human mutant tRNA show increased mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) production that triggers enhanced mitochondrial biogenesis as a compensatory response.
source_span: We demonstrate that the cells harboring the mouse or human mutant tRNA have exacerbated mitochondrial biogenesis triggered by an increase in mitochondrial ROS production as a compensatory response .
selection_reasoning: This finding explains a cellular compensatory mechanism relevant to disease penetrance.

fact: The combination of the pathogenic mechanism and the compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis can explain the variable penetrance of these mitochondrial tRNA mutations.
source_span: We propose that both the nature of the pathogenic mechanism combined with the existence of a compensatory mechanism can explain the penetrance pattern of this mutation .
selection_reasoning: This provides a key insight into why the same mutation can have different clinical outcomes.

fact: Mammalian mitochondrial DNA codes for 13 proteins of the oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) system, two rRNAs, and 22 tRNAs required for mitochondrial protein synthesis.
source_span: Mammalian mitochondrial DNA is a double-stranded circular molecule that codes for 13 of the 87 proteins that constitute the OXPHOS system , as well as two rRNAs and the 22 tRNAs required for mitochondrial protein synthesis .
selection_reasoning: This background fact is necessary to understand the biological context of mitochondrial tRNA mutations.

fact: Mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes impair the OXPHOS system and cause a wide variety of human diseases.
source_span: Mutations in mitochondrial DNA are known to be responsible for a wide variety of diseases in humans whose common characteristic is the impairment of the OXPHOS system .
selection_reasoning: This explains the clinical relevance of mitochondrial tRNA mutations.

fact: Mutations in mitochondrial tRNA genes can cause defects such as impaired aminoacylation, reduced tRNA half-life, impaired pre-tRNA processing, and decreased steady-state tRNA levels, leading to protein synthesis deficiency.
source_span: Different mutations produce a variety of defects [2] including impaired aminoacylation [3]–[5] , reduced tRNA half-life [6] , impairment of pre-tRNA processing [7]–[10] , decrease in the steady-state levels of tRNA [11] and others , promoting , therefore , protein synthesis deficiency .
selection_reasoning: This details the molecular consequences of tRNA mutations relevant to the study's mechanism.

fact: Mutations in mt-Ti tRNA genes in humans are usually associated with cardiomyopathy as a main or cardinal feature.
source_span: Different mutations produce a variety of defects ... mutations in mt-Ti , usually have cardiomyopathy as the main or one of the cardinal features [2] , [27] , [28] .
selection_reasoning: This clinical association contextualizes the importance of studying mt-Ti mutations.

fact: The mouse m.3739G>A mutation is located in the anticodon loop of the mt-Ti tRNA and creates a new potential Watson-Crick base pair in the loop.
source_span: The mutation is located in the anticodon loop of this tRNA , two bases downstream from the anticodon , and generates a new potential Watson and Crick pair between the first and last base of the loop .
selection_reasoning: This structural detail is key to understanding the mutation's molecular effect.

fact: Both the mouse and human mt-Ti mutations reduce the effective amount of functional isoleucyl-tRNAIle, impairing mitochondrial protein synthesis and the activity of respiratory complexes I, III, and IV.
source_span: We found that both , the human and the mouse mutations , promote a similar structural deficiency in the mt-tRNAIle that causes a reduction in the effective amount of functional isoleucyl-tRNAIle . As a consequence , mitochondrial protein synthesis and the activity of complexes I , III and IV are impaired , causing a mild but significant OXPHOS deficiency .
selection_reasoning: This links the mutation to functional mitochondrial defects central to disease.

fact: The ROS-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis compensatory response partially offsets the respiratory deficiency caused by the mutant mtDNA.
source_span: We describe also that cells harboring the mutant mtDNA show a higher ROS production that leads to a compensatory response to this respiration deficiency by enhancing mitochondrial biogenesis . This response is able to partially compensate the deficiency .
selection_reasoning: This explains a cellular mechanism that mitigates the mutation's impact.

fact: The ROS-mediated mitochondrial biogenesis mechanism may allow survival and reproduction of individuals carrying deleterious mitochondrial tRNA mutations, facilitating the evolution of compensatory mutations.
source_span: This increased mitochondrial biogenesis may allow the survival and reproduction of some individuals despite of harboring a deleterious allele , facilitating the appearance of a true compensatory mutation , the bona-fide epistatic mutation .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the evolutionary and pathological significance of the compensatory mechanism.

fact: A unique m.3739G>A mutation in the mitochondrial tRNAIle gene was identified in mutant mouse cell lines with defective oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source_span: Then , we fully sequenced the mtDNA of these cell lines and we found a unique mutation , consisting in an m . 3739G>A transition affecting the mt-Ti gene ( Figure 1A ) .
selection_reasoning: This mutation is central to the study as it underlies the observed mitochondrial dysfunction and is a core finding.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation affects a nucleotide in the tRNA anticodon loop that is 100% conserved across 150 mammalian species.
source_span: This nucleotide , 100% conserved in 150 species of mammals ( Figure 1B ) , is located at the tRNA anticodon loop , two bases downstream from the anticodon ( Figure 1B and 1C ) .
selection_reasoning: Conservation highlights the functional importance of the mutated site, supporting the mutation's pathogenic relevance.

fact: An identical mutation in the human mitochondrial tRNAIle gene has been associated with degenerative encephalopathy and oncocytic tumors.
source_span: An identical mutation ( m . 4296G>A ) has been found in humans associated with a degenerative encephalopathy ( Rossmanith , W , personal communication ) and in oncocytic tumors [35] .
selection_reasoning: This links the mouse mutation to human disease, emphasizing clinical relevance.

fact: Mutant cell lines carrying the m.3739G>A mutation show significantly decreased cellular respiration compared to controls.
source_span: As shown in Figure 2A , cell respiration was significantly decreased in the mutant cell lines ( an average reduction of 24% in mB77 and 46% in mB77p18 , relative to the respective control cell line ) .
selection_reasoning: Reduced respiration is a principal functional consequence of the mutation, a key finding.

fact: The respiratory defect in mutant cells affects the entire respiratory chain, consistent with a mitochondrial tRNA mutation.
source_span: Compatible with a tRNA mutation , Figure 2B illustrates that the reduction in respiration is maintained at any entry point of the electrons , suggesting an affectation of the whole respiratory chain ( see below ) .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains the broad impact of the mutation on mitochondrial function.

fact: Mutant cells show impaired growth in galactose medium compared to glucose, indicating defective OXPHOS capacity.
source_span: On the contrary , cells harboring mutant mtDNAs present a significant delayed growth in galactose with respect to glucose ( ratio DT Gal/Glu for mB77 , 1 . 201 and for mB77p18 , 1 . 304 ) .
selection_reasoning: Growth impairment in galactose is a functional assay demonstrating mitochondrial dysfunction.

fact: All respiratory complexes containing mtDNA-encoded subunits show significantly reduced activity in mutant cells, while complexes without mtDNA-encoded subunits show increased activity.
source_span: all the respiratory complexes harboring subunits encoded by mtDNA showed a significant activity reduction ( Figure 2E ) . ... mitochondrial enzymes with no mtDNA encoded subunits ( citrate synthase and complex II ) showed a small but significant increase in activity in mutant cells ( Figure 2D )
selection_reasoning: This differential effect supports the mutation's impact on mitochondrial protein synthesis and respiratory function.

fact: Mutant cells are more sensitive to inhibitors of respiratory complexes I, III, and IV but not complex II, consistent with mtDNA-encoded subunit defects.
source_span: the lethal dose 50 ( LD50 ) was significantly smaller for mutant versus wild type tRNAIle cells for complex I , III and IV inhibitors while the only respiratory complex without mtDNA encoded subunits , complex II , was equally affected by its inhibitor in control and mutant cells ( Figure 2F ) .
selection_reasoning: This pharmacological sensitivity confirms the functional impairment of mtDNA-encoded complexes.

fact: Mutant cells produce more mitochondrial hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), which triggers increased mitochondrial biogenesis as a compensatory response.
source_span: we also found that cells carrying the m . 3739G>A mutation produce more H2O2 ( Figure S1B ) and that ROS scavengers such as N-Acetyl-Cysteine ( NAC ) or Tiron added to the culture medium , abolish the signal that triggers mitochondrial biogenesis and equalizes the level of mtDNA and CS activity between mutant and wild type cells ( Figure 3 and Figure S1C ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding links oxidative stress to compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: Mutant cells have nearly double the amount of mitochondrial DNA and higher citrate synthase activity compared to control cells, indicating increased mitochondrial mass.
source_span: mutant cells almost double the amount of mtDNA with respect to control cells and have significantly higher citrate synthase ( CS ) specific activities ( Figure 3 and Figure S1A ) .
selection_reasoning: This supports the conclusion that mitochondrial biogenesis is upregulated in response to the mutation.

fact: Treatment with ROS scavengers reduces mitochondrial biogenesis and decreases respiration more in mutant cells than in controls, indicating that biogenesis compensates for the OXPHOS defect.
source_span: cell respiration decreased significantly more in mutant than in control cells after the NAC treatment indicating an effective compensation of the defect by the biogenesis activation ( Figure S1D ) .
selection_reasoning: This demonstrates the functional significance of ROS-induced mitochondrial biogenesis as a compensatory mechanism.

fact: Despite the mutation affecting a mitochondrial tRNA gene, in vivo mitochondrial protein synthesis rates per cell do not show significant differences between mutant and control cells.
source_span: Analysis of mitochondrial DNA translation products did not reveal significant quantitative differences or abnormal migration of any polypeptide in the mutant cells ( Figure 4A ) .
selection_reasoning: This unexpected observation is important for interpreting the mutation's effect on protein synthesis.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation in mitochondrial tRNAIle impairs mitochondrial protein synthesis, making mutant cells more sensitive to the mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibitor chloramphenicol.
source_span: When we analyzed this possibility, we found that, the LD50 for CAP was significantly lower for cells carrying m.3739G>A mutation when compared with wild type cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact shows a key functional consequence of the mutation on mitochondrial protein synthesis, central to the study's main question and findings.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation causes a disturbance in the assembly or stability of mitochondrial respiratory complexes I, III, and IV, while complex V is increased in mutant cells.
source_span: Blue Native gel electrophoresis (BNGE) analysis revealed that the amount of the assembled complexes is affected in mutant cells where complexes I, IV, and likely complex III, seemed to be reduced. On the contrary, complex V seems to be increased in mutant cells.
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a principal downstream effect of the mutation on mitochondrial respiratory complexes, a key mechanistic finding.

fact: Mutant cells with the m.3739G>A mutation accumulate subcomplexes of mitochondrial respiratory complexes III and IV that are not present in control cells.
source_span: When BNGE was followed by SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis of the labeled products we could observe the accumulation of subcomplexes affecting mainly complexes III and IV, both in the m.3739G>A original and transmitochondrial mutants. These did not appear in the control samples.
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a specific molecular defect caused by the mutation, supporting the conclusion about impaired complex assembly.

fact: The steady-state level of mitochondrial tRNAIle in mutant cells carrying the m.3739G>A mutation is nearly normal, at about 80% of control levels.
source_span: As shown in Figure 7A, the steady-state level of the mt-tRNAIle in mutant cells was almost normal, with a value of 80% of the amount in controls when normalized by tRNAGly signal.
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses whether the mutation affects tRNA abundance, an important background and mechanistic detail.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation does not cause a major defect in the 3′ and 5′ end processing or CCA addition of mitochondrial tRNAIle.
source_span: Since the major proportion of molecules showed a proper maturation of the 3′ and 5′ and CCA addition, we conclude that no major defect in the processing of the mt-tRNAIle can be attributed to the mutation.
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies that the mutation's effect is not due to impaired tRNA maturation, refining the understanding of the mutation's impact.

fact: A second slower migrating band of mitochondrial tRNAIle appears only in mutant cells, indicating a different structural conformation of the uncharged tRNA caused by the m.3739G>A mutation.
source_span: Interestingly, a second slower migrating band appeared only in the mutant mt-tRNAIle. This second band was present even after the deacylation treatment suggesting, therefore, a second structural conformation of the uncharged tRNA.
selection_reasoning: This fact reveals a novel structural alteration of the mutant tRNA, which may underlie functional defects.

fact: The slower migrating extra band of mitochondrial tRNAIle in mutant cells disappears under conditions that denature the tRNA, confirming it represents a different tRNA conformation.
source_span: We confirmed that the separation between the two bands of mt-tRNAIle was almost abolished when the tRNA was closer to full denaturation.
selection_reasoning: This fact supports the conclusion that the mutation alters tRNA structure, a key mechanistic insight.

fact: In organello aminoacylation experiments show that the slower migrating extra band of mutant mitochondrial tRNAIle is not aminoacylated, indicating it is an uncharged tRNA conformation.
source_span: As shown in Figure 7E, when in organello-aminoacylated tRNAs were isolated and electrophoresed under acidic conditions, only one band was observed.
selection_reasoning: This fact links the structural alteration to functional aminoacylation status, important for understanding the mutation's effect on tRNA function.

fact: A pathological G to A mutation at position 3739 in the mitochondrial tRNAIle anticodon loop was generated and characterized in mouse cells.
source_span: We describe here the generation and characterization of the first pathological mutation in a mitochondrial tRNA gene in mouse cells , a G to A transition at position 3739 within the mt-tRNAIle anticodon loop .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main experimental model and mutation studied, which is central to the article's focus.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation in mouse mt-tRNAIle causes an alternative folding of the tRNA that is not aminoacylated and thus reduces the amount of functional tRNA available for protein synthesis.
source_span: This alternative folded tRNAIle is not aminoacylated , representing a defective tRNA secondary/tertiary structure that cannot participate in protein synthesis and , therefore , reduces the amount of functional tRNA .
selection_reasoning: This explains the key molecular defect caused by the mutation, linking structure to function.

fact: The m.3739G>A mutation in mouse cells leads to a moderate defect in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) accompanied by accumulation of respiratory chain subcomplexes.
source_span: Together with that , we have established that both mutations , in humans and in mouse cells , cause only a moderate defect in OXPHOS that is accompanied by accumulation of subcomplexes of the respiratory chain .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the principal functional consequence of the mutation relevant to mitochondrial physiology.

fact: Cells carrying the m.3739G>A mutation are more sensitive to pentamidine, a drug that prevents proper folding of mitochondrial tRNAs, than wild type cells.
source_span: As shown in Figure 7F , cells carrying m . 3739G>A mutation are significantly more sensitive to pentamidine than wild type cells .
selection_reasoning: This finding supports the hypothesis that the mutation affects tRNA folding and has functional consequences.

fact: Human transmitochondrial cell lines harboring the m.4290T>C mutation in the tRNAIle anticodon loop show reduced respiration, increased mtDNA copy number, and increased H2O2 production compared to controls.
source_span: In agreement with the results obtained in mouse cells , the human tRNAIle mutant caused reduced levels of respiration when compared to control ( Figure 8A ) . More interesting , as shown in Figure 8B , both mtDNA copy number and H2O2 production were increased in human mutant cells as observed in mouse mutants .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the human mutation to similar mitochondrial dysfunctions observed in the mouse model, supporting translational relevance.

fact: The human m.4290T>C mutation promotes an alternative folding of the tRNAIle with similar probability to the canonical folding, resulting in a slower migrating band on acid gels that is resistant to deacylation.
source_span: Finally , when human mitochondrial tRNAs isolated under acidic conditions were electrophoresed through acid gels and hybridized with mt-tRNAIle specific probes , a slower migrating band appeared in mutant samples ... and is identical to the slower moving band described above for the mouse mutant tRNA .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key molecular phenotype shared by human and mouse mutations, supporting the pathogenic mechanism.

fact: Human mutant cells with the m.4290T>C mutation are more sensitive to inhibitors of mitochondrial complexes I, III, and IV and to uncouplers, but not to complex II inhibition, compared to wild type cells.
source_span: In addition , as in mouse cells , we confirmed that the human tRNAIle mutation promotes a higher sensitivity of cell growth to complex I , III and IV inhibitors , as well as to uncouplers , without modification of the sensitivity to complex II inhibition ( Figure 8D ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights functional mitochondrial defects caused by the mutation relevant to cellular bioenergetics.

fact: Human mutant cells are more resistant than wild type to ATPase inhibition by oligomycin and more sensitive to chloramphenicol but not to cycloheximide, similar to mouse mutant cells.
source_span: Again , human mutant cells were more resistant than wild type to inhibition of ATPase by oligomycin ( Figure 8D ) . Finally , human mutant cells were more sensitive to CAP but not to cycloheximide compared to wild type , as was observed in mouse cells ( Figure 8E ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact shows conserved drug sensitivity phenotypes between human and mouse mutants, supporting the model's validity.

fact: Thirteen mutations affecting the mitochondrial tRNAIle gene have been reported in humans, many of which impair tRNA biosynthesis or stability and lead to mitochondrial disease.
source_span: Thirteen mutations affecting mt-Ti gene have been reported to date in humans . Most of them seem to affect primarily tRNA biosynthesis , leading to a drop in its steady-state levels [41] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact contextualizes the importance of studying tRNAIle mutations in mitochondrial disease.

fact: The mouse m.3739G>A mutation is located at the same anticodon loop position as the human m.4296G>A mutation, which is associated with degenerative encephalopathy.
source_span: The mouse mutation described here ( m . 3739G>A ) is also located at the anticodon loop of the tRNAIle , at the same position that the human m . 4296G>A , and also induces a similar alternative folding of the tRNA to that promoted by the human m . 4290T>C .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the mouse model mutation to a known human pathogenic mutation, supporting translational relevance.

fact: Both the human and mouse tRNAIle anticodon loop mutations can reach homoplasmy because they cause only moderate OXPHOS deficiency, which may explain their variable clinical penetrance.
source_span: We would like to stress that both the human and the mouse mutations could reach homoplasmy because the OXPHOS deficiency they promote is moderate . Therefore , they represent an intriguing set of mitochondrial tRNA mutations with very variable penetrance than can cause no symptoms or , as it is the case of the tRNAIle mutation , a devastating neurological disease in members of the same family [16] .
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses the clinical significance and variability of disease expression caused by these mutations.

fact: The mouse mutation reproduces the molecular hallmarks of a human mitochondrial tRNA mutation that causes a moderate defect in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).
source_span: Therefore , the mouse mutation seems to fully reproduce the molecular hallmarks of a described human mtDNA mutation affecting a tRNA .
selection_reasoning: This establishes the relevance of the mouse model to human mitochondrial disease, a core background and motivation fact.

fact: Both the human and mouse mitochondrial tRNA mutations can reach homoplasmy because they cause only a moderate OXPHOS deficiency.
source_span: We would like to stress that both the human and the mouse mutations could reach homoplasmy because the OXPHOS deficiency they promote is moderate .
selection_reasoning: This explains a key biological property of the mutations relevant to disease penetrance and inheritance.

fact: Mitochondrial tRNA mutations can have highly variable penetrance, causing no symptoms in some carriers but devastating neurological disease in others within the same family.
source_span: Therefore , they represent an intriguing set of mitochondrial tRNA mutations with very variable penetrance than can cause no symptoms or , as it is the case of the tRNAIle mutation , a devastating neurological disease in members of the same family [16] .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the clinical variability and importance of understanding the mutation effects.

fact: A mother homoplasmic for the m.4290T>C mitochondrial tRNA mutation showed no symptoms, while her daughters developed disease at different stages.
source_span: In particular , the mother was homoplasmic for the m . 4290T>C mutation without showing any symptoms while her daughters suffered the diseases at different stages [16] .
selection_reasoning: This specific example illustrates the variable penetrance and motivates the study.

fact: The authors propose a 'functional epistasis model' to explain how mitochondrial tRNA mutations with variable penetrance can cause disease or remain asymptomatic.
source_span: Here we are proposing a model aimed to explain this behavior that we would like to call “functional epistasis model” ( Figure 9 ) .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal conceptual contribution of the study.

fact: The functional epistasis model suggests that a destabilizing mitochondrial tRNA mutation reduces functional tRNA availability, impairing mitochondrial protein synthesis and respiratory complex assembly.
source_span: First , a mitochondrial tRNA ( mt-tRNA ) mutation occurs that destabilizes the functional structure of the tRNA making a second but non-functional folding similarly feasible . If the mutation reaches homoplasmy , it substantially reduces the availability of functional tRNA and can compromise mitochondrial protein synthesis fidelity .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key mechanism underlying the mutation's effect.

fact: An imbalance in respiratory complex assembly caused by the tRNA mutation induces a compensatory increase in mitochondrial biogenesis through elevated basal production of reactive oxygen species (ROS).
source_span: As a consequence , an unbalance in the assembly of respiratory complexes induces a compensatory response by increasing mitochondrial biogenesis through a rise in the basal production of ROS ( H2O2 ) .
selection_reasoning: This explains the cellular response mechanism relevant to disease expression.

fact: The compensatory mitochondrial biogenesis response can sometimes fully compensate the deleterious effect of the mitochondrial tRNA mutation, preventing disease symptoms.
source_span: As has been described for mouse mt-tRNA non-pathological variants [31] , this response can be in some cases sufficient to compensate the deleterious effect of the mutation .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains why some carriers remain asymptomatic.

fact: Variations in gene context or environmental factors modulate the compensatory response, influencing whether the mitochondrial tRNA mutation causes disease or remains asymptomatic.
source_span: In other cases , differences in the amplitude of this response modulated by gene context or environmental factors can render this compensatory response insufficient to prevent the expression of the disease phenotype ( Figure 9 ) .
selection_reasoning: This highlights factors affecting disease penetrance, a key clinical implication.

fact: Excess ROS can trigger ROS defenses that, if very efficient, block mitochondrial biogenesis activation, preventing compensation and leading to disease manifestation.
source_span: For example , the excess of ROS can also trigger the expression of ROS defenses and if this response is very efficient the activation of mitochondrial biogenesis would be blocked , the effect of the mutation would not be compensated and the disease would manifest .
selection_reasoning: This explains a mechanism by which compensation fails, leading to disease.

fact: If ROS defenses are less efficient, mitochondrial biogenesis is activated, increasing functional tRNA levels and substantially compensating the mitochondrial protein synthesis defect, preventing or ameliorating disease.
source_span: Conversely , if ROS defenses are less efficient , mitochondrial biogenesis would be activated and the amount of functionally folded tRNA can grow to a level that can substantially compensate the mitochondrial protein synthesis defect . In this case , the disease would be prevented or substantially ameliorated .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains how disease severity can be reduced or avoided.

fact: The functional epistasis model suggests that homoplasmic mitochondrial tRNA mutations with variable penetrance can persist in populations long enough to allow the emergence of compensatory second mutations restoring tRNA function.
source_span: However , this scenario substantially increases the likelihood for the emergence of a second mutation in the same molecule , a true epistatic mutation that can render the tRNA fully functional again , and the new variant would behave as a neutral allele within the population .
selection_reasoning: This links the model to evolutionary implications and mutation dynamics.

fact: The emergence of compensatory second mutations may explain how mitochondrial tRNAs cross low-fitness valleys in evolution to reach functional fitness peaks.
source_span: This would be a plausible mechanism to cross low-fitness valleys in the evolution of mt-tRNAs [47] .
selection_reasoning: This fact connects the study findings to broader evolutionary biology concepts.

fact: Growth capacity of cells was determined by plating cells in glucose-containing or glucose-free galactose-containing medium and counting cells over 5 days.
source_span: Growth capacity was determined by plating 5*104 cells on 12 wells test plates in 2 ml of the appropriate medium ( DMEM , which contains 4 . 5 mg of glucose/ml supplemented with 5% FBS , or DMEM lacking glucose and containing 0 . 9 mg of galactose/ml , supplemented with 5% dFBS ) , incubating them at 37°C for 5 days and performing cell counts at daily intervals .
selection_reasoning: This describes a key method used to assess cell growth under different metabolic conditions, relevant to understanding cellular metabolism and viability.

fact: Oxygen consumption was measured in intact or permeabilized cells using a Clark-type electrode to assess mitochondrial respiratory function.
source_span: O2 consumption determinations in intact or in digitonine-permeabilized cells were carried out in an oxytherm Clark-type electrode ( Hansatech ) as previously described [50] with small modifications [34] .
selection_reasoning: Measuring oxygen consumption is a principal method to evaluate mitochondrial function, central to the study's investigation of cellular respiration.

fact: Mitochondria were isolated from cells and enzymatic activities of citrate synthase and respiratory complexes I, II, III, and IV were measured by spectrophotometry.
source_span: Mitochondria were isolated as described previously [51] and the different enzymatic activities were assessed by spectrophotometry . Citrate synthase and complexes I , II , III and IV activities were measured in isolated mitochondria as described before [32] , [52] .
selection_reasoning: Assessing mitochondrial enzyme activities is a key approach to characterize mitochondrial function and defects.

fact: Cell viability in response to different inhibitors was evaluated using the MTT reduction assay, which measures mitochondrial dehydrogenase activity in viable cells.
source_span: Effect of different inhibitors on the viability of control and mutant cells was evaluated using the MTT reduction assay according to Mosmann et al [53] . This is an indirect way of measuring cell viability in which mitochondrial dehydrogenases of viable cells reduce the yellowish water-soluble MTT to water-insoluble formazan crystals .
selection_reasoning: This method provides a functional readout of cell viability and mitochondrial activity, important for assessing drug effects.

fact: Mitochondrial DNA copy number per cell was quantified by real-time PCR using specific primers for mitochondrial and nuclear DNA sequences.
source_span: MtDNA quantification was performed by real-time PCR using an ABI PRISM 7000 Sequence Detector System ( AB Applied Biosystems ) and Platinum SYBR Green qPCR SuperMix-UDG ( Invitrogen ) . Total cellular DNA was used as template and was amplified with specific oligodeoxynucleotides for mtCo2 ... and SdhA ... mtDNA copy number per cell was calculated using SdhA amplification as a reference for nuclear DNA content as previously reported [31] .
selection_reasoning: Quantifying mtDNA copy number is essential to understand mitochondrial genome alterations relevant to the study.

fact: Production of hydrogen peroxide by cultured cells was measured using a fluorescent probe after incubation with 2′,7-Dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate.
source_span: Production of hydrogen peroxide was measured in cultured cells grown in the absence or in the presence of NAC for 1 week as previously described [31] . Briefly , 100 , 000 cells were incubated at 37°C for 30 minutes in the presence of 100 µM 2′ , 7-Dichlorodihydrofluorescein diacetate ( 2 , 7-DCFH2-DA , Fluka ) .
selection_reasoning: Measuring reactive oxygen species production is important for assessing oxidative stress in cells, a key factor in mitochondrial dysfunction.

fact: Mitochondrial DNA-encoded proteins were labeled with [35S]-methionine in intact cells to study mitochondrial protein synthesis.
source_span: Labeling of mtDNA-encoded proteins was performed with [35S]-methionine in intact cells as described elsewhere for 1 hour [54] .
selection_reasoning: This method allows assessment of mitochondrial translation, critical for understanding mitochondrial gene expression.

fact: The assembly and relative levels of mitochondrial respiratory complexes were estimated by Blue-Native electrophoresis followed by western blot analysis.
source_span: Estimation of the relative level of the assembled respiratory complexes in cell lines was performed by Blue-Native electrophoresis ( BNGE ) followed by western blot as described before [32] .
selection_reasoning: Analyzing respiratory complex assembly is central to evaluating mitochondrial function and defects.

The nutrition content of the Dox food ( e . g . 19% protein and 8 . 6% fat ) was very similar to the regular diet ( 20% protein , 9% fat ) used in our colony . Therefore the switching of food types did not result in change of cholesterol levels in mice .
selection_reasoning: This fact is relevant to the inducible system activation and controls for confounding dietary effects.

fact: Neural circuits use multiple coding strategies, including oscillations, synchronization, and precise spike timing, to encode sensory information.
source_span: Neuronal circuits implement a variety of coding strategies that differ in their reliance on precise timing and correlations between action potentials ( “spikes” ) . Among these strategies are oscillations , synchronization and precise spike timing on the one end of the spectrum; population codes and firing rate changes on the other one [1]–[6] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the diversity of neural coding mechanisms relevant to the study's focus on how multiple mechanisms interact.

fact: The locust olfactory system transforms dense, synchronized spike trains in the antennal lobe into a sparse representation in the mushroom body, which is associated with memory.
source_span: The locust olfactory system , in which dense , transiently synchronized spike trains across ensembles of antenna lobe ( AL ) neurons are transformed into a sparse representation in the mushroom body ( MB; a region associated with memory ) , provides a well-studied preparation for investigating the interaction of multiple coding mechanisms .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides essential background on the biological system studied and the key transformation of neural codes.

fact: Kenyon cells in the locust mushroom body respond sparsely and specifically to odors, with only a few cells responding reliably to any given odor.
source_span: Recordings made in vivo from the insect MB demonstrated highly specific responses to odors in Kenyon cells ( KCs ) . Typically , only a few KCs from the recorded population of neurons responded reliably when a specific odor was presented . Different odors induced responses in different KCs .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the sparse and odor-specific nature of the mushroom body responses, central to the study's focus.

fact: Plasticity at the synapses between antennal lobe projection neurons and mushroom body Kenyon cells can regulate synaptic weights to ensure the specificity of Kenyon cell responses to familiar or meaningful odors.
source_span: Here , we explored with a biologically plausible model the possibility that a form of plasticity may control and tune synaptic weights of inputs to the mushroom body to ensure the specificity of KCs' responses to familiar or meaningful odors .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the main research question and hypothesis tested in the study.

fact: A biologically plausible computational model showed that activity-dependent plasticity at antennal lobe to mushroom body synapses efficiently tunes the system to selectively filter oscillatory input and produce sparse odor representations.
source_span: We found that plasticity at the synapses between the AL and the MB efficiently regulated the delicate tuning necessary to selectively filter the intense AL oscillatory output and condense it to a sparse representation in the MB .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a principal finding about the role of plasticity in tuning odor representations.

fact: Plasticity mechanisms based on spike timing and spike rate were compared in the model to investigate their contributions to tuning odor representations in the mushroom body.
source_span: Two different forms of dynamic regulation of synaptic strength were compared , one based on the precise millisecond timing of individual spikes [22]–[24] and a second that depended on the rate of spike occurrence averaged over longer intervals [25] , [26] .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes the key methodological approach used to test different plasticity mechanisms.

fact: The model predicts that synaptic plasticity at antennal lobe to mushroom body synapses plays a critical role in generating sparse, reliable, and persistent odor representations.
source_span: Activity-dependent plasticity drove the observed specificity , reliability , and expected persistence of odor representations , suggesting a role for plasticity in information processing and making a testable prediction about synaptic plasticity at AL-MB synapses .
selection_reasoning: This fact states the significance and testable prediction derived from the study.

fact: The locust olfactory system is a favorable model for studying the interaction of neural coding strategies with plasticity mechanisms relevant to learning and memory.
source_span: Thus , this relatively simple system constitutes a favorable model for studying the interplay of neural codes with plastic mechanisms of learning and memory .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the broader significance and motivation for using the locust olfactory system.

fact: Learning rules based on spike rate- or spike timing-dependent induction of synaptic plasticity are central in influential models of cortical learning and neural development.
source_span: Learning rules based on spike rate- or spike timing-dependent induction of synaptic plasticity are central in influential models of cortical learning and neural development [22]–[26].
selection_reasoning: This provides important background on the biological relevance and motivation for studying these plasticity mechanisms.

fact: This study compared spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) with spike-rate dependent plasticity (SRDP) at synapses between projection neurons (PNs) and Kenyon cells (KCs) in the locust mushroom body.
source_span: Specifically, we compared spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP; Figure 1C) with a form of plasticity that depends on the rate, but not precise timing, of pre- and postsynaptic firing (Figure 1A and 1B). By analogy with STDP [27], we termed this spike-rate dependent plasticity (SRDP). In most of our computational experiments, we compared the effects of SRDP and STDP at the PNs-to-KCs synapses (Figure 1E).
selection_reasoning: This states the main question and key methods at a high level, essential for understanding the study focus.

fact: The computational model simulated small populations of conductance-based Kenyon cells receiving input from 100 projection neurons, replicating in vivo locust olfactory system activity.
source_span: Our simulations were based on small populations of conductance-based KCs receiving input from 100 PNs (i.e., ∼12.5% of total locust PN population). Each model KC received monosynaptic input from 10 PNs [7]. Following an approach that we previously applied in [8] the PN activity of the model (Figure 2B; see Materials and Methods) included dynamic ensembles of synchronized neurons replicating the behavior of PNs recorded in vivo (Figure 2A) [7], [28], [29] as well as of PNs in a complete AL model [9], [10].
selection_reasoning: This describes the modeling approach and biological relevance, important for understanding the methods.

fact: Before olfactory experience, stimulus-evoked responses in the mushroom body were dense and unselective, with many Kenyon cells responding to odors but firing less than one spike per trial.
source_span: Before olfactory experience, stimulus-evoked response patterns in the MB were dense, with olfactory representations characterized by the participation of a large fraction of the available KCs (often >25%; Figure 3A, left column). Most neurons fired less than one spike per trial (see spike raster in Figure 2D); thus, reliability was low. Population responses were unselective and largely overlapping across different odors (Figure 3A, left column).
selection_reasoning: This provides background on the initial state of the system before learning, important for framing the study findings.

fact: Both spike-rate dependent plasticity (SRDP) and spike-timing dependent plasticity (STDP) made Kenyon cell population responses sparser and more odor-specific after training.
source_span: Both learning mechanisms made KCs population responses sparser (Figure 3A, middle and right column), such that in most cases only one KC became specifically responsive to a given odor. After olfactory experience with SRDP or STDP over 3 blocks of presentations (150 trials in all), on average, only a few KCs developed sensitivity to a given odor leading to a sparse representation for that odor.
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing that both plasticity mechanisms enhance sparse and specific odor coding.

fact: The increase in sparseness after learning with SRDP or STDP was statistically significant compared to the naive case.
source_span: Overall, odor representations were significantly sparser after synaptic tuning through SRDP (p<0.0002, paired t-test on sparseness measures, see Materials and Methods; Figure 3B) and STDP (p<0.0003) compared to the naive case.
selection_reasoning: This supports the robustness and significance of the main finding.

fact: Activity-dependent synaptic tuning through SRDP or STDP normalized postsynaptic neuronal responses over a wide range of initial synaptic conductance values without requiring a global scaling signal.
source_span: Training with either SRDP or STDP made the population response much sparser (Figure 4A, mid and right column). Even for initial conductances in the 130–140% range, almost all neurons involved in the response fired a single spike after olfactory experience, whereas more than half of the KC population remained silent for all odors. ... Thus, activity-dependent synaptic tuning is able to normalize postsynaptic neuronal responses over a wide range of initial conditions, and can do so without a global scaling signal [30], [31].
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the robustness and generalizability of the plasticity mechanisms, important for understanding their functional significance.

fact: Both SRDP and STDP favor a sparser code within a fixed-size neuron population, which increases the global storage capacity of the olfactory system.
source_span: Finally, these forms of synaptic plasticity appear to favor a sparser code within a neuron population of fixed size, thereby increasing the global storage capacity of the system [5].
selection_reasoning: This fact relates the findings to the functional and computational significance of sparse coding.

fact: Synaptic plasticity mechanisms favor sparser coding within a fixed neuron population, increasing the global storage capacity of the olfactory system.
source_span: of synaptic plasticity appear to favor a sparser code within a neuron population of fixed size , thereby increasing the global storage capacity of the system [5] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains why sparse coding is important for olfactory memory capacity, motivating the study.

fact: The study tested whether synaptic plasticity mechanisms can support stable coexistence of multiple odor representations within a fixed pool of Kenyon cells.
source_span: We compared the ability of SRDP and STDP to tune synaptic strengths such that multiple odor representations could coexist in a stable manner within a fixed pool of KCs .
selection_reasoning: This states the main research question about how multiple odor memories are stored and maintained.

fact: The study used simulated olfactory circuits trained on sequences of four different odors to evaluate how odor representations are affected by training order and plasticity rules.
source_span: We trained simulated olfactory circuits on four different odor blocks ( odors 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ) delivered in various sequences ( Figure 5 ) . Each sequence consisted of 200 1-s trials in total , each odor block contributing the same 50 trials to every sequence .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key experimental approach used to test odor representation stability.

fact: After training with multiple odors, synaptic plasticity mechanisms produced sparser Kenyon cell population responses to single odors compared to naive conditions.
source_span: After SRDP- or STDP–based training with the multiple odor sequences , the observed KC population responses to single odors were significantly more sparse than in the naive case , and comparable across different sequences
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding showing that plasticity enhances sparse odor coding after multi-odor training.

fact: STDP-based training allowed odor representations to remain highly similar to those formed by training on single odors alone, supporting stable coexistence of multiple odor memories.
source_span: Olfactory representations for single odors acquired during training with STDP on multiple sequences had firing patterns that were very similar to those observed after learning each odor alone
selection_reasoning: This key result supports the conclusion that STDP preserves odor specificity after multi-odor training.

fact: Repeated consecutive presentations of the same odor are necessary to form stable odor representations; random odor sequences were less effective.
source_span: The random sequence was less effective at producing reliable odor representation , indicating that repeated consecutive presentations of 1-s trials from the same odor are needed to form a more stable representation .
selection_reasoning: This finding highlights the importance of odor presentation patterns for stable memory formation.

fact: Training with a set of distinct odors tunes the olfactory system broadly, enabling sparse and specific responses even to odors not included in the training set.
source_span: a set of more distinct odors would tune the whole system for all possible inputs including those not used for training .
selection_reasoning: This explains the significance of odor diversity in training for generalization and tuning.

fact: Animals raised in stable and impoverished odor environments may show poor discrimination among similar odors from novel chemical groups.
source_span: This result suggests some behavioral consequences , e . g , animals growing in a very stable and poor odor environment should show poor performance in discriminating among similar odors if these odors belong to a novel ( for that animal ) chemical group .
selection_reasoning: This implication connects the findings to potential behavioral and ecological relevance.

fact: The SRDP learning rule was less successful than STDP in storing multiple odor representations, often producing mixed or unreliable odor-specific firing patterns after multi-odor training.
source_span: We found that the rate-based learning rule was less successful in storing multiple odors . Exposure to a single odor after olfactory experience with multiple odor sequences with SRDP induced firing patterns with mixed degrees of similarity to those expected and observed after training with a single odor
selection_reasoning: This contrasts the two plasticity mechanisms, highlighting STDP's superiority for stable multi-odor memory.

fact: Under SRDP, the first odor in a training sequence had a major effect on synaptic strengths and odor representation specificity.
source_span: Interestingly , the best reproductions of the expected , single odor-trained olfactory representation were observed when presenting the first odor of each training sequence , e . g . odor 1 for 1234 , odor 2 for 2143 , etc . , indicating that under SRDP the first odor in the sequence had a major effect on the synaptic strengths of KCs .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains why SRDP leads to less flexible odor memory storage.

fact: STDP-induced synaptic changes are more specific and less disruptive than those induced by SRDP, allowing persistent coexistence of multiple olfactory representations.
source_span: Thus , although the two learning rules performed similarly in the previous experiments , the results with odor sequences indicate that synaptic changes induced by STDP are more specific and less disruptive than SRDP , allowing persistent coexistence of multiple olfactory representations .
selection_reasoning: This summarizes the main conclusion about the functional advantage of STDP in olfactory memory.

fact: The study compares two synaptic plasticity models, SRDP and STDP, in their ability to support persistent coexistence of multiple olfactory representations.
source_span: specific and less disruptive than SRDP , allowing persistent coexistence of multiple olfactory representations . This result can be explained in part by the more significant alternations of synaptic weights observed with SRDP model ( see below ) .
selection_reasoning: This fact addresses the main comparison of plasticity models and their impact on olfactory representation persistence, a core scientific claim.

fact: The SRDP model induces larger and more widespread synaptic changes than the STDP model during training with odor sequences.
source_span: While training with odor sequences , changes under SRDP affected most KCs , and most synapses at each KC ... The proportion of synapses undergoing strong changes was larger than for STDP , as shown by the wider and higher kurtotic distributions of synaptic efficacies for increasing number of training trials and learned odors ... In contrast , synaptic changes under the STDP rule were subtler , and restricted to fewer KCs and fewer synapses .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a key mechanistic difference between the two plasticity models relevant to their functional outcomes.

fact: STDP is more selective than SRDP, allowing a larger number of odors to be learned and represented with a fixed number of synapses.
source_span: After SRDP learning of the first odor in a sequence ( or 50 single odor learning trials ) , the average change was comparable to the value reached with STDP after exposure to the full 4-odor sequence ( 200 trials ) ... Thus , under these conditions , STDP is more selective than SRDP . This selectivity should allow for a larger number of odors to be learned and represented with a fixed number of synapses .
selection_reasoning: This fact conveys a principal finding about the functional advantage of STDP in odor representation capacity.

fact: Oscillatory synchronization of neuronal assemblies in the antennal lobe is essential for fine sensory discrimination of similar odors in honeybees.
source_span: In honeybees , it has been demonstrated that selective disruption of oscillatory synchronization by picrotoxin injections into the AL impaired the discrimination of molecularly similar odors .
selection_reasoning: This background fact explains the biological basis motivating the study of oscillatory synchronization and its role in odor discrimination.

fact: Kenyon cells (KCs) build distinct sparse representations for similar odors based on differences in stimulus-evoked oscillatory synchronization of projection neuron (PN) assemblies.
source_span: If oscillatory synchronization of neuronal assemblies is essential for fine sensory discrimination , and MB decoding in part depends on the identity of active KCs , then KCs must be able to build distinct sparse representations for similar odors based on differences in stimulus-evoked oscillatory synchronization of the PN neural assemblies .
selection_reasoning: This fact links the biological mechanism to the computational model's focus on KC sparse coding and odor discrimination.

fact: The model treats each odor stimulus as a sequence of independent pulses corresponding to cycles of local field potential (LFP) oscillations, with each cycle providing a unique combination of synchronized projection neurons.
source_span: In our model , each odor stimulus could be considered a sequence of independent pulses or bins , each bin corresponding to one cycle of LFP oscillations . Each cycle consisted of a unique combination of active PNs that were synchronized to each other , and all together provided an input that may be sufficient to induce spiking in a postsynaptic KC .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key high-level modeling approach necessary to understand how odor stimuli are represented and processed.

fact: Coincidence detection properties of Kenyon cells prevent integration across many LFP cycles, making each cycle essentially an independent brief odor pulse.
source_span: Coincidence detection properties of the KCs in our model prevented integration across many cycles making each cycle essentially independent . In other words , each unique pattern of PN activity at each LFP cycle during 1 sec odor presentation could be treated as a separate stimulus – brief odor pulses .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains a fundamental model assumption about how odor information is temporally segmented and processed.

fact: The sparseness of Kenyon cell responses guarantees little interaction between different odor representations, supporting coexistence of multiple odor memories.
source_span: Results of simulations support a coexistence of multiple odor representations; the sparseness of KC responses guaranteed little interaction between different odor representations .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights a principal finding about how sparse coding supports multiple odor representations without interference.

fact: STDP-based synaptic tuning improves the model's ability to discriminate very similar odors by increasing Kenyon cell sensitivity to fine synchrony structure.
source_span: After synaptic tuning , all single-trial responses to odor A were closer to its own corresponding response average ... This indicates that the strong increase in KC sensitivity to the fine synchrony structure induced by plasticity effectively improves discrimination of similar odors .
selection_reasoning: This fact states a key functional outcome of the plasticity mechanism on odor discrimination performance.

fact: Odor classification error rates decrease with training under STDP, reaching near-perfect discrimination after about 100 trials.
source_span: Distinct olfactory representations were already obtained with one training block . With two training blocks ( 100 trials ) , odor classification improved further ... The average evolution of the classification error rate across all odor pairs suggests that an asymptotically small ( ∼2% ) number of classification errors was reached after 100 trials .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes a principal quantitative finding about learning efficiency and accuracy.

fact: Plasticity-based tuning of synapses in the mushroom body improves the ability to discriminate between similar odors by increasing sensitivity to oscillatory synchronization patterns.
source_span: After olfactory experience , the error rate for most odor pairs plummeted to below 5% over the whole PN distance range ( Figure 8B , mid panel ) . This suggests that the strong enhancement of classification ability for similar odors ( Figure 8B , insert ) was provided by the increased sensitivity to oscillatory synchronization patterns after STDP , as expected [12] .
selection_reasoning: This fact captures a principal finding about how synaptic plasticity enhances odor discrimination, a core scientific claim likely emphasized in the abstract.

fact: The naive olfactory circuitry before synaptic tuning is unable to exploit synchrony information effectively, resulting in high classification error rates for similar odors.
source_span: Before synaptic tuning with STDP ( Figure 8B , upper panel ) , odor pairs with a high degree of similarity in slow structure gave a wide range of error rates ( 0–45% ) , suggesting that the naive circuitry is unable to exploit synchrony information to create distinct representations .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides background on the initial limitation of the system, motivating the study of plasticity effects.

fact: Activity-dependent synaptic plasticity in the mushroom body makes population responses highly selective and odor specific, increasing trial-to-trial reliability as observed experimentally in the locust olfactory system.
source_span: Activity-dependent modulation of relevant synapses made population responses in the MB highly selective and odor specific , and increased trial-to-trial reliability , to the extent observed experimentally in the locust olfactory system [7] , [33] .
selection_reasoning: This fact states a key mechanism and principal finding linking plasticity to improved odor coding reliability, central to the study's significance.

fact: Kenyon cells in the mushroom body act as selective coincidence detectors of synchronized input from projection neurons, a property that can be optimally tuned by synaptic plasticity.
source_span: In our computational model , plasticity could optimally tune KCs to become selective coincidence detectors of preferred simultaneous PN input .
selection_reasoning: This fact describes a key mechanism underlying odor encoding and the role of plasticity, important for understanding the main scientific claim.

fact: Excessively strong initial synaptic weights from projection neurons to Kenyon cells reduce sparseness and specificity of Kenyon cell responses, impairing odor discrimination.
source_span: Indeed , with excessively strong synaptic afferents , as in the case of high initial synaptic conductances ( Figure 4 ) , a few aligned PN spikes would be sufficient to induce spiking in a KC . ... Increasing the initial synaptic coupling from AL to MB would sacrifice sparseness .
selection_reasoning: This fact highlights the importance of synaptic tuning for maintaining sparse and specific odor representations, a core concept in the study.

fact: Synchronous spiking in odor-specific populations of projection neurons controls Kenyon cell response patterns during odor stimulation, independent of prior odor experience.
source_span: However , these results do not imply that odor encoding in the mushroom body depends solely on previous odor experience; synchronous spiking in odor specific populations of PNs controls the KCs response patterns during odor stimulation .
selection_reasoning: This fact clarifies the role of innate circuit dynamics alongside plasticity, important for a balanced summary of the findings.

fact: Experience-dependent plasticity complements the intrinsic olfactory circuit structure by stabilizing the interface between antennal lobe and mushroom body, increasing reliability and selectivity of sparse responses to time-varying input.
source_span: Here we propose a form of experience-dependent plasticity as a complementary mechanism to stabilize the interface between the two circuits , increasing reliability , providing persistence and maximizing the selectivity of sparse responses to time-varying input .
selection_reasoning: This fact captures the study's main conceptual contribution about the functional role of plasticity in olfactory processing.

fact: The fraction of projection neurons connected to a single Kenyon cell, the size of the Kenyon cell integration window, and the synaptic weights between antennal lobe and mushroom body jointly control the sparseness of mushroom body responses.
source_span: Indeed , the fraction of PNs connected to a single KC , the size of the KC integration window and the absolute synaptic weights between AL and MB constitute complimentary parameters that control the sparseness of MB responses .
selection_reasoning: This fact provides a high-level description of key parameters influencing odor representation sparseness, relevant to understanding the system's function.

fact: Plasticity-controlled synaptic tuning in sensory circuits employing coincidence detection is necessary to adjust for transmission delays and accurately tune spike arrival times.
source_span: Other sensory circuits employing coincidence detection have been shown to require plasticity-controlled synaptic tuning to adjust for transmission delays along axonal pathways of variable length , accurately tuning spike arrival times [22] .
selection_reasoning: This fact situates the study's findings in a broader sensory neuroscience context, supporting the significance of plasticity mechanisms.

fact: The locust olfactory system uses a combination of intrinsic circuit structure and experience-dependent plasticity to transform neural codes and improve odor discrimination.
source_span: Here we contend that in the locust all these properties can coexist in the same olfactory circuit and that their combined action on synchronized oscillatory activity contributes to the observed functional transformation of neural codes .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the principal conclusion about how plasticity and circuit structure interact to enhance olfactory coding.

fact: Up to 50% of the total projection neuron (PN) population in the locust antennal lobe (AL) may constitute the receptor field of a single Kenyon cell (KC).
source_span: Recent results indicate that a much larger fraction of the PN population ( up to 50% of the all PNs in the locust AL ) may constitute the “receptor field” of a single KC [43] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact defines the biological connectivity relevant to the study's model and is important for understanding the neural coding in the locust olfactory system.

fact: The sparseness of Kenyon cell (KC) responses in the mushroom body (MB) is controlled by the fraction of PNs connected to each KC, the size of the KC integration window, and the synaptic weights between the antennal lobe (AL) and MB.
source_span: Indeed , the fraction of PNs connected to a single KC , the size of the KC integration window and the absolute synaptic weights between AL and MB constitute complimentary parameters that control the sparseness of MB responses .
selection_reasoning: This identifies key parameters controlling neural response sparseness, central to the study's investigation of olfactory coding.

fact: Increasing the number of PNs projecting to a single KC, increasing synaptic weights, or increasing the KC integration window all lead to a loss of sparseness in the mushroom body.
source_span: The effect of increasing the number of PNs projecting to a single KC is similar to that of increasing synaptic weights or increasing the integration window in KCs – all lead to a loss of sparseness ( see , e . g . , Figure 4 ) .
selection_reasoning: This finding links changes in connectivity and synaptic strength to functional changes in neural coding sparseness.

fact: Rhythmic inhibitory input from local horn interneurons (LHIs) resets Kenyon cells at the end of each oscillatory cycle, preventing spike integration over longer time intervals and maintaining sparseness of KC responses.
source_span: Sparseness of KCs responses also depends on the input they receive from LHIs; this rhythmic inhibitory input resets KCs at the end of each oscillatory cycle , thus preventing the integration of spikes from PNs over longer time intervals [7] , [8] .
selection_reasoning: This mechanism is important background explaining how sparseness is maintained in the olfactory system.

fact: Changes in synaptic weights between the antennal lobe and mushroom body cannot be compensated by LHI input to maintain sparseness, requiring other mechanisms involving direct synaptic weight alterations.
source_span: a change in the synaptic weights between the AL and the MB does not affect the timing of the LHI firing . Therefore , an increase in synaptic weights to the MB would lead to immediate increases in response probability of KCs , which cannot be compensated by LHI input; under these conditions , other mechanisms involving direct alternations of synaptic weights are required to control sparseness .
selection_reasoning: This highlights the need for plasticity mechanisms to regulate sparseness beyond inhibitory timing control.

fact: In the model, a given odor typically induced responses in 5-10% of all Kenyon cells, with up to 15% active depending on the odor.
source_span: Between zero ( no specific response in any KC ) and ∼15% of all KCs , depending upon the odor , remained active after training in our model; a given odor usually induced responses in 5-10% of all KCs .
selection_reasoning: This quantifies the sparseness of odor representation in the model, a principal finding relevant to olfactory coding.

fact: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) selectively strengthens synapses that participate in postsynaptic action potentials within a potentiation time window, triggering competition among inputs to a neuron.
source_span: By selectively strengthening the synapses that participate in the generation of an action potential within the potentiation time window Δt>0 ( Figure 1C ) , STDP triggers competition among the inputs to a neuron [30] .
selection_reasoning: This describes the key plasticity mechanism studied, central to the model's learning and tuning.

fact: STDP was more effective than spike-rate-dependent plasticity (SRDP) at tuning postsynaptic neurons to select synchronized input ensembles and allowed a fixed number of synapses to represent a larger number of odors.
source_span: Thus the STDP mechanism was more effective than SRDP at tuning postsynaptic neurons to select synchronized ensembles . Synaptic changes under STDP were in general less intense and more selective ( Figure 6 ) , such that a fixed number of synapses could learn to represent a larger number of odors ( Figure 5 ) .
selection_reasoning: This principal finding supports the significance of STDP in olfactory learning and discrimination.

fact: STDP conveys global stability and normalizes synaptic strength locally at each synapse without requiring a global scaling signal.
source_span: In addition , acting locally at each synapse , STDP conveyed global stability and normalized synaptic strength [30] , [31] ( Figure 4 ) , without requiring a global scaling signal [27] .
selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how STDP maintains stable synaptic function, important for understanding plasticity.

fact: STDP favors sparse representations in the mushroom body by facilitating only a few input synapses per Kenyon cell and depressing others, leading to a decrease in net synaptic weight and requiring synchronized input to trigger spikes.
source_span: Thus , for each KC , plasticity acts to facilitate only a few of the input synapses and depresses the others . The overall effect of this dynamic is a decrease in net synaptic weight ( Figure 6 ) . Synaptic depression halts only when synaptic weights become sufficiently weak that the collective action of the majority of the input spikes is required to trigger a postsynaptic KC response . Because only a fraction of the PNs is synchronized during an odor response , only a few KCs may receive enough synchronized input to spike . So , the process converges to the state that is characterized by sparse odor representation in the MB .
selection_reasoning: This explains the mechanism by which STDP produces sparse odor coding, a key conclusion.

fact: Oscillatory synchronization in the insect antennal lobe is essential for fine perceptual discrimination of odors.
source_span: Whereas the functional significance of oscillatory synchronization in neural circuits is generally uncertain , in the insect AL it has been shown to be essential for fine perceptual discrimination [12] .
selection_reasoning: This background fact motivates the study of synchronization and plasticity in olfactory coding.

fact: The model showed that STDP tuning enhanced the ability of the circuit to discriminate among similar odors by efficiently selecting synchronized projection neuron firing patterns, significantly reducing classification errors.
source_span: Our model replicated this aspect of coding , as shown by simulations with PN firing patterns with the same slow temporal structure but different cycle-specific PN synchronization . Because of the intrinsic sensitivity to such synchronous ensembles , STDP tuning efficiently enhanced the ability of the circuit to discriminate among similar odors ( simulated by similar PN response patterns ) , significantly reducing classification errors .
selection_reasoning: This is a principal finding demonstrating the functional significance of STDP in odor discrimination.

fact: STDP was consistently more effective than SRDP across a wide range of parameters in the model of the locust olfactory system.

fact: The timing difference between pre- and post-synaptic spikes determined the direction and amount of synaptic modification, with presynaptic spikes preceding postsynaptic spikes causing potentiation and the reverse causing depression.
source_span: For every PN-KC synapse , the timing difference Δt = tpost−tpre between pre- and post-synaptic spiking events determined the direction and amount of synaptic modification . Thus , a presynaptic spike preceding a postsynaptic spike in an interval covered by the critical timing window produced a conductance increase . A presynaptic spike occurring after the postsynaptic spike produced a conductance decrease .
selection_reasoning: This fact explains the spike-timing-dependent plasticity rule implemented, a central mechanism for synaptic changes.

fact: A special metric based on convolving spikes with a Gaussian kernel and computing distances between PN spike trains was used to measure the divergence between two odor representations in PN space.
source_span: A special metric was defined to measure the distance ( divergence ) between two such odor representations . First , for every PN a time series was created by convolving every spike with a Gaussian Kernel ( σ = 5 ms , μ = 2σ , full-width-half-maximum = 11 . 8 ms ) . The 100 presynaptic spike trains representing the first odor were then compared pairwise with the 100 presynaptic spike trains representing the second odor using an L1-metric ( Manhattan distance ) ; this spawned a 100-D vector with the L1-distances . The Euclidean norm of this vector provided the distance measure between two odor representations in PN space .
selection_reasoning: This fact summarizes the key method used to quantify differences between odor representations, important for interpreting the results.

fact: Nidd/SJL carriers in the N2 progeny exhibited early onset hyperglycaemia and stopped gaining weight between weeks 10 and 12, unlike carriers of the NZO allele who became hyperglycaemic to a lesser degree and continued gaining weight.
source_span: Characterization of the N2 progeny indicated that Nidd/SJL carriers exhibited early onsetting hyperglycaemia with blood glucose levels approximately 150 mg/dl higher than in carriers of the NZO allele ( Figure 1B ) , and stopped gaining weight in week 10–12 ( Figure 1C ) . Similar results were obtained in the F2 intercross which showed an additive effect of Nidd/SJL ( Figure S1 ) . It should be noted that carriers of the NZO allele of Nidd/SJL also became hyperglycaemic , although to a much lesser degree than carriers of the SJL allele ( Figure 1B ) , presumably due to other diabetogenic alleles from NZO chromosomes 1 and 15 [10] , [11; Vogel et al . , unpublished] . These mice , however , continued to gain weight ( Figure 1C ) , indicating that the weight development could be used as an additional criterion to determine the presence or absence of the causal gene in Nidd/SJL .

Thus , the critical interval of chromosome 4 comprising the diabetogenic allele was defined by the markers D4Mit76 and D4Mit12 ( Figure 2A ) .

fact: Model reduction by removing intermediate components preserves stable states and complex attractors but may lose some trajectories and introduce additional cyclical attractors.
source_span: A solution consists in reducing the model by removing ( intermediate ) components . We have recently proposed an algorithm to automatically compute the logical rules for a user-defined reduced model [22] . Starting with a detailed model , the computation of a reduced model is performed by iteratively removing regulatory components . Auto-regulated components are not entitled for removal , thereby avoiding the loss of dynamical properties associated with regulatory circuits ( see below ) . Removing a regulatory component G implies a revised wiring where all targets of G are directly regulated by the regulators of G . The logical rules of the targets of G are modified accordingly to conserve the ( indirect ) effects of its regulators . This reduction method ensures the preservation of a number of dynamical properties of the original model . In particular , stable states and more complex attractors are conserved . However , additional cyclical attractors may arise from the isolation of transient cycles of the original system . An attractor which is reachable in the reduced model is also reachable in the full model , but the reverse is not always true , as the reduction may lead to the loss of some trajectories ( see [22] for further details ) .

fact: β3K mutants are widely used to study noncatalytic functions of eukaryotic protein kinases, but conformational differences among these mutants may affect these noncanonical functions.
source_span: β3K mutants are widely utilized to decipher these noncanonical functions [45] . Our findings show that these mutations should be designed with caution , as the conformational differences between the different mutants may interfere with these noncanonical functions as well .
selection_reasoning: This finding is important for experimental design and interpretation in kinase biology.

fact: Molecular dynamics simulations revealed that mutations at β3K cause distinct conformational changes in the kinase N-lobe that affect catalytic activity.

selection_reasoning: This mechanistic insight explains how β3K mutations alter kinase structure and function.
